Each deck keys its own question by repeating the slide with the correct option bolded, but **none carries a written rationale** - the explanations below are reasoned from [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]].
stem: True or false: GIP levels are decreased in those with type 2 diabetes. (originally one slide carrying five true/false statements; split into Q71-75, one per statement)
answer:
The correct answer is B, false. This is the one most people get backwards. In T2DM GIP levels are normal or raised - what is lost is the beta cell's insulin response to GIP, not the hormone itself. It is GLP-1 whose levels fall.

That split is the whole reason GLP-1RAs work and a GIP analogue alone historically did not: you can replace the hormone that is missing, but not rescue a receptor response that has been lost.

stem: True or false: renal reabsorption of glucose is increased in those with type 2 diabetes.
answer:
The correct answer is A, true. T2DM upregulates SGLT2 in the proximal convoluted tubule, which raises the renal threshold for glucose. The kidney reclaims more glucose exactly when the body least needs it - a maladaptive response that defends the hyperglycemia.

This is the defect SGLT2 inhibitors were designed against, and it is why they lower glucose independently of beta-cell function.

Each deck keys its own question by repeating the slide with the correct option bolded, but **none carries a written rationale** - the explanations below are reasoned from [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]].
stem: True or false: glucose production by the liver is increased in those with type 2 diabetes.
answer:
The correct answer is A, true. Hepatic gluconeogenesis is increased, driven by insulin resistance in the liver and by the raised free fatty acid flux from insulin-resistant adipocytes. It is the main reason for fasting hyperglycemia, since overnight glucose comes from the liver rather than from a meal.

This is metformin's principal target - it suppresses hepatic glucose output via AMPK, which is why it works best on the fasting number.

stem: True or false: elevated GLP-1 levels lead to increased satiety in those with type 2 diabetes.
answer:
The correct answer is B, false. The trap is that the physiology in the statement is right while the premise is wrong. Incretins genuinely do promote satiety, acting on the hypothalamus and the mesolimbic reward system - that is why semaglutide causes weight loss.

But GLP-1 levels are decreased in T2DM, not elevated. There is no endogenous excess doing this work; the satiety effect only appears once you supply a pharmacological GLP-1 receptor agonist.

stem: True or false: beta cell function is not impaired in those with prediabetes.
answer:
The correct answer is B, false. By the time a patient is merely in the prediabetes range, ⭐ about 80% of beta-cell function has already been lost.

This is the single most clinically loaded fact in the deck. Prediabetes sounds like a warning shot, but most of the secretory damage is already done and not recoverable - which is the argument for intervening at prediabetes rather than waiting for the diagnostic threshold to be crossed.

stem: Which of the following insulins presents the slowest onset of action?
answer: The correct answer is D. The onset of action of the human regular insulin varies between 30 to 60 minutes. The onset of action of the analogs is much faster, starting at 5 minutes for some of them.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (3 questions).
stem: What are some of the advantages of using rapid-acting analogues compared to the regular insulin? Select all that apply.

options.html: Analogues provide better postprandial control of glucose
Analogues have faster onset of action
Analogues are associated with lower risk of hypoglycemia
Analogues are more efficacious than regular insulin
Analogues can be taken every other day
Analogues present longer duration of action

answer: The correct answers are A, B, and C. In terms of efficacy, meaning reduction in HbA1C levels, analogues as as efficacious as the human regular insulin. Nonetheless, analogues provide more flexibility to patients and present a better safety profile. Like the human regular insulin, analogues must be taken at least twice a day. The prandial insulins only provide coverage for a few hours and must be injected multiple times a day. Insulin lispro and the human regular insulin can be taken intravenously. When regular insulin is administered IV, it dissociates immediately in the bloodstream. The duration of action of analogues is similar to the human regular insulin. However, given the unpredictability of the rate of absorption of regular insulin, its duration of action may be longer compared to the rapid-acting analogues.

lecture: Concept Checks - Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnosis & Epidemiology
lectureMeta: Source: the lecture slide deck (`Hashmi T2DMellitus`), 1 question, posed in-deck as an "Alertness Check". **The Elentra module for this lecture carries no knowledge checks**, so this is the only question it has. **Keyed** - the deck marks each option in place with a **✓ or ✗ glyph**, and option 2 carries the ✓. The deck's two patient cases live in [[New Questions - Endocrinology]].
stem: Which of the following is correct? (originally a numbered "Alertness Check" with a ✓/✗ against each statement; rewritten as a single-best-answer MCQ)

options.html: T2DM is diagnosed by the blood glucose level associated with risk for developing cardiovascular disease (e.g. MI)
T2DM is associated with increased risk for stroke, MI and forefoot amputation
metabolic syndrome is most common in middle-aged people with type 1 diabetes for > 30 years
T2DM is diagnosed by the blood glucose level associated with risk for foot numbness and tingling

answer:
The correct answer is B. The deck marks option 2 with a ✓ and the other three with a ✗.

⭐ The whole question turns on one distinction: what the diagnostic threshold was set by, versus what the disease is associated with.

  • B is true. T2DM genuinely does carry increased risk of stroke, MI and forefoot amputation - these are its macrovascular complications.
  • ⭐ A is the classic distractor. The cut-points are not based on cardiovascular risk. They mark the glycemic level at which the risk of diabetic retinopathy rises sharply - a microvascular endpoint. Being associated with MI is not the same as being defined by it.
  • D is the same error wearing different clothes, substituting neuropathy (foot numbness and tingling) for cardiovascular disease. Retinopathy is the specific endpoint, not neuropathy and not nephropathy.
  • C inverts the type. metabolic syndrome clusters with insulin resistance, so it belongs to T2DM, not T1DM. And in a patient who already has T2DM, metabolic syndrome ⭐ raises cardiovascular risk further still, above other people with T2DM who do not have it.

Why it matters: the threshold is the same for T1DM and T2DM, and it is retinopathy that set it. That is the fact two of these four options are built to test.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (9 questions).
stem: Which of the following pharmacological strategies can be used to lower blood glucose levels? Select all that apply.

options.html: Increase secretion of insulin by the pancreatic beta cells
Increase the secretion of glucagon by the pancreatic alpha cells
Increase the sensitivity of target tissues to insulin

answer: The correct answers are A, B, and D. Glucagon opposes the actions of insulin, stimulating hepatic production of glucose, increasing plasma glucose levels. Increasing the secretion of this hormone is not a good strategy to decrease hyperglycaemia. Similarly, drugs that stimulate hepatic production of new molecules of glucose (gluconeogenesis) will worsen hyperglycaemia. The increased digestion of carbohydrates can potentially increase the amount of monosaccharides available for absorption, worsening hyperglycaemia.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (9 questions).
stem: Which of the following pharmacological strategies will be directly affected by the functionality of the pancreatic beta cells?

options.html: Use of drugs to decrease glucose absorption
Use of drugs to increase glucose excretion
Use of drugs to increase insulin-sensitivity of target cells
Use of drugs to increase insulin secretion
Use of drugs to decrease the hepatic production of glucose

answer: The correct answer is D. Overall, the efficacy of all antihyperglycemic drugs is affected by the ability of the pancreatic cells to produce insulin - some directly, others indirectly. Without an adequate level of insulin (endogenous or exogenous), these drugs won't be able to fully control the blood glucose level. Drugs that stimulate the secretion of insulin can only work if the beta cells are able to produce and secrete this hormone; thus their efficacy is directly affected by beta cell functionality. Drugs that improve insulin sensitivity are also affected by beta cell functionality, but in an indirect manner.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (9 questions).
stem: How are metformin and pioglitazone similar?

options.html: Both drugs present comparable efficacy in lowering A1C
Both drugs present cardiovascular protective effects
Both drugs are associated with weight gain
Both drugs are metabolized by the liver into active and inactive metabolites
Both drugs are associated with increased risk of bone fracture

answer: The correct answer is A. Metformin presents cardiovascular protective effects, is associated with weight loss, is excreted unchanged by the kidney, and is not associated with increased risk of bone fracture. Pioglitazone is associated with an increased risk of heart failure, weight gain, and increased risk of bone fracture; this drug is extensively metabolized by the liver. They present comparable efficacy in lowering A1C.

stem: Which of the following is a serious adverse effect associated with the use of metformin? (originally a fill-in-the-blank; rewritten as MCQ)
answer: The correct answer is A. lactic acidosis. The accumulation of metformin can lead to a build up of lactate, which can result in lactic acidosis.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (9 questions).
stem: A 45-year old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your office with poorly controlled plasma glucose levels. He was initially prescribed metformin but due to GI intolerance, he was switched to gliclazide six months ago. Which of the following may be related to the decreased efficacy of gliclazide in reducing hyperglycemia in this patient? Select all that apply.

options.html: Decreased ability of the adipose cells to reduce free fatty acids
Decreased ability of the pancreatic beta cells to secrete insulin

answer: The correct answers are B and D. Gliclazide, a sulfonylurea, increases the secretion of insulin by acting on the ATP-sensitive potassium channels. It has been observed that over time, patients develop tolerance to the SU drugs. This may be explained by desensitization of the receptors and loss of functionality by the pancreatic beta cells. The decreased ability of the adipose cells to reduce circulating fatty acids would affect the efficacy of the TZDs more than the SUs - that being said, accumulation of fat in the body could contribute to poor control of blood glucose (energy balance). Renal dysfunction would affect the elimination of gliclazide but not its ability to reduce glycemia.

stem: A 43-year-old woman with Type-2 diabetes has been taking insulin with meals as well as metformin. Her blood glucose remains poorly controlled. Her doctor prescribes an additional drug, which is an analog of an endogenous peptide that inhibits glucagon secretion. What is the most likely medication this patient is taking?
answer: The correct answer is E. Pioglitazone is a TZD that activates PPAR. Repaglinide is a meglitinide that inhibits the ATP-sensitive potassium channel in the beta cells. Sitagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor that targets the DPP-4 enzyme. Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea that also inhibits the ATP-sensitive potassium channel. Liraglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that is an analog of the endogenous GLP-1 peptide and inhibits the secretion of glucagon.

stem: Which of the following are side effects associated with the use of canagliflozin? Select all that apply.
answer:
The correct answers are A, B, and E. For this SGLT2 inhibitor:

  • Genitourinary infections = increased delivery of glucose to the genitourinary tract
  • Orthostatic hypotension = hypovolemia
  • Reduction in bone mineral density = potential increase in calcium & phosphate excretion and reduction in the levels of vitamin D

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (9 questions).
stem: Which of the following antihyperglycemic drugs have a greater effect on reducing postprandial glucose than fasting glucose level? Select all that apply.
answer: The correct answers are A, D, and F. The alpha-glucosidase inhibitors decrease the peak of postprandial glucose (PPG) by delaying the absorption of carbohydrates in the GI tract. Meglitinides promote insulin secretion; their fast onset and short duration of action make this class suitable for the control of postprandial glucose. DPP-4 inhibitors promote insulin secretion in a nutrient-dependent manner, with great effect on PPG. The other classes listed here also help to decrease PPG and fasting glucose levels; however, given their mechanism of action and PK properties, their effects on PPG aren't as pronounced as for the 3 classes listed above.

stem: Sophie has been taking semaglutide at the maximally tolerated dose for 12 weeks and has lost only 2% of their initial body weight. What is your most appropriate next step?

options.html: Encourage increased activity to achieve further weight loss.
Consider switching to tirzepatide because the treatment goal has not been achieved.
Refer immediately for bariatric surgery regardless of eligibility.

answer: The correct answer is C. The goal of pharmacotherapy is to achieve at least 5% weight loss after 12 weeks at the maximally tolerated dose. If this is not achieved, it is important to consider changing medications. While increased activity is important, the 5% weight loss target with pharmacotherapy is an important threshold for considering efficacy, as some patients may not achieve weight loss with a particular agent.

stem: Raul presents two months after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with persistent nausea, poor oral intake, and confusion. His vitals reveal a BP of 90/56 mmHg, HR 120 bpm. You have started him on Ringer's lactate IV fluids. What else should be done immediately?

options.html: Nothing else needs to be done at this time.

answer: The correct answer is B. Thiamine deficiency can occur within 1-3 months after surgery, particularly with poor oral intake and nausea. Recognizing thiamine deficiency is critical as there are serious neurologic sequelae - importantly, thiamine should always be given immediately before any glucose to prevent onset of Wernicke's encephalopathy.

lecture: Concept Checks - Prevention of Chronic Complications of Diabetes
lectureMeta: Source: the lecture slide deck (`PreventionofDMComplications Hashmi 2024`), 2 questions, posed in-deck as "POP QUIZ". **The Elentra module for this lecture carries no knowledge checks**, so these are the only questions it has. The deck's third pop quiz is a patient case and lives in [[New Questions - Endocrinology]].
stem: According to the 1993 DCCT results: after 6.5 years of tight blood-glucose control vs less tight control, patients in the tight control arm had decreased risk of which of the following? (originally a check-all-that-apply poll over five items; rewritten as an MCQ over complete sets, so the whole grouping still has to be known)

options.html: Worsening retinopathy, de novo retinopathy and renal impairment only
Worsening retinopathy and de novo retinopathy only
Worsening retinopathy, de novo retinopathy, renal impairment, heart attack and stroke

answer:
The correct answer is A. The deck highlights 1, 4 and 5 in green. DCCT (1993) randomised 1441 T1DM patients to conventional vs intensive insulin for 6.5 years, and intensive control moved microvascular outcomes only:

OutcomeEffect
De novo retinopathy (primary prevention)⭐ ↓ 76%
Worsening retinopathy already present (secondary prevention)↓ 54%
Clinical neuropathy↓ 60%
Microalbuminuria / albuminuria (renal impairment)↓ 39% / ↓ 54%
⚠ hypoglycemia↑ 2-3x

⭐ What is deliberately absent from that list is MI and stroke. Within the trial period, intensive glycemic control did not move macrovascular outcomes, which is what rules out C and D. B is the near-miss: it drops renal impairment, which the trial did reduce.

Principle: ⭐ glycemic control buys microvascular protection; blood pressure control is what buys macrovascular protection.

The caveat worth carrying: the CV benefit did eventually appear, but only in the legacy-effect observational follow-up more than 10 years later (adverse CV outcomes ↓ 42%), not in the 6.5-year trial this question asks about.

lecture: Concept Checks - Prevention of Chronic Complications of Diabetes
lectureMeta: Source: the lecture slide deck (`PreventionofDMComplications Hashmi 2024`), 2 questions, posed in-deck as "POP QUIZ". **The Elentra module for this lecture carries no knowledge checks**, so these are the only questions it has. The deck's third pop quiz is a patient case and lives in [[New Questions - Endocrinology]].
stem: According to the main findings of the initial UKPDS study in people with type 2 diabetes, which of the following statements are true? (originally a check-all-that-apply poll over three statements; rewritten as an MCQ over complete sets)
answer:
The correct answer is A. The deck highlights 2 and 3 in green. UKPDS (1998)07019-6/abstract) followed 3867 newly-diagnosed T2DM patients for 10 years.

  • Statement 3 is true - intensive glucose control gave ⭐ ↓ 25% microvascular complications, and the glucose-to-risk relationship is linear, so any improvement helps.
  • Statement 2 is true - the blood pressure arm is what delivered the broad benefit: BP under 144/82 reduced strokes, diabetes-related death, heart failure, microvascular complications and vision loss. In T2DM it is the BP arm, not the glucose arm, that bought the macrovascular gain.
  • ⭐ Statement 1 is false, and it is the one the question is built around. Intensive glucose control had no significant effect on macrovascular disease or all-cause mortality in the initial trial. The all-cause mortality reduction (↓ 33% in DCCT, diabetes-related death ↓ 17% in UKPDS) belongs to the legacy-effect follow-up published more than a decade later - and the stem says "the initial UKPDS study", which is precisely what excludes it.

Principle: be strict about which intensive arm and which publication a mortality claim comes from.

stem:
You are seeing a 25-year-old woman with GDM in your Endocrine Pregnancy Clinic. She is managing her GDM with metformin. She is also following the GDM diet with 45 g meals 3x/day and 20g snacks 3x/day. In the last few days, she feels that her sugars are increasing despite walking 10 min after each meal. What would you recommend based on her on log:

DateacB1h pcB1h pcL1h pcS
Aug 55.37.79.08.8
Aug 65.47.88.88.8
Aug 75.48.27.87.9
Aug 85.57.78.97.8
Aug 95.88.08.87.7

options.html: Stop metformin as her blood sugars are well below target.
Do nothing as her sugars are well controlled.
Recommend she decreases her carbohydrate intake by 50% and increase the intensity of her exercise.
Recommend adding insulin as all her blood glucose readings are well above target..

answer:
The correct answer is D. Read the log against the pregnancy targets - fasting < 5.3 and 1 hour post-meal < 7.8 mmol/L - and every column fails:

  • acB runs 5.3 → 5.8, at or above the fasting target every day, and trending upward.
  • 1h pcB, pcL and pcS run 7.7 → 9.0, at or above the post-meal target on almost every reading.

She is already on metformin, already on the GDM diet, and already walking after meals, so the non-pharmacological levers are spent - A and B misread a failing log as a good one, and C asks more of the two things that have not worked. Insulin is the next step, and it is the only agent that can be titrated to bring both fasting and post-prandial numbers to target in pregnancy.

lecture: Concept Checks - Can We Prevent Type 2 Diabetes?
lectureMeta: Source: the lecture slide deck (`Diabetes Prevention Slides 2021`), 5 questions, spread across the deck's three sub-decks (lifestyle, medications, surgery). **The Elentra module for this lecture carries no knowledge checks**, so these are the only questions it has. The deck keys each one by repeating the slide with the correct option bolded; rationales below are reasoned from [[12 - Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes]].
stem: What percent weight loss was found to be effective in reducing risk of developing diabetes in randomized controlled trials?
answer:
The correct answer is D. The Diabetes Prevention Program set a 7% weight loss target, but the weight loss the lifestyle arm actually achieved was only 5% - and that was enough to produce the 58% reduction in progression to diabetes.

⭐ The teaching point is that the target is aspirational while the benefit is real well below it. A patient who loses 5% has already bought most of the risk reduction, which is a far more useful thing to tell them than a number they will not hit. A and C overstate what the evidence required; B is below the level at which benefit was demonstrated.

lecture: Concept Checks - Can We Prevent Type 2 Diabetes?
lectureMeta: Source: the lecture slide deck (`Diabetes Prevention Slides 2021`), 5 questions, spread across the deck's three sub-decks (lifestyle, medications, surgery). **The Elentra module for this lecture carries no knowledge checks**, so these are the only questions it has. The deck keys each one by repeating the slide with the correct option bolded; rationales below are reasoned from [[12 - Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes]].
stem: In the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), lifestyle interventions for diabetes prevention were more effective than the effect of metformin.
answer:
The correct answer is A, true. In the DPP's three arms, measured against placebo:

Arm↓ cumulative incidence of diabetes
⭐ Lifestyle58%
metformin31%

⭐ 58% vs 31% is the single most testable number in this lecture - lifestyle is roughly twice as effective as metformin. The lifestyle intervention itself was fat- and calorie-restricted diet plus 150 minutes of aerobic activity per week.

The nuance worth holding alongside it: metformin's 31% is not uniform. It performs closest to lifestyle in the younger (< 60 years), the obese (BMI > 35), and women with previous GDM.

lecture: Concept Checks - Can We Prevent Type 2 Diabetes?
lectureMeta: Source: the lecture slide deck (`Diabetes Prevention Slides 2021`), 5 questions, spread across the deck's three sub-decks (lifestyle, medications, surgery). **The Elentra module for this lecture carries no knowledge checks**, so these are the only questions it has. The deck keys each one by repeating the slide with the correct option bolded; rationales below are reasoned from [[12 - Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes]].
stem: Which medication is approved for diabetes prevention in Canada?
answer:
The correct answer is E. ⭐ No medication is approved in Canada for the prevention of diabetes. Several have real evidence behind them - metformin 31%, TZDs ~70%, acarbose ~25-36%, orlistat ~37%, and the GLP-1RAs - but evidence is not the same thing as an indication, and none carries the approval.

What blocks approval is the deck's own closing point: side effects, uncertain long-term safety, and lack of affordability. TZDs make the case neatly - the largest drug effect of any agent (~70%) and still unusable at scale because of peripheral edema, heart failure, osteoporosis and fractures.

This is the conclusion of the whole lecture, so expect it to be examined: everything in the medication section is evidence, not indication.

lecture: Concept Checks - Can We Prevent Type 2 Diabetes?
lectureMeta: Source: the lecture slide deck (`Diabetes Prevention Slides 2021`), 5 questions, spread across the deck's three sub-decks (lifestyle, medications, surgery). **The Elentra module for this lecture carries no knowledge checks**, so these are the only questions it has. The deck keys each one by repeating the slide with the correct option bolded; rationales below are reasoned from [[12 - Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes]].
stem: Which medication does not have evidence for diabetes prevention?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea - an insulin secretagogue that flogs the beta cell into releasing more insulin. It has no evidence for preventing diabetes, and mechanistically you would not expect any: it does nothing about insulin resistance, and driving an already-failing beta cell harder is not a plausible way to preserve it.

The other three all have prevention data behind them - metformin 31% (DPP), pioglitazone as a TZD at ⭐ ~70%, and semaglutide among the GLP-1RAs.

Principle: the agents with prevention evidence are the ones that ⭐ improve insulin sensitivity or produce weight loss. Secretagogues do neither.

lecture: Concept Checks - Can We Prevent Type 2 Diabetes?
lectureMeta: Source: the lecture slide deck (`Diabetes Prevention Slides 2021`), 5 questions, spread across the deck's three sub-decks (lifestyle, medications, surgery). **The Elentra module for this lecture carries no knowledge checks**, so these are the only questions it has. The deck keys each one by repeating the slide with the correct option bolded; rationales below are reasoned from [[12 - Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes]].
stem: Which are the two most commonly performed surgeries for weight loss in Canada?

options.html: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and laparoscopic banding
Duodenal switch and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
Sleeve gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass

answer:
The correct answer is D. ⭐ The two are the Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and the sleeve gastrectomy, both done laparoscopically, both achieving 30-35% weight loss. They differ in mechanism: ⭐ Roux-en-Y is restrictive AND malabsorptive, the sleeve is restrictive only.

The distractors are both retired procedures. Laparoscopic banding is no longer performed, which kills A and B; the duodenal switch is not among the common two, which kills C.

On prevention specifically: bariatric surgery is ⭐ the most effective approach of any in this lecture, and still ⚠ not first line for prevention - cost, procedural risk and invasiveness rule it out for that purpose. Effectiveness and appropriateness are different questions, which is exactly the discrimination the lecture wants.

lecture: Concept Checks - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs (2026)
lectureMeta: Source: in-deck "CONCEPT CHECK" slides from the same lecture deck (Fabiana Crowley), 5 questions. Answers are the ones **highlighted in OneNote** on `Pharmacology of glucose lowering drugs_edited` (`B1 Endo` > `Asynch W1`).
stem: Which of the following patients on metformin is at greatest risk of developing lactic acidosis?

options.html: A 45-year-old with T2DM and an eGFR of 75 mL/min, stable on metformin 1000 mg BID for two years
A 68-year-old with T2DM and stable CKD (eGFR 50 mL/min), no recent changes in health status
A 72-year-old with T2DM and heart failure, admitted with a two-day history of vomiting and reduced oral intake
A 55-year-old with newly diagnosed T2DM, started on metformin 500 mg once daily one week ago, mild nausea reported

answer:
The correct answer is C, highlighted on the slide. Metformin is eliminated unchanged by the kidney, so risk comes from acute accumulation. Vomiting and reduced oral intake → volume depletion → acute drop in renal clearance, and the heart failure adds tissue hypoperfusion, which independently raises lactate.

The red margin note gives the number to watch: eGFR < 40. B is a stable, chronic eGFR of 50 with no acute change. D is mild GI upset, the expected early side effect. A is stable and well within range.

Principle: the danger is the acute illness on top of metformin, not the baseline eGFR.

lecture: Concept Checks - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs (2026)
lectureMeta: Source: in-deck "CONCEPT CHECK" slides from the same lecture deck (Fabiana Crowley), 5 questions. Answers are the ones **highlighted in OneNote** on `Pharmacology of glucose lowering drugs_edited` (`B1 Endo` > `Asynch W1`).
stem: For which of the following patients would pioglitazone be contraindicated?
answer:
The correct answers are B and E - both are highlighted on the slide.

  • E, heart failure: TZDs cause fluid retention via ↑ Na⁺ channel expression in the kidney → fluid retention worsens CHF.
  • B, hepatic cirrhosis: TZDs are extensively metabolized by the liver, so impaired liver function is a contraindication.

The two distractors are the teaching point:

  • C, osteopenia - caution, but not a contraindication. TZDs ↑ fracture risk, so it is osteoporosis that contraindicates them.
  • D, well-controlled hypertension - monitor. Fluid retention → ↑ blood volume → ↑ blood pressure.
  • A, CKD is not a contraindication; TZDs are not renally cleared (contrast metformin, Q36).

lecture: Concept Checks - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs (2026)
lectureMeta: Source: in-deck "CONCEPT CHECK" slides from the same lecture deck (Fabiana Crowley), 5 questions. Answers are the ones **highlighted in OneNote** on `Pharmacology of glucose lowering drugs_edited` (`B1 Endo` > `Asynch W1`).
stem: In this classic experiment, oral and IV glucose were administered to produce matched blood glucose levels over time. What is the main conclusion that can be drawn from the graph?

options.html: IV glucose is a stronger stimulus for insulin secretion than oral glucose, since it reaches the pancreas more directly
Oral and IV glucose produce a similar insulin response, since blood glucose is the main driver of insulin secretion
Oral glucose produces a substantially greater insulin response than IV glucose at matched blood glucose levels
The difference in insulin response reflects faster glucose absorption with the oral route compared to the IV route

answer:
The correct answer is C, highlighted on the slide. This is the definition of the incretin effect. The shaded area between the two curves is the incretin effect. Because blood glucose was matched between the two arms, the extra insulin released after oral glucose cannot be explained by glucose itself - it comes from gut-derived incretins (GLP-1 and GIP) released in response to nutrients passing through the GI tract.

D is wrong because the design controls for absorption rate by matching glucose curves.

Why it matters: this experiment is the entire rationale for the incretin drug classes.

lecture: Concept Checks - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs (2026)
lectureMeta: Source: in-deck "CONCEPT CHECK" slides from the same lecture deck (Fabiana Crowley), 5 questions. Answers are the ones **highlighted in OneNote** on `Pharmacology of glucose lowering drugs_edited` (`B1 Endo` > `Asynch W1`).
stem: Which of the following adverse effects is associated with the use of α-glucosidase inhibitors?
answer:
The correct answer is A, highlighted on the slide and annotated "GI effects". The margin note gives the chain:

↑ glucose downstream in the large intestine → fermentation → flatulence

AGIs block cleavage of complex carbohydrates at the intestinal brush border, so undigested carbohydrate reaches the colon and is fermented by bacteria.

B is wrong - AGIs carry no hypoglycemia risk as monotherapy (they don't alter insulin release). C is wrong - they are weight neutral. D is the wrong direction for the listed GI profile.

lecture: Concept Checks - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs (2026)
lectureMeta: Source: in-deck "CONCEPT CHECK" slides from the same lecture deck (Fabiana Crowley), 5 questions. Answers are the ones **highlighted in OneNote** on `Pharmacology of glucose lowering drugs_edited` (`B1 Endo` > `Asynch W1`).
stem: Which of the following adverse effects are associated with the use of SGLT2 inhibitors? Select all that apply.
answer:
The correct answers are B, C and D, all three highlighted on the slide. They follow directly from the mechanism - blocking the Na⁺/glucose co-transporter in the proximal convoluted tubule leaves glucose in the urine:

  • glucose in the urinary tract → genital and urinary infections
  • osmotic diuresis → polyuria → ECF volume contraction

A is wrong - SGLT2 inhibitors cause weight loss, because glucose (and therefore calories) is excreted.

The module's own version of this question is Q34 above, where the graded key was A, B, E for a different option set. See also 13 - Antihyperglycemic Drug Choices for T2DM (CBL) Case 4, where this mechanism produced prerenal AKI and shock.

lectureMeta: Source: "UME P2 Endocrine Pharmacology (Pharmacology of T2DM)" Microsoft Forms quiz, 9 questions (Q1-7 and Q9 multiple choice, Q8 short answer). All content maps to [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]].
stem: Which of the following combinations is most likely to cause hypotension?
answer:
D. SGLT2 inhibitors cause osmotic diuresis - glucose is dumped into the tubule and drags Na⁺ and water with it - producing ECF volume contraction. Adding a loop diuretic gives two drugs emptying the same compartment, so the volume loss is additive and hypotension follows. The lecture states this directly: "be careful when prescribing other diuretics."

C is the tempting distractor - valsartan does lower blood pressure - but an ARB drops BP by vasodilation, not by further depleting volume, and is a routine, deliberate co-prescription in T2DM with diabetic nephropathy. B is the wrong direction: pioglitazone causes fluid retention, which offsets the diuresis. A is wrong because insulin does not lower blood pressure.

Principle: the risk is mechanism stacking, not simply "two BP-lowering drugs".

lectureMeta: Source: "UME P2 Endocrine Pharmacology (Pharmacology of T2DM)" Microsoft Forms quiz, 9 questions (Q1-7 and Q9 multiple choice, Q8 short answer). All content maps to [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]].
stem: Which class of antihyperglycemics should be avoided in a patient making use of a GLP1-RA for the treatment of T2DM?
answer:
A. Both act on the same incretin pathway. A GLP-1 RA already delivers ~10x normal GLP-1 activity with a molecule that DPP-4 does not degrade; a DPP-4 inhibitor only prolongs endogenous GLP-1 to ~2-3x. Adding it to a receptor agonist buys no additional glycemic benefit while adding cost and adverse-effect risk.

The other four all act by different mechanisms (sensitizers, secretagogues, renal glucose excretion) and are legitimate add-ons.

Principle: the contraindication here is pharmacodynamic redundancy, not toxicity.

lectureMeta: Source: "UME P2 Endocrine Pharmacology (Pharmacology of T2DM)" Microsoft Forms quiz, 9 questions (Q1-7 and Q9 multiple choice, Q8 short answer). All content maps to [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]].
stem: Which of the following drug classes is less affected by the ability of the pancreatic beta cells to secrete insulin?
answer:
C. SGLT2 inhibitors work in the kidney, blocking the Na⁺/glucose co-transporter in the proximal convoluted tubule. The lecture calls this action insulin-independent and relatively independent of beta cell function - glucose leaves in the urine whether or not the pancreas can respond. Their efficacy depends on renal function, not beta cell reserve.

A and B are insulin secretagogues - they close the K⁺/ATP channel on a functioning beta cell, so they fail in advanced disease. D is the subtle distractor: GLP-1 analogs still act on the beta cell to release insulin, just in a glucose-dependent way, so they too need beta cell function.

Why it matters: this is the reason SGLT2 inhibitors keep working late in T2DM when secretagogues have failed.

lectureMeta: Source: "UME P2 Endocrine Pharmacology (Pharmacology of T2DM)" Microsoft Forms quiz, 9 questions (Q1-7 and Q9 multiple choice, Q8 short answer). All content maps to [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]].
stem: Which of the following drug classes lowers glycemia by delaying the reabsorption of glucose in the GI tract?
answer:
B. AGIs (acarbose) competitively inhibit the alpha-glucosidase enzymes on the intestinal brush border, so complex carbohydrates are broken down more slowly. The effect is to blunt the post-prandial glucose peak and spread absorption out over time, giving existing insulin reserves time to cope.

C is the trap - SGLT2 inhibitors also block a glucose transporter, but in the kidney, and they block reabsorption of glucose already filtered, not GI uptake.

Note the wording: the quiz says "reabsorption in the GI tract"; the actual mechanism is delayed digestion and absorption.

lectureMeta: Source: "UME P2 Endocrine Pharmacology (Pharmacology of T2DM)" Microsoft Forms quiz, 9 questions (Q1-7 and Q9 multiple choice, Q8 short answer). All content maps to [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]].
stem: Which of the following antihyperglycemics would be the best option for a patient with a compelling need to minimize or lose weight?
answer:
C. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 RA and the only option that causes weight loss rather than merely avoiding gain - via ↓ gastric emptying and ↑ satiety.

Sorted by weight effect, from the lecture's comparison table:

  • loss - GLP-1RAs (semaglutide), SGLT2 inhibitors
  • neutral - DPP-4 inhibitors (alogliptin), acarbose, metformin
  • gain - TZDs (rosiglitazone), SUs (glyburide), meglitinides

Read the stem carefully: "minimize or lose" asks for the strongest option, so weight-neutral D and E lose to weight-losing C.

lectureMeta: Source: "UME P2 Endocrine Pharmacology (Pharmacology of T2DM)" Microsoft Forms quiz, 9 questions (Q1-7 and Q9 multiple choice, Q8 short answer). All content maps to [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]].
stem: Which of the following drug classes presents the highest risk of hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy?
answer:
E. SUs close the K⁺/ATP channel on the beta cell and drive insulin release regardless of the blood glucose level - the release is not glucose-dependent, so it continues into a normal or low glucose. This is why they should not be prescribed to the elderly, people who live alone, or people who drive for a living.

C is the near-miss: meglitinides share the mechanism, but their rapid onset and short duration confine the insulin spike to the meal, which the lecture credits with a ↓ risk of hypoglycemia relative to SUs. A, B and D carry no hypoglycemia risk as monotherapy - the sensitizers do not alter insulin release, and the incretins act glucose-dependently.

Principle: hypoglycemia risk tracks glucose-independent insulin release.

lectureMeta: Source: "UME P2 Endocrine Pharmacology (Pharmacology of T2DM)" Microsoft Forms quiz, 9 questions (Q1-7 and Q9 multiple choice, Q8 short answer). All content maps to [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]].
stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to the use of metformin?
answer:
A. Metformin is renally excreted unchanged. Below an eGFR of 30 mL/min it accumulates, and because its mechanism includes ↓ conversion of lactate to glucose, accumulation raises the risk of lactic acidosis.

Every other option is a contraindication belonging to a different class - a good class-attribution check:

  • medullary thyroid cancer (and MEN2) → GLP-1RAs
  • pancreatitis → incretin agents (GLP-1 RAs and DPP-4 inhibitors)
  • heart failure and bladder cancer → TZDs / pioglitazone
  • retinopathy is not a contraindication to any of these

lectureMeta: Source: "UME P2 Endocrine Pharmacology (Pharmacology of T2DM)" Microsoft Forms quiz, 9 questions (Q1-7 and Q9 multiple choice, Q8 short answer). All content maps to [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]].
stem: TZDs are contraindicated in patients with heart failure. What is the pharmacological basis of this contraindication? (short answer)
answer:
TZDs activate the PPAR-γ receptor, and one downstream transcriptional effect is ↑ expression of Na⁺ channels in the kidney. The resulting Na⁺ and water retention expands plasma volume → edema → increased preload on a ventricle that already cannot handle it, so heart failure decompensates.

The key nuance: TZDs are not cardiotoxic and not negative inotropes. The problem is entirely a volume effect - a predictable extension of the drug's own mechanism, which is exactly what "pharmacological basis" is asking for.

Worth adding: the same PPAR-γ mechanism also drives the class's weight gain, through expansion of adipose tissue - a separate effect from the fluid retention.

lectureMeta: Source: "UME P2 Endocrine Pharmacology (Pharmacology of T2DM)" Microsoft Forms quiz, 9 questions (Q1-7 and Q9 multiple choice, Q8 short answer). All content maps to [[07 - Pharmacology of Glucose-Lowering Drugs]].
stem: Which of the following antihyperglycemics can be used in patients with eGFR < 30 ml/min?
answer:
A. DPP-4 inhibitors are the caution, not contraindicated row in the lecture's comparison table - alogliptin can be continued at a reduced dose in severe renal impairment.

The other three are all contraindicated below eGFR 30:

  • C metformin - renally excreted, accumulates, lactic acidosis risk (this is the explicit < 30 mL/min cut-off)
  • D dapagliflozin - an SGLT2 inhibitor, and its efficacy depends on filtration, so it both stops working and stays contraindicated
  • B glyburide - a sulfonylurea with renally cleared active metabolites; ↓ clearance → accumulation → hypoglycemia

Related: the in-class Menti asked the same idea one step further - at GFR < 15 mL/min the class answered insulin (marked correct), the fallback when every oral option is gone.

stem:
Which of the following statements about team care for people with diabetes are true?

(originally select all that apply; rewritten as a combinations MCQ)

  1. A certified diabetes educator (someone with the title CDE) can advise patients about diet, glucose and insulin adjustments
  2. Pharmacists can show patients how to use insulin pens
  3. Pharmacists will help patients adjust insulin doses when the insulin prescription is refilled
  4. Pharmacists will advise patients on the side effects of medications
  5. Pharmacists will help patients adjust the dose of oral medications when the prescription comes up for renewal
answer:
A. The line the question draws is who may change a dose. A CDE is credentialed to advise on diet, glucose interpretation and insulin adjustment - dose changes are inside the role (1). A pharmacist teaches device technique and counsels on adverse effects, which is why 2 and 4 are true, but does not independently retitrate insulin (3) or oral agents (5) at the point of refill.

Original select-all key: statements 1, 2 and 4.

Principle: every option is a real member of the team; the discriminator is scope of practice, not competence.

stem: Complication screening is a routine part of diabetes care. Which of the following is true for a teenager who has gone through puberty with Type 1 diabetes?

options.html: Screening for nephropathy is done with an annual urinalysis for microalbuminuria
Screening for retinopathy should begin at diagnosis in all patients with Type 1 diabetes
Blood pressure measurements should be recorded on an annual basis
Hypothyroidism is less common in Type 1 diabetes than in the general population, and so screening is only done based on symptoms

answer:
A. Annual urine albumin screening for diabetic nephropathy is the standard once a post-pubertal patient has had type 1 diabetes long enough to be at risk.

  • B has the wrong disease. Screening from diagnosis is the type 2 rule, because type 2 has been present unnoticed for years before it is found. Type 1 has a datable onset, so diabetic retinopathy screening starts some years after it.
  • C is too infrequent, not wrong in kind. Blood pressure is taken at every visit, not annually.
  • D is the wrong direction. Type 1 is autoimmune and clusters with other autoimmune disease, so hypothyroidism is more common, and that is exactly why it is screened for rather than waited for.

stem:
Your patient who works in construction was just diagnosed with type 1 diabetes and is going to start testing his blood glucose. He asks you what he should consider when he goes to buy a capillary blood glucose meter. Which of the following are issues you should discuss with him?

(originally select all that apply; rewritten as a combinations MCQ)

  1. Does he have a medical plan for coverage
  2. How does he feel about pricking his finger with a lancet
  3. Would he find it helpful to see his blood glucose results on his cell phone screen
  4. Does he have access to hand washing facilities at work
  5. Would it be helpful if his wife could also see his glucose results on her cell phone device
answer:
E. All five. The question is testing that meter choice is a fit-to-the-life decision rather than a technical one: cost and coverage (1), tolerance of lancing (2), how results are displayed and whether they reach a phone (3), whether hands can be washed on a construction site before a capillary sample (4), and whether a partner can see the data (5).

Original select-all key: all five statements.

Each distractor drops a real consideration, which is the point: A keeps only the tidy ones and discards hand washing and the partner, C discards the partner alone, and D discards coverage - the one most likely to decide whether he buys the meter at all.

Principle: a meter the patient will not or cannot use accurately is the wrong meter, whatever its specifications.

stem:
You follow a 29 year old woman in your practice who wishes to conceive her first baby. She has a 9 year history of type 1 DM. She wants the best outcome for her baby. Which of the following are true statements that you should review with her?

(originally select all that apply; rewritten as a combinations MCQ)

  1. The pre-conception A1C goal is 6.5% or less for the least risk of associated baby malformations
  2. Serious maternal hypoglycemia during pregnancy increases the offspring's risk for childhood seizures
  3. During pregnancy, the aim for capillary blood glucose before breakfast is 5.2 mM or less
  4. The A1C goal throughout pregnancy is 6.5% or less
  5. She should start taking folic acid 1 mg daily in preparation for conception
answer:
A. The three true statements are the three pre-conception actions: an A1C at or below 6.5% before conceiving, when organogenesis is at stake (1); a fasting capillary target of 5.2 mM or less once pregnant (3); and folic acid 1 mg daily started before conception rather than after a positive test (5).

Original select-all key: statements 1, 3 and 5.

  • C is the trap for anyone who read statement 1 and carried the number forward. The target does not stay at 6.5% - it tightens once she is pregnant, which is why statement 4 is false. Same patient, different number, and the question is checking that the two are held apart.
  • Statement 2 is keyed false.

stem: Luigi is awaiting a knee replacement which will occur in the next 6 months. He has been advised that he needs to lose at least 20 pounds before his surgery to help with his post-operative recovery. His past medical history is significant for pancreatitis and myocardial infarction. He is on ASA, bisoprolol, atorvastatin, and perindopril. His current BMI is 32 kg/m2. In addition to lifestyle changes, which medication(s), if any, would you recommend?
answer:
D. Transcribed from Elentra: "Correct answer: d. Naltrexone-bupropion (Pancreatitis is a contraindication for a and b; metformin is not a weight-loss med)."

So the history does the work: pancreatitis rules out semaglutide and tirzepatide, and metformin is not an anti-obesity agent at all, which leaves naltrexone-bupropion.

Pair this with Q18, which is the same question with the contraindication moved. There the seizure history knocks out naltrexone-bupropion and the two incretins are the answer.

stem: Your 65 year old patient has had type 2 DM for 20 years. He has had retinal laser therapy for retinopathy and can no longer see well enough to drive. He describes tripping over a mat the night before when he got up in the dark and cannot feel the bath water temperature when he steps into it. What category of diabetic complication do his symptoms suggest?
answer:
A. Two findings, one category. Retinopathy needing laser and a loss of protective sensation in the feet - tripping in the dark, not feeling bath water - are diabetic neuropathy and retinopathy, both microvascular.

  • B would be myocardial infarction, stroke or peripheral arterial disease. Nothing here is vascular occlusion of a large vessel.
  • C is the distractor worth naming: neuroglycopenic describes the brain being starved of glucose in hypoglycemia - confusion, slurred speech - and is an acute state, not a chronic complication. The word contains "neuro" and this patient has neuropathy, which is the whole reason it is on the list.

stem:
You are called to the Emergency department to see a patient who is acutely ill with elevated blood glucose. He/she is taking no medications and has been very healthy in the past. Which of the following lab test results are consistent with your suspicion that he/she has diabetic ketoacidosis?

(originally select all that apply; rewritten as a combinations MCQ)

  1. Blood glucose 5 mM
  2. Low pH on blood gases
  3. Absence of ketones in urine
  4. Low serum bicarbonate
  5. High anion gap
  6. Presence of ketones in blood
answer:
B. DKA is a triad, and the four true statements are that triad's lab signature: acidosis (low pH, 2), consumed buffer (low bicarbonate, 4), the unmeasured anions doing the consuming (high anion gap, 5), and the ketones themselves (6).

Original select-all key: statements 2, 4, 5 and 6.

Statements 1 and 3 are the same wrong answer twice. A glucose of 5 mM is normal, and absent urine ketones is the negative of the finding being looked for - each contradicts one leg of the triad. A is the near miss: it has the acid-base picture right but leaves out the ketones, which is the one finding that names the diagnosis.

stem:
You are called to the Emergency department to see an elderly man with confusion that has developed over a week. He has known Type 2 DM and was recently started on prednisone for a flare of gout. His BG is 50 mmol/L and his creatinine is significantly elevated at 300 micromol/l even though he has no history of renal impairment. Which of the following would be helpful emergency department care of this man?

(originally select all that apply; rewritten as a combinations MCQ)

  1. Start an intravenous line
  2. Assess his breathing, heart rate and blood pressure
  3. Check an ECG for ischemia or infarct
  4. Ask the RN to start running 5% dextrose intravenously at 100 cc/hour
  5. Check his serum bicarbonate and pH levels
  6. Administer rapid acting insulin through the intravenous line
answer:
B. The picture is HHS: a week of confusion, glucose 50 mM, and a creatinine of 300 in someone with no renal history, which is pre-renal failure from osmotic diuresis. Prednisone for the gout flare is the precipitant.

Original select-all key: statements 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6.

Everything true is either resuscitation or the workup that separates HHS from DKA: access (1), ABCs (2), an ECG because hyperglycemic crises are precipitated by and precipitate ischemia (3), and a bicarbonate and pH to establish whether he is acidotic (5). Insulin by the same line (6) treats the hyperglycemia.

Statement 4 is the only false one and the point of the question, which is why C and E are the options to be careful with - both include it. He is profoundly hyperglycemic and volume depleted. He needs saline. Running 5% dextrose adds glucose to a patient already at 50 mM and does nothing for the deficit.

stem:
Paul is a 59 year old man who has been struggling with his weight for a long time. His BMI is 34.4 kg/m2. He is on phenytoin for seizures. He has tried diet at least 3 times, and struggles each time with weight regain. In addition to lifestyle changes, which medication(s) would you recommend as option(s) for Paul?

(originally select all that apply; rewritten as a combinations MCQ)

  1. Semaglutide
  2. Tirzepatide
  3. Metformin
  4. Naltrexone-bupropion

options.html: None of these is an appropriate option for Paul

answer:
A. Transcribed from Elentra: "Metformin is not approved for weight loss. Seizures are a contraindication for naltrexone-bupropion. Semaglutide and Tirzepatide are both approved agents for weight management."

Original select-all key: options 1 and 2.

Phenytoin tells you the diagnosis being guarded against: bupropion lowers the seizure threshold, so naltrexone-bupropion is out (4). Metformin is not an anti-obesity agent (3). That leaves semaglutide and tirzepatide.

Pair this with Q14, the same options with pancreatitis instead of seizures, where the answer inverts to naltrexone-bupropion.

stem: Which of the following is true regarding results of the Diabetes Prevention Program?

options.html: A lifestyle modification program comprising 200 minutes of physical activity and low fat, low calorie diet was less effective than metformin in diabetes prevention.
A lifestyle modification program comprising 150 minutes of physical activity and low fat, low calorie diet was more effective than metformin in diabetes prevention.
Metformin was more effective than a lifestyle modification program comprising 150 minutes of physical activity and low fat, low calorie diet in diabetes prevention.
Neither metformin, nor a lifestyle modification program was effective in diabetes prevention.

answer:
B. Two things have to be right at once, which is what makes this more than recall. The dose of lifestyle is 150 minutes of activity a week, and lifestyle beat metformin. Both arms worked; lifestyle worked better.

  • A has the right ranking spoiled by the wrong number (200 minutes) and then inverts the result anyway.
  • C keeps the correct 150 minutes and inverts only the ranking, so it is the option to be careful with.
  • D denies the trial's central finding.

Principle: this is the evidence behind 12 - Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes - prevention is achievable, and the behavioural arm outperformed the drug.

stem: How does the thyroid gland obtain and concentrate iodine?

options.html: Iodine is abundant in the food supply so no special mechanism is needed for the thyroid to uptake iodine.
The thyroid cell expresses specialized molecules, including thyroperoxidase and transthyretin to help take up iodine.
Specialized transporters, including pendrin and the sodium iodide symporter, allow the thyroid cell to take up iodine against the concentration gradient.
Thyroglobulin and thyroxine binding globulin are specialized proteins that bind iodine in the plasma for transport to the thyroid follicle cell.
Uptake of iodine by the thyroid cell occurs largely by passive diffusion in the wake of water uptake through the actions of 11β-HSD2 in the kidney.

answer: The correct answer is C. The sodium iodide symporter (NIS) brings in iodine from the basolateral side of the thyroid follicle against a concentration gradient. From the inside the thyroid follicle, pendrin acts to transport iodine to the apical side of the thyroid follicle whereby it can be acted upon by TPO to generate T3/T4 conjugated to thyroglobulin.

stem: Which of the following regarding Thyroid Hormones is INCORRECT?

options.html: Iodination and coupling of tyrosine residues in thyroglobulin takes place at the apical microvillus surface of the thyroid follicular cell.
Thyroxine (T4) can be directly converted to either T2 or reverse T3 (rT3) by the actions of deiodinase-3 (D3).
Thyroid hormones are permissive for the induction of surfactant.
TPO synthesizes T3/T4 first by coupling tyrosine residues followed by iodination of tyrosine residues.

answer: The correct answer is E. This is tough question! Answer B is incorrect as Thyroxine (T4) cannot be directly converted to T2 by the actions of deiodinase-3 (D3). D2 first must convert T4 to T3 and then D3 can be converted to T2. Answer D is also incorrect as TPO first iodinates then couples tyrosine residues to synthesize T3/T4. So Answer E is the correct answer.

stem: Thyroid hormones increases metabolism by stimulating
answer: The correct answer is B. Answer B is correct as alterations in cardiac Na+/K+ ATPase activity will have direct impact on heart rate, stroke volume, and basal metabolic rate (BMR) all influencing metabolism. Answer A is incorrect as thyroid hormones promote lipid breakdown for more energy, and Answers C and D are not directly linked to metabolism.

stem: All of the following are properties of thyroxine (T4) EXCEPT:

options.html: T4 is composed of amino acid subunits
T4 binds to thyroid binding globulin (TBG) with less affinity than T3
T4 has greater half-life than T3

answer: The correct answer is C. T4 , though a weaker thyroid hormone than T3 can still elicit thyroid hormone effects including increase metabolic rates. It is also derived from tyrosine residues and does have a great half-life (7 vs 1 day) than T3. TBG can bind both T3 and T4 with equal affinity (75% of both circulating T3/T4).

stem: Dietary iodine deficiency often presents as a goiter (an enlarged thyroid gland). Which of the following statements offers the best explanation for this phenomenon?

options.html: The thyroid enlarges so that it can secrete more thyroid hormones to compensate for the lack of iodine.
Decreased plasma iodine levels are detected by the hypothalamus, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete more thyroid stimulating hormone.

Without iodine, the thyroid gland cannot produce thyroid hormones. Thyroid hormones normally act as a negative-feedback signal for the hypothalamus and pituitary gland. Loss of this signal results in excessive secretion of thyroid stimulating hormone resulting in thyroid hyperplasia and hypertrophy.

In an attempt to move more iodine into the colloid for iodination, thyroid follicle cells increase the expression of the sodium iodide symporter (NIS) and pendrin, thus enlarging the cells, and ultimately, the thyroid gland.

answer: The correct answer is C. When there is a lack of iodine, less or no T3/T4 production occurs by the thyroid gland leading to lower levels of T3/T4 in circulation. With diminished T3/T4 in circulation, there is 'less' of a negative feedback on circulating TSH levels leading to further activation of the TSH receptor. Prolonged activation of the TSH receptor lead to thyroid follicular cell hypertrophy, ultimately resulting in a goiter.

stem: A patient comes to you with a problem. She has been tired, unable to concentrate, has put on a little weight, has a little trouble swallowing and feels like her neck is swollen. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms and the easiest solution to her problem?

options.html: These are classic symptoms of hypothyroidism. You suggest she be put on thyroid hormone therapy.
These are classic symptoms of hyperthyroidism and she should decrease her salt intake.

These are classic symptoms of hypothyroidism, most likely due to a lack of thyroid stimulating hormone secretion from the anterior pituitary. She should have a head/neck CT scan and follow-up with her doctor.

These are classic symptoms of hypothyroidism, most likely due to to thyroid hormone levels. Since she shows signs of a goiter, she should increase her intake of iodine and see if the symptoms disappear.

answer: The correct answer is D. This is a tricky question! The key to the answer was to realize what is the easiest solution (from a medical standpoint) for her problem. While this is definitely a case of hypothyroidism, answer A is incorrect as it would be premature to put the patient on thyroid hormone replacement therapy, without first trying to naturally boost T3/T4 production with increased dietary intake of salt (iodine). Answer C is also too drastic and premature. Therefore, Answer D is correct.

stem: Normal physiological function requires serum calcium to be maintained within a very narrow range. What effects will be noted after a decrease in plasma calcium ion levels in an otherwise normal person?

options.html: an increase in plasma parathyroid hormone level, a decrease in plasma 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D3 level and a decrease in nerve and muscle excitability.
an increase in plasma parathyroid hormone level, plasma 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D3 level and in nerve and muscle excitability.
since the patient is otherwise normal, no change in hormone levels or nerve and muscle function would be noted.
a decrease in plasma parathyroid hormone level, and an increase in plasma 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D3 level and an increase in nerve and muscle excitability.

answer: The correct answer is B. Plasma calcium is tightly regulated by both PTH and Vitamin D3. So drop in plasma calcium triggers PTH from the parathyroid gland and this will ultimately lead to more Vitamin D3 production. Collectively, both hormones will act to increase plasma ("free") calcium which would promote nerve/muscle activity.

stem: All of the following will lead to increased serum calcium EXCEPT:

options.html: increased parathyroid hormone binding to receptors in GI tract
increased parathyroid hormone binding to receptors in the bone

answer: The correct answer is A. Answer A is correct as there are no PTH receptors in the GI tract. PTH leads to more 1α-hydroxylase in the kidney promoting more Vitamin D3 production and ultimately Vitamin D3 leads to more calcium reabsorption in the GI tract.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding calcium homeostasis is/are true?

options.html: Vitamin D binding to its receptor in the bone leads to increased bone resorption but only when there is high circulating calcium.
Activation of PTH receptors in the GI tract further lead to calcium absorption.
Sunlight converts the vitamin D3 precursor to 25-dihydroxycholcalciferol in the skin.
PTH related peptide (PTHrP) binding to the PTH receptor can lead to hormone-related hypercalcemia (HHM).
Calcium absorption can by upregulated by activation of PTH receptors in the Loop of Henle.

answer: The correct answer is D. Answer A is incorrect as Vitamin D leads to increased bone resorption only wehen there is low circulating calcium. Answer B is incorrect as there are no PTH receptors in GI tract. Answer C is incorrect as sunlight (UV) coverts D3 precursor in our skin to cholecalciferol, NOT 25-dihydroxycholcalciferol. And answer E is incorrect as PTH activates calcium resorption, in an active process (not passive), in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). Answer D is correct.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (11 questions) - 6 from the Thyroid mini-lecture, 4 from Parathyroid, 1 from the Putting it All Together consolidation.
stem: Which of the following statement(s) are true regarding hyperparathyroidism?

options.html: Primary hyperparathyroidism is associated with elevated PTH but not calcium.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is associated with both elevated PTH and calcium
Jansen's metaphyseal chrondroplasia can lead to hyperparathyroidism due to an inactivating mutation of the PTH receptor.
Primary hyperparathyroidism results in low or normal calcium levels
None of the above is true.

answer: The correct answer is E. Primary hyperparathyroidism is associated with both elevated PTH and calcium while secondary hyperparathyroidism is associated with low-normal calcium resulting from PTH or Vitamin D resistance. Jansen's metaphyseal chrondroplasia occurs due to an activating mutation of the PTH receptor.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (11 questions) - 6 from the Thyroid mini-lecture, 4 from Parathyroid, 1 from the Putting it All Together consolidation.
stem: Which of the following regarding thyroid and parathyroid hormones are correct?

options.html: SRIF inhibits both TSH production in the anterior pituitary and PTH production from the parathyroid gland.
Excessive production of thyroid hormones or parathyroid hormones can result from activating autoimmune antibodies or activating mutations in target endocrine receptors.
T3/T4 require carrier proteins to transport in the blood because they are steroid hormones.
Hormone-related hypercalcemia occurs when PTHrP binds to the Vitamin D receptor in the GI tract.

answer: The correct answer is B. Answer A is incorrect as SRIF only inhibits TSH production. Answer C is incorrect as T3/T4 are not steroid hormones, but do require carrier proteins due to their aromatic structure. Answer D is incorrect as PTHrP binds to the PTH receptor, not the Vitamin D receptor. Finally Answer B is correct because activating antibodies lead to hyperthyroidism is the autoimmune Grave's disease, while hyperparathyroidism occurs due to activating mutations of PTH receptor in Jansen's metaphyseal chondroplasia.

stem: Which of the following represents a key difference in the actions of Vitamin D and PTH on calcium and phosphate homeostasis?

options.html: Vitamin D increases the intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate while PTH decreases the absorption of both ions.
Vitamin D has direct actions on renal cells regulating the reabsorption of these ions while PTH has indirect actions.
PTH increases the renal excretion of phosphate while Vitamin D increases the reabsorption of this ion.
PTH increases its own secretion via its action on the calcium sensing receptors while Vitamin D decreases PTH secretion.

answer: The correct answer is C. PTH and Vitamin D have similar actions on calcium and phosphate homeostasis but one key difference is that PTH decreases the renal reabsorption of phosphate while Vitamin D increases it. PTH doesn't have direct actions in the GI tract; it affects the GI absorption of calcium and phosphate indirectly via the actions of Vitamin D.

stem: Which of the following statements is correct about bisphosphonates?

options.html: These drugs have high distribution in lipophilic tissues such as bone and fat tissues
These drugs act by inhibiting the actions osteoblasts, increasing bone formation
These drugs are poorly absorbed in the GI tract and should be taken with food
These drugs are well tolerated but high doses of the most potent agents can cause ONJ
These drugs depend on hepatic function for elimination

answer: The correct answer is D. Bisphosphonates are drugs with high affinity for calcium and bone tissue. These drugs present poor bioavailability and must be taken on an empty stomach. They act on osteoclasts, decreasing their ability to promote bone resorption. Bisphosphonates are elminated unchanged in the urine. These drugs are associated with the development of a rare but very serious condition called Osteonecrosis of the jaw bone. Most cases happen with high doses of the high potency bisphosphonates such as zoledronic acid.

stem: Which of the following would be contraindications to the use of bisphosphonates? Select all that apply.
answer:
The correct answers are C and E. The module keys the question but gives no rationale, so the reasoning below is mine, from the lecture note.

The lecture's contraindication list for bisphosphonates has exactly three entries - eGFR < 30 mL/min, esophageal disease, and established or predisposed hypocalcemia - and two of them are on offer here:

  • C, severe renal disease - ⭐ bisphosphonates are excreted unchanged in the urine, with no hepatic metabolism to fall back on, so a failing kidney means the drug accumulates. This is the reason ⭐ denosumab is the antiresorptive of choice when renal function is poor: it is a monoclonal antibody and does not depend on the kidney for elimination. Teriparatide is out below 30 mL/min as well
  • E, esophageal abnormalities - oral bisphosphonates cause direct esophageal and gastric irritation, which is why they are taken on an empty stomach with water and the patient must sit or stand upright for 30 minutes afterwards. A stricture, achalasia or significant reflux turns that irritation into ulceration
  • A, hypercalcemia is the right ion in the wrong direction. Every antiresorptive drives serum calcium down, so ⭐ hypercalcemia is an indication for a bisphosphonate, not a contraindication - it is the treatment for hypercalcemia of malignancy. What contraindicates them is hypocalcemia, which the option set never offers
  • B, hyperglycemia has nothing to do with this class

flags.title: D is a caution, not a contraindication
flags.html: “Inability to stand” is about the route, not the drug. The upright-for-30-minutes rule exists to keep an oral tablet moving through the esophagus, so a patient who cannot stay upright is a patient you do not hand the pill to - you give IV zoledronate instead, and the bisphosphonate itself is still on the table. ⭐ C and E take the whole class away whatever the route; D only rules out one formulation. That is the line this question is drawn along.
