stem: Steve's fingerstick values over two weeks range from 2 to 20 mmol/L. Before escalating his regimen, which step does the facilitator put first? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Immediately switch him to an insulin pump
Identify the sources of his glycemic variability
Add a sulfonylurea to his existing insulin regimen
Increase every one of his insulin doses by 20%

answer:
The correct answer is B. A range of 2 to 20 mmol/L is a variability problem, and you cannot fix variability by adding insulin. Look first for:

  • injection-site problems - is there lipohypertrophy?
  • timing of the NovoRapid relative to meals (~15 minutes before)
  • over-correcting lows
  • whether he has a system for pre-meal bolus dosing based on the glucose level plus expected carbohydrate intake
  • possible gastroparesis

Then offer referral to the Diabetes Education Centre, especially if it has been a while.

C is wrong outright - a secretagogue does nothing in T1DM, where there are no functioning beta cells to stimulate.

lecture: DSSG Case 2 - Steve Dedalus (Longstanding Type 1 Diabetes, A1c 11.0%)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q26-29. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]] and [[08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes]].
stem: Having addressed the sources of variability, which escalation does the facilitator identify as preferred for all individuals with type 1 diabetes? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)
answer:
The correct answer is C, an insulin pump - stated in the deck as preferred for all individuals with T1DM.

The full escalation pathway: address variability → DEC → full basal-bolus MDI, with rapid-acting insulin before breakfast, lunch and supper dosed on a correction factor plus carbohydrate intake, and a longer-acting basal (glargine, degludec) instead of Levemir/detemir → CGM, subject to coverage → insulin pump.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: A family doctor calls you at 4:30 pm on the Friday before the May long weekend about Fitzwilliam Darcy, a 55-year-old man with a random plasma glucose of 55 mmol/L. He has no history of diabetes but has had two weeks of increased thirst, blurred vision and polyuria every half hour. Which type of diabetes is most likely? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Type 1 diabetes, because of the severity of the hyperglycemia
Type 2 diabetes, the most common form overall
Gestational diabetes, given her age and presentation
Drug-induced diabetes from a recent prescription

answer: The correct answer is B. Type 2 diabetes is most likely and it is the most common form of diabetes overall. Severity of hyperglycemia alone does not classify the diabetes - a glucose of 55 mmol/L is entirely compatible with T2DM presenting as HHS.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: You ask the family doctor for the serum creatinine, electrolytes including sodium and bicarbonate with an anion gap, and Mr. Darcy's mental status. What are you screening for? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)
answer:
The correct answer is A. Both are potentially lethal and both need to be excluded before anything is deferred over a long weekend.

  • HHS - suggested by impaired mental status plus an effective serum osmolality ≥ ~320 mosm/kg.
  • DKA - suggested by an anion-gap metabolic acidosis, which is why the bicarbonate and anion gap were requested.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: How is the effective serum osmolality calculated in this context? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)
answer:
The correct answer is A. Effective serum osmolality = (2 × [Na⁺]) + [glucose], and a value ≥ ~320 mosm/kg together with impaired mental status is the concern for HHS.

Urea is excluded because it crosses cell membranes freely and so is not an effective osmole - it does not drive the water shift that produces the neurological findings.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: What advice should you give the family doctor at 4:30 pm on the Friday of a long weekend? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Send him to the Emergency Department now
Book him into your clinic on Tuesday and start metformin in the meantime
Advise oral rehydration with fruit juice and review after the weekend
Arrange outpatient labs for the following week

answer:
The correct answer is A. If he has not had the tests needed to rule out HHS and DKA, or he has had them and the results are consistent with either, the safe thing is the Emergency Department now. Both are potentially lethal if not treated quickly, so leaving it over the long weekend is not a good idea.

He should also stop drinking anything except water and diet juices - which is why C is actively harmful.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Why is insulin the drug of choice for Mr. Darcy's severe new hyperglycemia, even though he most likely has type 2 diabetes? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: It is the only agent licensed in new-onset diabetes
It controls severe hyperglycemia fastest, and may not be needed long term
All oral agents are contraindicated in type 2 diabetes at diagnosis
It is the only agent that does not require renal dose adjustment

answer: The correct answer is B. Because there is concern about acute decompensation, the threshold to start insulin ahead of all other anti-hyperglycemic drugs is very low. It is the most effective option for quickly controlling severe uncontrolled hyperglycemia. He may not need insulin long term - the choice is driven by the acuity, not by the eventual classification.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: At the Diabetes Education Centre, Mr. Darcy is seen by a nurse and a dietician. Which best describes what the nurse will cover? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Survival skills - safe insulin use, hypoglycemia and sick-day rules
A calorie-reduced, balanced diet plan and carbohydrate counting teaching
Screening for retinopathy and nephropathy at this visit
Titration of his statin and his antihypertensive medication

answer:
The correct answer is A. The nurse concentrates on survival skills:

  • safe use of insulin - dose setting, how to inject, injection timing, storage
  • hypoglycemia - detection, prevention, treatment
  • glucose monitoring
  • driving guidelines
  • sick-day management

B is the dietician's role - assess his current diet, then build a plan on the Diabetes Canada 2018 guidelines: nutritionally balanced and, if he is overweight, calorie-reduced for weight loss. He also learns about carbohydrates generally, and may later be taught carbohydrate counting, especially if he ends up on MDI.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Mr. Darcy's father died in his early 60s of kidney failure after a leg amputation. Which statement about protecting his kidneys is correct? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Use an ACE inhibitor or an ARB, but never both together
Use an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together for additive renal protection
Neither class has a role once diabetes is diagnosed
An ARB is only indicated once dialysis has begun

answer:
The correct answer is A. For prevention of renal failure: screening urine ACR annually, blood glucose control, blood pressure control, and an ACE inhibitor or an ARB - but not both.

Dual RAAS blockade adds hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury without an offsetting benefit, which is why the "or" in that sentence is the examinable part.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Is ASA used for primary or secondary cardiovascular prevention in diabetes? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Primary prevention in all patients with diabetes over 40
Neither - ASA has no role in diabetes

answer:
The correct answer is B, secondary prevention only. Meta-analyses and RCTs show that in primary prevention the benefit does not clearly exceed the harm, so ASA is not used for that indication in diabetes.

The rest of the macrovascular prevention package for coronary heart disease, ischemic stroke and peripheral vascular disease: blood pressure control, LDL-C control with a statin, smoking cessation, and anti-hyperglycemic drugs proven to prevent MACE in the cardiovascular outcome trials.

lecture: DSSG Case 3 - Fitzwilliam Darcy (Random Plasma Glucose 55 mmol/L)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q30-38. Tests [[06 - Acute and Chronic Complications of Diabetes]] and [[10 - Prevention of Complications of Diabetes]].
stem: Which set of interventions is used to prevent vision loss from diabetic eye disease? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Eye exam, glucose and BP control, smoking cessation, fenofibrate
An annual screening eye exam and nothing further
Blood glucose control and nothing further
Laser photocoagulation for every patient at diagnosis

answer:
The correct answer is A. For diabetic eye disease: a screening eye exam roughly annually, blood glucose control, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, and fenofibrate.

Set against the other structural complications from the same slide:

  • Renal failure - screening urine ACR annually, BG control, BP control, an ACE inhibitor or an ARB.
  • Peripheral sensory neuropathy - BG control.
  • Foot ulcers / amputation - everything that prevents neuropathy and peripheral vascular disease, plus regular foot exams and patient education, especially in high-risk feet.

lecture: DSSG Case 4 - Agnes Wickfield (32-year-old Pilot with New Hyperglycemia)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q39-41. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]] and [[02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes]].
stem: Agnes Wickfield is a 32-year-old Air Canada pilot with polyuria and polydipsia. She is not pregnant, her random blood glucose is 25.4 mmol/L, and urinalysis shows 3+ glucosuria but is negative for ketones. Which pairing of clinical features with the diabetes type they favour is correct? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: acanthosis favours type 1; DKA at presentation favours type 2
DKA at presentation favours type 1; acanthosis favours type 2
Both DKA and acanthosis favour type 1
Neither feature has any discriminating value

answer:
The correct answer is B. DKA at presentation favours T1D; acanthosis favours T2D.

The other features available from history and exam: ethnicity (T2D more common in First Nations, African American, Asian and Hispanic populations), family history (stronger in T2D - identical-twin concordance ~100%, and ≥half of T2D patients have a close relative with diabetes, versus only ~15% of new-onset T1D having a first- or second-degree relative with T1D), past GDM (favours T2D), older age (favours T2D), and obesity (favours T2D).

flags.title: No single factor is decisive
flags.html: T1D has been described in patients in their 80s, being overweight does not protect against immune-mediated beta-cell loss, and DKA can occur in T2D. The features are combined, not applied individually.

lecture: DSSG Case 4 - Agnes Wickfield (32-year-old Pilot with New Hyperglycemia)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q39-41. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]] and [[02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes]].
stem: Which investigations would specifically support a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes in Agnes? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Pancreatic autoantibodies and a low serum C-peptide
A high serum C-peptide and a fasting insulin level
An OGTT and a fructosamine level

answer:
The correct answer is A.

  • Pancreatic autoantibodies - GADA, IAA, ZnT8A, IA-2A, ICA - marking immune-mediated beta-cell loss.
  • A low serum C-peptide - favours T1D, because C-peptide is co-secreted with endogenous insulin and so falls as beta-cell function is lost.
  • HLA typing - T1D is associated with DR3, DR4, DQ8.

lecture: DSSG Case 4 - Agnes Wickfield (32-year-old Pilot with New Hyperglycemia)
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q39-41. Tests [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]] and [[02 - Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes]].
stem: Why does it matter whether Agnes has type 1 or type 2 diabetes? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Only because the long-term complication risk differs
Type 1 means insulin, which has occupational implications for a pilot
It does not change management at this glucose level
Only because type 1 requires a different A1c target

answer:
The correct answer is B. Two reasons are given:

  • If she has type 1 diabetes, insulin is the required treatment - not an option among others.
  • She is a commercial pilot, so the diagnosis and the need for insulin carry direct occupational and regulatory implications.

lecture: DSSG Cases 5-7 - Adjusting Insulin from the Glucose Record
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q42-47. Three patients on insulin: read the record, decide whether to change the regimen and what to change. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]] and [[08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes]].
stem:
Patient 5 is a 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and an A1c of 8.4%, on rapid-acting NovoRapid before each meal and glargine 16 units at bedtime. His week of readings (mmol/L):

DayBreakfastLunchSupperBedtime
Mon4.26.812.316.7
Tue3.912.514.618.2
Wed6.88.59.212.6
Thu3.26.98.54.7
Fri4.15.211.916.5
Sat2.811.413.48.4
Sun3.99.414.315.9

Which description of his pattern is correct? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Morning hypoglycemia, with hyperglycemia at supper and at bedtime
Morning hyperglycemia, with hypoglycemia at supper and at bedtime

answer:
The correct answer is A. Reading down the columns: the breakfast values run low (2.8, 3.2, 3.9, 3.9, 4.1) - morning hypoglycemia; the supper values run high (up to 14.6) - hyperglycemia at supper; and the bedtime values run high (up to 18.2) - hyperglycemia at bedtime.

Reading the record by time of day rather than by day is the whole technique here - the pattern is in the columns, not the rows.

lecture: DSSG Cases 5-7 - Adjusting Insulin from the Glucose Record
lectureMeta: Source: Week 2 DSSG "Diabetes Mellitus Cases", facilitator deck by Mohammed Alagha. Q42-47. Three patients on insulin: read the record, decide whether to change the regimen and what to change. Tests [[03 - Pharmacology of Insulin]] and [[08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes]].
stem: Which set of insulin adjustments does the facilitator recommend for Patient 5? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Decrease bedtime glargine; increase lunch and supper NovoRapid
Increase bedtime glargine; decrease lunch and supper NovoRapid
Decrease every one of her doses by 20%
Make no change and repeat the A1c in three months

answer:
The correct answer is A.

  • Decrease bedtime Lantus/glargine by 10-20% - it is the insulin acting overnight, and he is waking low.
  • Increase lunch NovoRapid by 10% - it covers the interval ending at the pre-supper reading, which is high.
  • Increase supper NovoRapid by 10% - it covers the interval ending at bedtime, which is high.

stem: What is the general principle for adjusting a basal-bolus regimen from a glucose record? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Adjust the insulin acting before the abnormal glucose, typically by 10-20%
Adjust the insulin given after the abnormal glucose
Adjust the basal insulin only, whatever the pattern
Change all components simultaneously to reach target faster

answer:
The correct answer is A. Adjust the insulin acting before the abnormal glucose, typically by 10-20%:

  • morning low → decrease the bedtime basal
  • high pre-supper → increase the lunch rapid-acting
  • high bedtime → increase the supper rapid-acting

The reading tells you which insulin was responsible for the interval that just ended.

stem: Patient 6 is a 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a seizure disorder. Her A1c is 6.9%, and her record shows many single-digit readings with occasional highs. What is the concern, and what should be done? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Too tight for her seizure disorder - reduce degludec, loosen the target
Too loose for her age - increase the degludec dose by 20%
Her A1c is ideal, so make no change to her regimen
Stop the insulin entirely and start a sulfonylurea

answer:
The correct answer is A. An A1c of 6.9% is probably too tight given her seizure disorder - hypoglycemia can provoke seizures, and she is already running lots of single-digit values. The occasional high readings are likely corrections or over-corrections of a previous low, not true loss of control.

  • Reduce the Tresiba/degludec by 10-20%.
  • Consider a higher A1c target (e.g. 7.5%), especially if she has no glycemic-responsive (eye, kidney, nerve) complications.

The deck qualifies this by whether her seizures are controlled and whether she has eye, renal or neuropathic complications.

stem: Patient 7 is an 81-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, advanced dementia, living in a nursing home with caregiver-administered insulin. His A1c is 9.1% and most readings sit above the 4.0-7.0 mmol/L ac-meal target. What insulin adjustment is recommended? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Add rapid-acting insulin at every meal

answer:
The correct answer is C, none. His glucoses are high relative to the ac-meal targets needed to reach an A1c of ~7.0% - but given his dementia, older age and limited life expectancy, the glycemic goals of care shift away from preventing structural complications through a lower A1c and toward keeping him free of symptomatic hypo- and hyperglycemia.

This is the case that makes the point: the right answer to "would you change the regimen?" is sometimes no, and tightening control here would buy complication prevention he will not live to benefit from at the cost of hypoglycemia he cannot reliably report.

stem: What determines the glycemic target in an older adult? (originally an open-ended DSSG discussion question; rewritten as MCQ)
answer:
The correct answer is B, functional status and life expectancy - not age. As frailty increases, targets loosen to reduce hypoglycemia risk.

StatusA1c targetIdea
Functionally independent≤7.0%treat like a younger adult
Functionally dependent<8.0%some relaxation of target
Frail / dementia<8.5%prioritise avoiding hypoglycemia
End of lifeno A1c targetavoid symptomatic hyper- and any hypoglycemia

The exact numbers are not the point - the concept is that the frailer or more dependent the patient, the looser the target, because the harm of hypoglycemia starts to outweigh the benefit of tight control. This is exactly why no adjustment was recommended for Patient 7.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a history of PCOS and a mother with type 2 diabetes. She conceived her first pregnancy by fertility intervention and is now at 25 weeks. Her weight is 100 kg and her BP is 135/95 on three measurements. Which feature of this presentation is not a recognised risk factor for gestational diabetes? (originally a narrative case slide; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: A first-degree relative with type 2 diabetes
None - all of these are recognised risk factors

answer:
The correct answer is D - every feature listed is a risk factor, which is exactly why the slide stacks them.

  • PCOS is an insulin-resistant state in its own right, and is independently associated with GDM.
  • A mother with T2DM gives a strong family history.
  • Age ≥35 and obesity (100 kg) are both standard risk factors.
  • Conception by fertility intervention travels with PCOS and with older maternal age.

Two details on the slide are not GDM risk factors but still matter: BP 135/95 on three occasions puts her diastolic at or above 90, so she needs assessment for hypertension in pregnancy and pre-eclampsia alongside the diabetes; and her 12-hour physically demanding job and drug plan shape what treatment is actually feasible (see Q51).

stem: She has a 50 g screening test of 8.5 mmol/L, and proceeds to a 75 g OGTT which returns 6.5 / 10.9 / 10.6 mmol/L (fasting / 1h / 2h). How should this be interpreted? (originally a narrative case slide; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: GDM is diagnosed; all three values are above target
Only the fasting value is diagnostic; repeat the test
The 50 g screen was normal, so the 75 g test should not have been done

answer:
The correct answer is B. The 50 g screen of 8.5 sits in the 7.8-11.0 grey band, which is precisely the band that sends her for the 75 g OGTT - so D is wrong.

On the 75 g test, all three values clear their thresholds (fasting ≥ 5.3, 1h ≥ 10.6, 2h ≥ 9.0):

Her valueThreshold
Fasting6.5≥ 5.3
1 hour10.9≥ 10.6
2 hours10.6≥ 9.0

One value at or above threshold is enough to diagnose GDM; she has three.

stem: Immediately after the diagnosis is made, what are the next steps in her care? (originally a narrative case slide; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Start insulin at once, before any other intervention
Referral to a registered dietitian for diet, and to a nurse to learn blood glucose testing
Start metformin and review in one month
Repeat the 75 g OGTT in two weeks to confirm

answer:
The correct answer is B. The slide's next steps are an interview with the RD for diet and an interview with the RN to learn how to test blood glucoses.

Management of GDM starts non-pharmacologically - diet and activity - with glucose monitoring put in place first, because the monitoring is what tells you whether diet alone is going to be enough. Starting insulin before there is any log to read (A) has nothing to titrate against. D is wrong because the diagnosis is already made.

stem: After one week on diet and walking after meals, her log shows high fasting (acB) and post-breakfast (pcB) values, with no real trend after lunch or supper. The team suggests insulin aspart 4 units before breakfast and insulin detemir 6 units at bedtime. What is the logic of that particular regimen? (originally a narrative case slide; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Each insulin is aimed at the interval that is actually out of range
Both are started at full replacement doses to normalise every reading
Rapid-acting insulin is given at every meal regardless of the log
Basal insulin alone would be sufficient for both abnormalities

answer:
The correct answer is A. This is the same principle as the DSSG insulin cases (Q42-44): treat the interval that is out of range, with the insulin that acts over it.

  • The high fasting (acB) value is an overnight problem → detemir at bedtime.
  • The high post-breakfast (pcB) value is a prandial problem at one specific meal → aspart before breakfast only.
  • Lunch and supper show no trend, so they get no insulin - which is why C is wrong.

The slide notes that high fasting and post-breakfast values are a common pattern in GDM. Note also how small the starting doses are (4 and 6 units): you start low and titrate, rather than aiming to normalise everything immediately (B).

Her drug plan and her 12-hour physically demanding job are on the case slide for a reason - the drug plan makes analogue insulins affordable, and the long physical shifts raise the stakes on hypoglycemia, which is an argument for the cautious dosing and for not covering meals that do not need it.

stem: By 37 weeks her insulin requirements are aspart 40 units at breakfast, 10 at lunch, 10 at supper, and detemir 60 units at bedtime - up from 4 and 6 units. What best explains this escalation? (originally a narrative case slide; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: She has developed type 1 diabetes during the pregnancy
Placental hormones drive progressively increasing insulin resistance as pregnancy advances
The original doses were calculated incorrectly
Insulin requirements fall in the third trimester, so this represents a dosing error

answer:
The correct answer is B. Insulin requirements rise steeply through the second and third trimesters because the placenta produces hormones that antagonise insulin - the deck names prolactin among the pregnancy hormones behind the higher insulin needs. A tenfold rise in the breakfast dose is a normal trajectory in GDM, not a failure of treatment.

D has the direction backwards for late pregnancy. It is worth holding the contrast: insulin requirements fall in the first trimester (which is the module's own knowledge check, Q48) and then climb for the rest of the pregnancy.

stem: Her obstetrician books induction at 38 weeks because the baby is judged to be at the 97th percentile. The baby is delivered vaginally with a small tear, weighs 4.5 kg, and spends two days in the NICU with low blood glucoses and under UV light. Which explanation of the newborn's low blood glucose is correct? (originally a narrative case slide; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: The newborn's pancreas was damaged by the maternal hyperglycemia
Fetal hyperinsulinemia outlasted the maternal glucose supply at delivery
Insulin crossed the placenta from the mother and lowered his glucose
It was caused by the induction rather than by the diabetes itself

answer:
The correct answer is B. Glucose crosses the placenta; maternal insulin does not - which is what makes C wrong. Chronic maternal hyperglycemia therefore drives the fetal pancreas to oversecrete insulin. That fetal hyperinsulinemia is responsible for both findings here:

  • macrosomia - 4.5 kg and the 97th percentile, insulin being a growth factor. This is what prompted the induction at 38 weeks, and what put her at risk of shoulder dystocia and of the perineal tear she sustained.
  • Neonatal hypoglycemia - at delivery the glucose supply is cut but the high insulin level persists for a time, so the newborn goes low.

The UV light is phototherapy for neonatal jaundice, also more common in infants of diabetic mothers.

stem: By six months postpartum she has lost 40 pounds (BMI now 28), is active daily, follows a low-fat, high-fibre diet and is still breastfeeding. Her 75 g OGTT shows fasting 5.0 mmol/L and 2-hour 7.5 mmol/L. What does this result mean? (originally a narrative case slide; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: The result is normal, and it confirms her GDM has resolved - but she remains at long-term risk of type 2 diabetes
The result is normal, so she carries no further risk and needs no further screening
The result is diagnostic of type 2 diabetes
The result is diagnostic of impaired glucose tolerance

answer:
The correct answer is A. Fasting 5.0 and 2-hour 7.5 mmol/L are both normal, so the GDM has resolved as expected - and the slide has you congratulate her on the diabetes prevention she has done, because the weight loss, daily activity, diet and continued breastfeeding are all working in her favour.

B is the trap. GDM identifies a woman whose beta cells could not meet the demand of pregnancy, and the deck puts the long-term risk of type 2 diabetes at up to 60%, depending on length of follow-up and ethnic background. A normal postpartum OGTT resets the clock; it does not remove the risk, and she needs ongoing periodic screening.

stem:
She is six weeks post-partum after a pregnancy managed as gestational diabetes. What is the caveat about that label, and what would give it away?

(originally a narrative case slide; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Some are pre-existing type 2 - the glucose never returns to normal
Some never had diabetes, and the OGTT is unreliable in pregnancy
GDM cannot be distinguished from type 2 diabetes at any point
They should be re-tested during the pregnancy rather than after it

answer:
The correct answer is A. Because glucose is first tested at 24-28 weeks, a woman with undiagnosed pre-existing type 2 - or, less often, early type 1 - diabetes will be picked up then and labelled "GDM", since that is simply when the test happens.

Two things give it away:

  • During the pregnancy, the glucoses and the medication needed to control them are quite high - a hint that there is more going on than GDM.
  • After delivery, in true diabetes the blood glucoses do not return to normal - which is the definitive discriminator, and the reason the postpartum OGTT in Q54 is not optional.

stem: A 35-year-old man has a history of type 2 diabetes of 2 years. He also has hypertension. He is on metformin monotherapy for his diabetes and amlodipine for his hypertension. He has no structural complication of diabetes (retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy). What should be his target A1c?

options.html: No specific target; treat symptoms only

answer:
The correct answer is A, ≤ 6.5%. The deck's own factors to consider:

  • Young and otherwise healthy, so a longer life expectancy in which to accrue benefit
  • Short duration of diabetes
  • ⭐ No structural complications yet - they can still be prevented
  • Low risk of hypoglycemia: he is on monotherapy, and not on any medication that can cause hypoglycemia

This is the ≤ 6.5% tier: ⭐ T2DM at low risk of hypoglycemia, tightened to further reduce CVD, CKD and retinopathy. metformin alone does not cause hypoglycemia, which is what makes the tighter target safe to chase. Everything that would argue for loosening is absent.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has longstanding type 1 diabetes (30 years) managed with insulin on multiple daily injections. Her past medical history includes coronary artery disease, hypertension and dyslipidemia. She has no history of severe hypoglycemia or hypoglycemia unawareness. She has neuropathy but no nephropathy or retinopathy. She works as an administrator and maintains an active lifestyle. What should be her target A1c?

options.html: No specific target; treat symptoms only

answer:
The correct answer is B, ≤ 7.0%. The deck's own factors to consider:

  • Prolonged history of diabetes
  • ⚠ Is on medications that can cause hypoglycemia (insulin)
  • Has both macrovascular and microvascular complications
  • ⭐ No indications of frailty, functional decline, or limited life expectancy

This is the validated default tier - most patients with T1DM or T2DM sit here.

She is the instructive middle case. The insulin and the established complications rule out tightening to 6.5%, because the hypoglycemia risk is real and the complications she has are no longer preventable. But she is active, working and not frail, which rules out loosening as well. ⭐ Being complicated is not the same as being frail, and that is the discrimination this case exists to test.

stem: An 85-year-old woman has type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease with severe dementia. She is dependent for all her ADLs and IADLs. She is managed with an oral regimen of metformin, gliclazide and canagliflozin, plus weekly semaglutide. Her daughter administers all her medications. What should her target A1c be?

options.html: No specific target; treat symptoms only

answer:
The correct answer is C, 7.1 - 8.5%. The deck's own factors to consider:

  • Dementia
  • Functionally dependent
  • ⚠ On a medication that can cause hypoglycemia (gliclazide)

⭐ In the frail elderly, hypoglycemia is more dangerous than hyperglycemia - it causes falls, and severe hypoglycemia carries increased mortality. A patient with severe dementia cannot reliably report or self-treat a low, which is what makes the sulfonylurea the dangerous drug in her regimen.

D is the trap. Loosening the target is not the same as abandoning it: the minimum goal of care is still that she be free of clinically significant symptoms of hypo- and hyperglycemia, so a target range is still set, just a higher one.

flags.title: The deck and the lecture note state this tier differently
flags.html: The closing slide gives 7.1 - 8.5% as a range, while 08 - Glycemic Goals of Care in Adults with Diabetes and the guidelines phrase the same tier as ≤ 8.5%. They are the same recommendation; the deck's lower bound just makes explicit that you are not aiming below 7.1% in this patient.

lecture: Module Case - Staging Type 1 Diabetes (Diabetes Pathophysiology)
lectureMeta: Q59, the case posed in the `Diabetes Pathophysiology T1DM` slide deck. **Keyed** - the deck reveals the answer by repeating the slide with the correct option bolded, but gives no written rationale, so the explanation is reasoned from [[01 - Intro to Diabetes]]. Previously banked as a module concept check; moved here because it is a patient case.
stem: You are seeing a 10 year old with a sibling with T1DM. He has anti-GAD and anti-insulin antibody positivity. His fasting glucose is 6.5 mmol/L. He is at which stage of developing T1DM?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Every stage of T1DM is defined by beta-cell autoimmunity already being present; what separates the stages is the glucose and the symptoms.

  • Stage 1 - autoantibodies with normoglycemia, pre-symptomatic
  • Stage 2 - autoantibodies with dysglycemia, still pre-symptomatic
  • Stage 3 - symptomatic diabetes

His fasting glucose of 6.5 mmol/L sits in the impaired fasting glucose band (6.1-6.9 mmol/L), so he is dysglycemic but not yet diabetic, and he has no symptoms. That is Stage 2. D is a pure distractor - there is no Stage 4.

Worth noticing separately: he carries two antibodies (GAD and insulin). Antibody count, not mere presence, is what carries risk - one antibody leaves him at the ~0.4% background risk, two confers ~25% within 5 years, three ~40%.

lecture: Module Case - Clarifying the Type of Diabetes (Case Illustration)
lectureMeta: Q60-62, the "Case Illustration" from the `Hashmi T2DMellitus` deck (Objective 2). **Keyed** - the deck lists five candidate next steps and the lecturer's own commentary on each appears on the following slide, transcribed into the answers below.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 28-year-old, previously well, is found to have a blood glucose of 12 mmol/L. The only symptom is fatigue, and he is on no medications. His mother has type 1 diabetes (DKA at age 6) and his grandfather has type 2 diabetes (diagnosed at 70, on metformin alone).

stem: Why does this patient need a repeat or confirmatory test before the diagnosis is made?

options.html: Because his only symptom is fatigue, so he is effectively asymptomatic
Because a single glucose of 12 mmol/L is below the diagnostic threshold
Because his family history makes the result unreliable
Because A1c must always be measured before a diagnosis can be made

answer:
The correct answer is A. The deck's own comment is "absolutely, get a confirmatory test as he has negligible symptoms of high BGs."

⭐ The rule turns on symptoms, not on the size of the number. A single abnormal glucose is diagnostic only when the patient is symptomatic with polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss. Fatigue alone does not count, so he needs a second abnormal result on a separate day.

B is factually wrong - 12 mmol/L is well above the random threshold of 11.1 mmol/L; it is the absence of symptoms, not the value, that forces the repeat. C confuses risk assessment with diagnosis. D is too absolute: a repeat fasting glucose or an OGTT would serve equally well.

lecture: Module Case - Clarifying the Type of Diabetes (Case Illustration)
lectureMeta: Q60-62, the "Case Illustration" from the `Hashmi T2DMellitus` deck (Objective 2). **Keyed** - the deck lists five candidate next steps and the lecturer's own commentary on each appears on the following slide, transcribed into the answers below.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 28-year-old, previously well, is found to have a blood glucose of 12 mmol/L. The only symptom is fatigue, and he is on no medications. His mother has type 1 diabetes (DKA at age 6) and his grandfather has type 2 diabetes (diagnosed at 70, on metformin alone).

stem: You are clarifying which type of diabetes he has. Which of these next steps is not done routinely?

options.html: Repeat the blood glucose, OGTT or A1c

answer:
The correct answer is C. The deck's comment: "theoretically he could have pancreatic insufficiency from islet cell destruction from pancreatic Ca. However, that would be quite odd at his age, and with no other symptoms of illness would be unlikely. So, we don't tend to do imaging routinely."

The other three are all endorsed, and each is a discriminating question rather than a general one:

  • Activity level - if he was very active and then stopped, the lost muscle work alone could tip him into the diabetic range, which argues for type 2
  • Recent weight change - gain points to type 2; ⚠ a sudden dramatic loss should raise concern for severe hyperglycemia and incipient type 1
  • Repeat testing - needed to confirm the diagnosis at all, as in Q60

Principle: imaging is not part of working out which type of diabetes someone has.

lecture: Module Case - Clarifying the Type of Diabetes (Case Illustration)
lectureMeta: Q60-62, the "Case Illustration" from the `Hashmi T2DMellitus` deck (Objective 2). **Keyed** - the deck lists five candidate next steps and the lecturer's own commentary on each appears on the following slide, transcribed into the answers below.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 28-year-old, previously well, is found to have a blood glucose of 12 mmol/L. The only symptom is fatigue, and he is on no medications. His mother has type 1 diabetes (DKA at age 6) and his grandfather has type 2 diabetes (diagnosed at 70, on metformin alone).

stem: If this patient does have type 2 diabetes, what would his C-peptide and anti-GAD antibodies be expected to show?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The deck states it directly: "C-peptide would be high and anti-GAD Ab would be low if type 2 DM."

C-peptide is released with insulin in equal amounts, so it measures endogenous insulin production. In T2DM the pancreas is still secreting - the problem is resistance - so C-peptide is preserved or high. In T1DM the beta cells are destroyed, so C-peptide is low and anti-GAD, the most specific marker, is positive. That makes B the T1DM pattern.

flags.title: Why they are often not ordered
flags.html: The deck is candid that this is optional: "sometimes we do these, but usually we just let time and response to medications indicate which type of DM he has… not often necessary, and might incur a cost at the lab as not all tests are covered by OHIP." ⭐ The response to treatment over time is itself a diagnostic test, and a cheaper one.

lecture: Module Case - Inherited and Intrauterine Risk (Alertness Check)
lectureMeta: Q63-64, the "Alertness Check" scenario from the `Hashmi T2DMellitus` deck (Objective 4). **Keyed** - the deck poses both questions and prints its own answer under each.

preamble.title: The scenario
preamble.html: The scenario. Your patient's mother had type 1 diabetes during the pregnancy with her, and she was born at 34 weeks following premature rupture of membranes, unrelated to the diabetes.

stem: Is she at increased risk for type 2 diabetes?

options.html: Yes - both the intrauterine glucose exposure and the prematurity raise her risk
Yes, but only because of the prematurity
No - maternal type 1 diabetes carries no type 2 risk for the child
No, provided maternal glycemic control was excellent

answer:
The correct answer is A. The deck: "Yes, technically; she had exposure to higher glucose in the womb (even with excellent maternal control), and premature birth is itself a risk factor for later metabolic dysfunction."

Two independent mechanisms stack here, which is why B is incomplete and D is the trap: ⭐ good maternal control reduces but does not abolish the intrauterine exposure.

This sits inside the deck's wider point that birth weight extremes at both ends - underweight and overweight infants alike - show increased metabolic risk decades later. The intrauterine environment is a T2DM risk factor in its own right, alongside inheritance, lifestyle, obesogenic diet and lower socio-economic status.

preamble.title: The scenario
preamble.html: The scenario. Your patient's mother had type 1 diabetes during the pregnancy with her, and she was born at 34 weeks following premature rupture of membranes, unrelated to the diabetes.

stem: Is she at increased risk for type 1 diabetes?

options.html: No, maternal type 1 diabetes confers no inherited risk

answer:
The correct answer is A. The deck: "Yes, slightly, but only about 3% lifetime risk. The inherited risk for Type 1 DM is much lower than for Type 2 DM."

⭐ This is the counterintuitive pairing worth holding. T1DM feels like "the genetic one" because it presents in childhood, but the inherited risk is far lower than for T2DM - monozygotic twin concordance is 50% in T1DM versus 90% in T2DM, and 40% of people with T2DM have an affected parent.

B is roughly the figure for two autoantibodies within 5 years, a different question entirely (see Q59). C is the monozygotic twin concordance, not the offspring risk.

lectureMeta: Q65, the third "POP QUIZ" in the `PreventionofDMComplications Hashmi 2024` deck. **Keyed** - the deck shows no answer slide but draws a **green highlight box** around the correct options in place. Previously banked as a module concept check; moved here because it is a patient case.
stem: A 31-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes for 20 years presents to your clinic. She has persistent microalbuminuria and does not wish to conceive. Which of the following medications to prevent diabetes complications would you suggest to her? (originally a check-all-that-apply poll over four drugs; rewritten as an MCQ over complete sets)

options.html: ASA 81 mg and an ACE inhibitor

answer:
The correct answer is C. ⭐ The deck highlights both option 3 and option 4 - she needs a statin and an ACE inhibitor, and picking either alone is a half-answer.

Why the ACEi: persistent microalbuminuria is diabetic nephropathy, and ACEi (or an ARB) is given for nephropathy even in a normotensive patient - the indication is renal protection, not blood pressure. The detail that she does not wish to conceive is not scene-setting: ACE inhibitors are teratogenic, so the stem is clearing the one contraindication that would otherwise block it.

Why the statin: the lecture's own criteria are age ≥ 30 AND diabetes > 15 years. She is 31 with 20 years of diabetes, so she qualifies on both counts.

A is wrong on type - metformin is not a T1DM drug and does nothing for microalbuminuria - and ASA is not given for primary prevention in a 31-year-old without established cardiovascular disease, which rules out D.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Mr. X is a 30-year-old man just diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. BMI 35, blood glucose 15 mmol/L, A1c 14%, normal creatinine, LDL 4.0 mmol/L, triglycerides 10 mmol/L.

stem: Mr. X has just been diagnosed. Which set of referrals and actions should follow at diagnosis?

options.html: Dietitian, diabetes nurse and optometry, with bloodwork every 3 months
A dietitian referral only, with annual bloodwork thereafter
Immediate referral to both nephrology and cardiology
Nothing until the diagnosis is confirmed on a second sample

answer:
The correct answer is A. The deck's at-diagnosis bundle:

  • Dietitian - low fat, high fibre, portion control
  • Diabetes education nurse - what diabetes is, how to test, how to manage a low, how to manage sick days
  • Optometrist - and note the patient can self-refer
  • Aim for very good glucose control in the next few months
  • A1c every ~3 months, with lipids and renal function
  • Check BP, and if not < 130/80, get him monitoring at the pharmacy or at home

⭐ Prevention starts at diagnosis, not at the first complication, and most of it is education and allied health rather than drugs. C inverts that - he has normal creatinine and no cardiac disease, so specialist referral is not indicated. D misapplies the confirmation rule: with a glucose of 15 and an A1c of 14%, the diagnosis is not in doubt.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Mr. X is a 30-year-old man just diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. BMI 35, blood glucose 15 mmol/L, A1c 14%, normal creatinine, LDL 4.0 mmol/L, triglycerides 10 mmol/L.

stem: What determines whether Mr. X starts on insulin rather than metformin?

options.html: Whether he is very symptomatic - thirst, polyuria, weight loss
His body mass index and waist circumference at diagnosis
His A1c value considered entirely on its own
Whether he has already failed a trial of lifestyle measures

answer:
The correct answer is A. The deck is explicit: insulin if very symptomatic (very thirsty, polyuria, yeast infections, weight loss, malaise); if not very symptomatic, and with no concern about liver or renal impairment, metformin is the usual first medication.

⭐ The trigger is the symptom burden, not the number. An A1c of 14% is alarming, but it is how he feels that decides whether he needs insulin now, which is why C is wrong.

The reassurance worth knowing: patients ask whether insulin can ever be stopped, and ⭐ the answer is potentially yes, depending on the glucose response. Starting insulin is not a life sentence in T2DM.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. Mr. X is a 30-year-old man just diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. BMI 35, blood glucose 15 mmol/L, A1c 14%, normal creatinine, LDL 4.0 mmol/L, triglycerides 10 mmol/L.

stem: Mr. X is now some years into treatment and attending regular visits. What should you both expect over that time?

options.html: That his medication needs will likely increase over time, and neither of you should be surprised
That once at target, he can be reviewed annually
That medication can be steadily withdrawn as his weight falls
That his A1c target should be tightened each year

answer:
The correct answer is A. Every 3-4 months: a weight check with encouragement of any weight loss, and a review of his home glucose record to reinforce the goals. And explicitly: ⭐ "he and you would not be surprised if BG control medication needs to be increased with time."

This is the progressive-disease point. T2DM involves ongoing beta-cell decline, so needing more medication is the expected course, not a failure - by the patient or by you. Framing it that way in advance is what stops escalation being heard as blame.

C is the mirror-image error; weight loss can genuinely reduce requirements, but it is not the expectation to set. D contradicts individualised targets, which loosen rather than tighten as complexity and frailty accumulate.

lecture: Module Case - Growth Failure in Hashimoto's Disease (Thyroid Physiology)
lectureMeta: Q69, the case illustration on the Hashimoto's slide of the `Thyroid Part 2 2023` deck. **Reasoned, not keyed** - the deck presents the case as an illustration and poses no question, so the stem and the answer are both written here, from [[01 - Thyroid and Parathyroid Gland Physiology]], which carries the same case.
stem: An 8-year-old with Hashimoto's disease is 3'6" with an immature body phenotype. One year after starting thyroid hormone replacement he is 4' tall with a normal body phenotype. What best explains the change? (originally a one-line case illustration on a teaching slide with no question posed; written up as an MCQ)

options.html: Thyroid hormone is permissive to growth hormone action, so replacing it restored growth that had been arrested
Levothyroxine directly stimulates the epiphyseal growth plate independently of growth hormone
The anti-TPO antibodies were suppressing growth hormone secretion directly
The growth was unrelated to treatment and reflects normal pubertal timing

answer:
A. In Hashimoto's disease, anti-TPO antibodies block the iodination of thyroglobulin, so T3 and T4 cannot be made and the child becomes hypothyroid.

Thyroid hormone is required for growth hormone secretion and permissive to its action. Without it, GH cannot drive linear growth however much is present, so growth arrests and skeletal maturation is delayed - hence the immature body phenotype at 3'6". Replace the T4 and the permissive signal returns: ⭐ six inches in a single year is catch-up growth, and the phenotype normalises with it.

The teaching point is recoverability. Untreated childhood hypothyroidism stunts linear growth and delays development, and ⭐ both are largely recoverable once T4 is replaced - which is what makes the delay worth catching.

B inverts the mechanism: the effect is permissive, exerted through GH, not a direct action on the plate. C invents an antibody target - anti-TPO acts on the thyroid, not the pituitary. D is ruled out by the timing and by an 8-year-old being pre-pubertal.

flags.title: Contrast this with congenital hypothyroidism
flags.html: Here the neurological outcome is intact because the deficiency began after early neural development. In maternal or congenital deficiency the same hormone is missing during neural development itself, and that damage is not recoverable - which is why maternal iodine deficiency is the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide. Same hormone, same deficiency, different window, different reversibility.

lecture: Concept Checks - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hyperparathyroidism and Hypoparathyroidism
lectureMeta: Source: the `Hyper Hypo Parathyroidism and Calcemia Slides` deck (Dr. Khan), 1 question. **Keyed** by the deck repeating the slide with the correct option bolded, with no written rationale, so the explanation is reasoned from [[04 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hyperparathyroidism and Hypoparathyroidism]].
stem: All of the following are treatments for hypoparathyroidism except:
answer:
The correct answer is D. ⭐ Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion, which is the last thing you want in a patient who is already hypocalcemic. They treat hypercalcemia, not hypoparathyroidism.

The drug that belongs here instead is a ⭐ thiazide, which reduces calcium excretion and lowers stone risk during long-term replacement. Thiazide for low calcium, loop for high calcium - deliberately counter-intuitive, because thiazides cause hypercalcemia in other settings.

The three real treatments: 1-2 g elemental calcium in divided doses; calcitriol 0.25 mcg b.i.d., monitoring calcium and phosphate and keeping 25-OH-D above 75 nmol/L; and rhPTH, approved in the US and Europe.

Whatever the regimen, aim for the low-normal range and monitor for ectopic calcification - renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis, head MRI for basal ganglia calcification, calcium-phosphate product under 4.4 mmol²/L².

stem: A patient of yours tells you that her sister recently underwent a hemithyroidectomy and was diagnosed with papillary thyroid carcinoma. She asks you what the prognosis is. You tell her:

options.html: That it is a benign tumour and she should be cured
That it is an aggressive tumour with a poor prognosis
That it is malignant and generally has a very good prognosis
That it is malignant and generally has a very good prognosis if a completion thyroidectomy and lymph node dissection are done
That it is malignant and generally has a very good prognosis if radioactive iodine therapy is given

answer:
The correct answer is C. The deck's own annotation: “Correct - can't say more about management as don't have details of report.”

  • A - “PTC is a malignant neoplasm; adenoma is a benign neoplasm.”
  • B - “PTC generally behaves indolently; anaplastic ca has a poor prognosis.”
  • D and E ⭐ attach a condition to the prognosis that you have no basis to state. They are not wrong that those treatments exist; they are wrong because ⭐ you do not have the pathology report, and the report is what decides whether completion thyroidectomy, nodal dissection or RAI is indicated at all.

The numbers behind C: PTC is the most common primary thyroid malignancy (85-90%) with 93% 10-year survival.

⭐ The teaching point is as much communication as pathology: give the prognosis you can support, and do not promise a management plan before the report is in.

stem: Akio has a 2 cm palpable enlarging thyroid nodule. TSH is normal. He has a family history of thyroid cancer in his father. Your next steps will be:
answer:
The correct answer is C. Transcribed from the deck's explanation slide.

“This nodule needs investigation given enlargement and family history of cancer. Remember to choose the least invasive and most cost-effective test first for a mass. Ultrasound is an important first step for a thyroid nodule to determine risk of malignancy and need for nodule sampling.”

  • A is ruled out by two risk features already present: ⭐ enlargement and a ⭐ first-degree family history.
  • E - “A CT scan would not be indicated as a first line test here, since thyroid nodule sampling cannot be performed with the CT scan and it is an expensive test.”
  • B - “Needle core biopsy (NCB) is not used to sample neck nodules in general, and especially thyroid nodules. The needle is large bore, and there is a risk of tumour seeding and hematoma. One exception is for lymphoma in a neck lymph node, where NCB is first line sampling in some patients.”
  • D puts surgery before risk stratification, inverting the pathway.

⭐ A normal TSH is what sends you to ultrasound rather than to a radioactive iodine scan - a low TSH would have gone to RAI first.

stem: The imaging report indicates a TI-RADS score of 4. What type of nodule sampling would you choose for Akio?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Transcribed from the deck's explanation slide.

“For thyroid, which is a vascular organ, FNAB is the preferred biopsy type for sampling a nodule. As well, given the risk of tumour seeding and hematoma formation the large bore needles (needle core biopsy) would be avoided if possible.”

  • B and D - “Incisional biopsies are not performed for thyroid, due to the vascularity of the organ, such that surgery would either be a lobectomy or thyroidectomy.”
  • A - “Punch biopsy is used only for skin related lesions, not for deep lesions under the skin.”
  • E - “FNAB needs to be performed first for risk stratification before any decision about surgery usually.”

⭐ Vascularity is the reason for all of it. It is why a fine needle is right, why a large-bore core needle risks hematoma and seeding, and why there is no such thing as a partial cut into the thyroid.

stem: Kiaria has a 2.7 cm mildly symptomatic thyroid nodule and a normal TSH. The ultrasound report indicates a mixed cyst with a TI-RADS score of 2. You remove clear fluid with a fine needle aspiration biopsy and the cyst disappears. On follow-up the cyst does not reappear. The most likely diagnosis is:
answer:
The correct answer is B. Transcribed from the deck's explanation slide.

“With disappearance of the cyst with aspiration, a not suspicious TIRADs score and no reappearance of the cyst, this is in keeping with a benign cyst.”

  • A - “An abscess is unusual in the thyroid, and the aspirate should reveal pus. The clinical features do not indicate the classic signs of inflammation.” The fluid here was clear.
  • C - “Papillary carcinoma can be cystic, but would show increase in size on follow-up and some solid component.”
  • D - “An adenoma, which can be cystic would not disappear with aspiration in that there would be a solid component left.”
  • E - “Lymphoma is typically firm solid tissue, and not a cyst.”

⭐ Three findings have to line up, and all three are in the stem: clear fluid, complete disappearance, and no recurrence. A surviving solid component is what would have pushed this to C or D.

stem:
Ms. Smith is a 65-year-old lady who is being assessed for osteoporosis. The diagnosis of osteoporosis can be made if:

  1. Her BMD T-score is < −2.5
  2. She has had a skull fracture
  3. She has had a hip fracture as a result of a fall from standing height
answer:
The correct answer is D. Two of the three statements are diagnostic, and the one that is not is the point of the question.

  • 1 is diagnostic. A T-score ≤ −2.5 makes the diagnosis on its own.
  • 3 is diagnostic. A hip fracture from a fall from standing height is a fragility fracture, and ⭐ a fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis irrespective of the BMD.
  • 2 is not. ⭐ The definition explicitly EXCLUDES fractures of the skull, hands, feet and ankles, and any fracture involving real trauma. A skull fracture tells you nothing about bone quality.

The third route to the diagnosis, not tested here, is a 10-year fracture risk above 20% with no fragility fracture and a T-score above −2.5.

⭐ The exclusion list is the examinable part. “Fragility fracture” is not “any fracture” - those sites are excluded precisely because they break for reasons other than low bone mass.

stem: What percentage of patients are treated for osteoporosis following a hip fracture in Canada?
answer:
The correct answer is C, 15%.

The comparison the deck draws is why the number matters: ⭐ 15% of patients are treated for osteoporosis after a fracture, against 80% who are started on a beta blocker after a heart attack. The slide's framing is “a fracture is to osteoporosis what a heart attack is to cardiovascular disease” - the same sentinel event, treated at a fifth of the rate.

A, 80%, is the beta-blocker figure, which is what makes it the strongest distractor.

The consequences of the gap: over age 50 the lifetime risk of hip fracture is 12.1%, and one year after a hip fracture 80% cannot carry out more than one IADL, 40% cannot walk independently, and ⭐ 29% are dead. Five-year mortality is 23.5% after hip fracture and 15.7% after vertebral fracture.

stem: Which of these is not included in calculating fracture risk using FRAX?
answer:
The correct answer is B. ⭐ FRAX asks about a parental history of HIP fracture, not vertebral fracture.

Everything else listed is a genuine FRAX input: personal prior fracture, current smoking, alcohol of 3 or more units daily, and height and weight (needed for BMI). Its other inputs are age, sex, glucocorticoid use, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary osteoporosis, and optionally femoral neck BMD.

The distractor works by swapping one word in a real risk factor, which is the most common way this kind of question is built.

Easy to conflate, and worth keeping separate: prior fragility fracture after age 40 and prolonged corticosteroid therapy each move the patient up one risk category after the risk is calculated, and prior hip or vertebral fracture, or more than one non-vertebral fragility fracture, puts them straight into high risk. Those are modifiers on the output, not inputs to the calculation.

stem: Mrs. Jones is 65 years old and presents for assessment of osteoporosis. The presence of which of these factors would NOT warrant consideration of pharmacologic therapy?
answer:
The correct answer is B. ⭐ A T-score above −2.5 is, on its own, a reason NOT to treat - it is the threshold defining the no-treatment band when nothing else is present.

  • A and D - ⭐ a hip or vertebral fracture is a strong recommendation to treat, and carries more weight still if the fracture was within the last 2 years. A fragility fracture also makes the diagnosis outright, whatever the BMD shows.
  • C - a 10-year risk above 15% puts her at least in the moderate band, where treatment is suggested; above 20% it is recommended.

B is only a reason not to treat in isolation, and that is the trap: Mrs. Jones could have a T-score above −2.5 and still need treatment if she has had a fragility fracture or her calculated risk is high. ⭐ BMD is a surrogate for fracture, not the diagnosis itself, which is exactly why the fracture-based routes to treatment exist alongside it.

stem: Mrs. Davidson was on treatment with denosumab for 5 years, and has recently sustained a hip fracture. She received her injections on time, without any delays or missed treatments. She has no contraindications for any osteoporosis treatments. Which of the following would be the best treatment option for her?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Read the stem carefully: she took the drug correctly, on schedule, for 5 years, and fractured her hip anyway. That is ⭐ failure of antiresorptive therapy, one of the three named indications for bone-forming therapy - alongside a recent severe vertebral fracture and more than 2 vertebral fractures with a T-score below −2.5. Adherence is stated explicitly so that you cannot explain the fracture away as a missed dose.

  • A repeats a strategy that has already demonstrably failed in this patient.
  • B swaps one antiresorptive for another, which does not change the class that failed.
  • C is the worst option here: ⭐ raloxifene has no hip fracture data at all. It covers the spine only, so it is the wrong drug in a patient whose problem is a hip.
  • D moves her to an anabolic agent, and ⭐ romosozumab is the anabolic with hip fracture benefit (versus alendronate) - whereas teriparatide has no hip data either.

One thing not to forget after choosing D: ⭐ anabolic therapy must be followed by an antiresorptive, after 1 year for romosozumab. Also worth weighing first: romosozumab carries a cardiovascular signal (MI, stroke, death), and stopping denosumab without a follow-on antiresorptive risks rapid bone loss.

stem: Mrs. Smith is a 65-year-old lady who was on alendronate treatment for 10 years. She had aching pain in her thigh for 6 months and sustained an atypical femoral fracture as a result of no trauma, which required surgical repair. Her fracture risk remains high over the next 10 years. Her alendronate has been stopped. Which among these would be used for treatment of osteoporosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

She has had an atypical femoral fracture on long-term alendronate. ⭐ AFF is an adverse effect of BOTH the bisphosphonates AND denosumab, so every antiresorptive on this list is off the table:

  • B and D are more bisphosphonates - the same class that caused it, and bisphosphonates stay bound in bone, so the risk does not reset when you switch within the class.
  • A is a different class but shares the AFF risk.
  • C is anabolic, does not carry the AFF risk, and her fracture risk remains high, so she cannot be left on nothing.

⭐ The 6 months of aching thigh pain was the warning sign, present in 70% of AFF patients, and it is why that complaint in anyone on long-term therapy is taken seriously rather than treated as arthritis.

Also relevant: ⭐ teriparatide is not associated with ONJ and may even help treat it. Its own limits are no hip fracture data, it must be followed by an antiresorptive after 2 years, and it is contraindicated in hypercalcemia, eGFR under 30, and metabolic bone disease.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with a history of celiac disease presents with a history of falls, muscle weakness, and the x-ray shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Atypical fractures due to bisphosphonate use
Pseudofractures due to vitamin D deficiency
Femoral neck fracture due to osteoporosis

answer:
The correct answer is B, keyed by the Elentra module, which asks this question identically. The slide deck gives it no answer slide, no bolded option and no highlight box, so on the deck alone it looked unkeyed. The module settles it. The reasoning below is written from the lecture note, since neither source gives a rationale.

Three features in the stem point the same way, and none of them fits the alternatives.

  • ⭐ Celiac disease is the deck's named common cause of osteomalacia, because vitamin D is fat-soluble and malabsorbed.
  • ⭐ Proximal muscle weakness (myopathy) that contributes to falls is the osteomalacia feature that osteoporosis does not share. This is the most useful discriminator between the two, since they can look alike on x-ray and on BMD.
  • ⭐ Pseudofractures - healed microfractures - are the radiological hallmark of osteomalacia.

A requires a drug she is not on, and at 23 would be extraordinary. C names a single acute fracture, which explains neither the weakness nor the falls - and osteomalacia is routinely mistaken for osteoporosis, which is precisely the error this option offers. The tell is that osteomalacia has overt symptoms while osteoporosis is indolent.

Confirmatory labs: ↓ calcium, ↓ phosphate, ↑ ALP, ↑ PTH, ↓ 25-OH-D and ↓ urine calcium. ⭐ Both calcium and phosphate being low separates osteomalacia from Paget's, where both are normal.

stem: You are seeing a patient with Paget's disease involving the left femur. His ALP is 3 times greater than the upper limit of normal. Which of the following would be the best treatment for this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

  • ⭐ Zoledronate is the treatment, and IV zoledronate is better than an oral bisphosphonate in Paget's - which is what puts it ahead of B.
  • ⭐ A is actively contraindicated. Bone-forming agents must not be used in Paget's, because the disease already is disordered bone formation: increased osteoclastic resorption, followed by osteoblasts laying down structurally abnormal, fragile bone. Stimulating that further is the opposite of the goal.
  • D - denosumab has not been studied in Paget's.
  • Calcitonin is a real option the deck lists, but it loses effectiveness after a few treatments, so it belongs early and only for pain.

The raised ALP is why this patient is treated at all. ⭐ Even an asymptomatic patient is treated when there is evidence of active disease - a raised ALP or scintigraphy showing active lesions - plus disease in the skull, long bones, spine, or bone abutting a joint. A femur is a long bone, so he qualifies on both counts.

The other two treatment triggers: ⭐ a surgical procedure planned in a pagetic site (the lesions are vascular and can hemorrhage) and ⭐ coexisting congestive heart failure, which Paget's vascularity can worsen. ALP also doubles as the monitoring marker on treatment.

stem: A 17-year-old woman with a history of osteogenesis imperfecta type 1 presents for a routine annual evaluation. She has had 5 fractures of various long bones in the last year, without any atypical fractures and without trauma. She is having regular menstrual periods and has normal vitamin D levels. What is the most appropriate treatment for her?
answer:
The correct answer is D. ⭐ IV bisphosphonates are the mainstay of treatment for osteogenesis imperfecta, and zoledronate is the IV bisphosphonate.

She meets the criteria to be treated: the indications are long bone deformities, vertebral compression fractures, or ⭐ more than 3 fractures per year - and she has had 5.

The stem's negatives are doing deliberate work, ruling out the alternative explanations for fractures at her age:

  • no atypical fractures and no trauma - not drug-induced AFF, not simple injury
  • regular menstrual periods - not hypoestrogenic bone loss, which also removes the rationale for C
  • normal vitamin D - not osteomalacia on top of the OI

A is anabolic but is not the established treatment in OI, and the underlying defect is qualitative, not quantitative: ⭐ OI is a lack of, or poorly formed, type I collagen (COL1A1 and COL1A2, 85-90% of cases), so building more of the same defective matrix is not the fix. B is not the mainstay either.

The optimal duration of bisphosphonate therapy in OI has not been studied. Her type 1 disease carries a normal life span - type 2 is lethal in the perinatal period.

lecture: Module Case - The Worked Thyroid Nodule (Pathology of Thyroid Masses)
lectureMeta: Source: the worked case opening the `Wehrli_ThyroidGlandPathology_slides_nv` deck. **Reasoned, not keyed** - the deck walks the case through the diagnostic pathway to show what an appropriate workup looks like and poses no question, so the stem and the answer are both written from [[05 - Pathology of Thyroid Masses]]. Banked as a case rather than a concept check because a patient is presented and reasoned through.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 42-year-old female with no risk factors and no family history has a lump in her neck, present and slowly enlarging over 6 months, causing some difficulty swallowing. She reports no symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. On examination there is a solitary, firm but not hard, 2-3 cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe, with no neck adenopathy and no signs of thyrotoxicosis. TSH is normal. Ultrasound confirms a solitary 3.2 cm nodule, TI-RADS 3. FNA is satisfactory and returns FLUS (follicular lesion of undetermined significance). After discussion she elected to undergo a hemithyroidectomy.

stem: Her ultrasound is low-risk (TI-RADS 3) and her cytology is FLUS. On the risk-adapted pathway, what makes hemithyroidectomy a defensible choice here rather than simple surveillance? (originally a worked case illustration with no question posed; written up as an MCQ)

options.html: FLUS is indeterminate, and the nodule is symptomatic and enlarging
A TI-RADS 3 nodule always requires excision regardless of cytology
FLUS is a malignant result, so completion thyroidectomy is mandated
Her normal TSH excludes a benign cause, leaving surgery as the only option

answer:
A. Two of the four risk-adapted management routes point at surgery, and neither of them is “the ultrasound said so”.

FLUS is an indeterminate Bethesda result, not benign and not malignant. The routes that apply are surgery (for malignancy, ⭐ some indeterminate cytology, or ⭐ benign but symptomatic) and repeat biopsy (insufficient or some indeterminate cytology). ⭐ She qualifies twice over: indeterminate cytology AND a symptomatic, enlarging nodule. Surveillance is the answer for low-risk ultrasound plus benign cytology, which is not what she has.

There is a deeper reason surgery resolves this and a repeat FNA might not. ⭐ FNA cannot distinguish a follicular adenoma from a follicular carcinoma - their nuclei are identical, and only capsular or vascular invasion separates them, visible only in the resected specimen. Repeating the aspirate would sample the same cells and return the same uncertainty. This is the opposite of papillary carcinoma, whose nuclear features are diagnostic on FNA.

  • B inverts the pathway. TI-RADS decides whether to biopsy, not whether to operate; a TR3 with benign cytology gets clinical follow-up only.
  • C misreads the cytology. FLUS is indeterminate. Bethesda III and IV carry 12-30% and 23-34% risk of malignancy - real, but a long way from the 97-100% of a Bethesda VI.
  • D misuses the TSH. ⭐ A normal TSH excludes nothing malignant - it establishes she is euthyroid, and its role here is to send her to ultrasound rather than a radioactive iodine scan. A low TSH would have gone to RAI, where a hot nodule is benign.

What the operation then delivers, and why the deck opens with this case: the surgical pathology report gives the definitive diagnosis, the elements needed for staging and prognosis, and the answer to whether further management is needed. ⭐ Cytology stratifies; only the specimen stages.

lecture: Module Case - Hypercalcemia Found on an Osteoporosis Workup (Hyperparathyroidism)
lectureMeta: Source: the case study in the `Hyper Hypo Parathyroidism and Calcemia Slides` deck (Dr. Khan). **Reasoned, not keyed** - the deck advances the case across four slides, asking “What next?” and “Diagnosis? Further studies?” without stating an answer, so the reasoning is written from [[04 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hyperparathyroidism and Hypoparathyroidism]] and the deck's own subsequent slides.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 65-year-old woman presents for assessment of osteoporosis. She complains of back pain, and has fractured her right radius and ulna at age 52 and her left ulna at 61. She had a hysterectomy at 35. Evaluation shows normal thyroid function and normal renal function, with Ca 2.95 mmol/L and albumin 45 g/L. Repeat testing gives Ca 2.73 mmol/L, phosphate 0.69 mmol/L, PTH 14 pmol/L (reference 1.6-6.9) and 25-OH vitamin D 70 nmol/L.

stem: Her repeat panel shows a high calcium with a clearly elevated PTH and a low phosphate. What is the diagnosis, and which single further test separates it from its main mimic? (originally a multi-slide case study whose closing slides ask “Diagnosis? Further studies?” without stating an answer; written up as an MCQ)

options.html: Primary hyperparathyroidism, separated from FHH by a 24-hour urine collection for calcium and creatinine to calculate the fractional excretion of calcium
Secondary hyperparathyroidism, separated from primary disease by a 25-OH vitamin D level
Hypercalcemia of malignancy, separated from parathyroid disease by a PTHrP level
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism, separated from primary disease by an eGFR

answer:
A. The four-analyte pattern names the disease, and the urine names the mimic.

First, correct the calcium for albumin - her albumin is 45, so the correction is small and the calcium is genuinely high. Then: calcium 2.73 (high), PTH 14 against a ceiling of 6.9 (⭐ inappropriately high in the face of hypercalcemia), phosphate 0.69 (low, because ⭐ PTH is phosphaturic), and 25-OH-D 70, which rules out vitamin D deficiency as the driver.

⭐ A high calcium with a high PTH is the definition of primary hyperparathyroidism - a normal gland would have switched off. 80% are a single parathyroid adenoma.

Why the urine test. FHH produces the same picture, because an inactivating CaSR mutation shifts the calcium-PTH curve right. The urine separates them: ⭐ FECa < 0.01 means FHH, ⭐ > 0.02 means likely primary hyperparathyroidism, and 20% of FHH lands in the 0.01-0.02 overlap, where nothing is decided. The result only means something off thiazides for 3 months, with a normal magnesium and a 25-OH-D above 50 - hers is 70, so that condition is met.

  • B - secondary hyperparathyroidism runs a normal or low-normal calcium. Her renal function is normal and her vitamin D adequate, so there is nothing for the gland to be reacting to.
  • C - in hypercalcemia of malignancy the PTH is suppressed, because the driver is PTHrP or osteolysis. Her PTH is elevated, which excludes the whole PTH-independent branch. PTHrP would be the right test if PTH had come back low.
  • D - tertiary hyperparathyroidism arises on long-standing CKD and runs a high phosphate. ⭐ Her phosphate is LOW and her renal function normal, which is the cleanest way to tell primary from tertiary when both show a high calcium.

Why she was found at all. She came in for osteoporosis, with a fragility fracture history and back pain. ⭐ Chronic hypercalcemia from primary hyperPTH resorbs bone, and this is the presentation that catches it. She also meets surgical criteria on more than one count once confirmed. And while she is being worked up: ⭐ keep her hydrated and avoid thiazides and lithium.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents with tremor and heat intolerance, but is otherwise well. No neck pain or tenderness. No family history of autoimmune disease. Thyroid is mildly enlarged, more on the right than left, with no definite nodule. There is no evidence of Graves' orbitopathy or dermopathy. TSH is <0.01 (0.3-4.5), FT4 is 28 (11-22), FT3 is 11.0 (3.5-6.5). What tests would you order?

options.html: Pituitary hormone assessment and pituitary MRI

answer:
The correct answer is A. The biochemistry has already made the diagnosis: TSH suppressed with both free hormones high is overt thyrotoxicosis. What is missing is why, and ⭐ RAI uptake and scan is the single best test for the etiology of thyrotoxicosis.

Read the negatives in the stem, because they are what remove the shortcut:

  • no family history of autoimmune disease, no orbitopathy or dermopathy, and an asymmetric goiter with no definite nodule. ⭐ Graves is symmetric and usually carries eye signs; asymmetry points at autonomous nodular tissue (TMNG or a toxic adenoma). Without the clinical picture of Graves you cannot diagnose it on signs alone, so imaging has to settle it
  • no neck pain or tenderness argues against subacute thyroiditis

C is the wrong antibody in the wrong direction: anti-TPO is a hypothyroid test, and even there it rarely changes management. B, ultrasound, tells you about structure, not about whether the gland is synthesizing. D would be for central disease, which is excluded here because ⭐ the TSH is suppressed in the presence of high hormone, which is exactly the appropriate pituitary response.
