stem: A healthy 68-year-old man presents with dry skin, cold intolerance and mild fatigue. No clear cause is determined after appropriate investigations. Initial TSH is 7.5 (0.35-4.5), repeat TSH 8.4, FT4 14 (11-22). He requests a trial of levothyroxine. After 75 mcg for 3 months he feels no change and TSH is 2.5. What do you recommend?

options.html: Increase the dose to 100 mcg daily and repeat TSH in 6 weeks
Decrease the dose to 50 mcg and repeat the TSH in 6 weeks
Continue current levothyroxine and monitor TSH yearly
Stop levothyroxine and monitor for overt hypothyroidism

answer:
The correct answer is D. This is subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH raised, FT4 normal) treated as a therapeutic trial, and ⭐ the rule for a trial is that it ends if nothing changes.

He has now been biochemically euthyroid on treatment (TSH 2.5) for 3 months and feels no different. That is the trial answering its own question: his symptoms were not from his thyroid. ⭐ Stop after 3 months of no response and watch for progression to overt disease instead.

The other options all treat the number rather than the patient:

  • A chases a TSH that is already normal, which would push him toward iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis
  • B keeps him on a drug that has demonstrably done nothing
  • C commits a 68-year-old to lifelong therapy on no evidence of benefit

⭐ There is no evidence of benefit in treating subclinical hypothyroidism, with the exceptions being pregnancy, TSH > 10, anti-TPO positive, and exactly this kind of time-limited symptomatic trial. His TSH of 7.5-8.4 is below 10, so nothing else here argued for treating him indefinitely.

stem: A 51-year-old woman with obesity and hypothyroidism has adopted a healthier lifestyle and lost 10% of her body weight. She has developed a mild tremor and increased heat intolerance with worse and more frequent menopausal hot flashes. You measure TSH and it is <0.01 (0.3-4.5); the lab reflexively adds FT4, which is 27 (11-22). What do you suggest?

options.html: Stay on the same dose of levothyroxine and start HRT
Decrease the levothyroxine dose and repeat TSH in 2 weeks
Decrease the levothyroxine dose and repeat TSH in 6 weeks
Measure anti-TPO antibodies and order a thyroid ultrasound

answer:
The correct answer is C. She is over-replaced. ⭐ levothyroxine is weight-based at roughly 1.5 mcg/kg/day, so losing 10% of her body weight makes a dose that used to be right now excessive, and the tremor, heat intolerance and worsened flushes are iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis rather than menopause.

The discriminator between B and C is the interval, and it comes from one number: ⭐ levothyroxine's half-life is 1 week, so a level checked at 2 weeks has not reached steady state and will mislead you into another dose change. Recheck at 6 weeks, which is the same interval used for every other titration.

A treats the symptom as menopausal and leaves her thyrotoxic. D investigates a diagnosis she already has, and ⚠ anti-TPO and ultrasound almost never change management in hypothyroidism — they certainly do not explain a suppressed TSH in someone taking thyroid hormone.

stem: A 38-year-old healthy woman presents with a tender thyroid and pain on swallowing 3 weeks after a mild respiratory infection. She is having heat intolerance, tremor and tachycardia with bothersome palpitations, but is hemodynamically stable. What treatment do you recommend?

options.html: Beta blocker pending radioactive iodine ablation

answer:
The correct answer is D. The stem describes subacute (post-viral) thyroiditis: ⭐ a tender, painful thyroid with odynophagia, 3 weeks after a respiratory infection. Tenderness is the giveaway — post-partum and autoimmune thyroiditis are painless.

⭐ This is a LEAKAGE thyrotoxicosis, not a production one. The gland is not synthesizing hormone, it is releasing preformed hormone as it is damaged, which is why treatment is supportive only:

  • beta blocker for the palpitations, tachycardia and tremor
  • NSAID for the pain

A is the error the question is built around: ⭐ thionamides block synthesis, and synthesis is not the problem, so methimazole does nothing here. B is worse — RAI needs iodine uptake, and uptake in thyroiditis is low. E ignores treatable symptoms. C is not wrong so much as premature: ⭐ glucocorticoids are the second step, reserved for pain the NSAID does not control.

The thing to warn her about: watch for the hypothyroid phase as the gland recovers.

stem: A 24-year-old healthy man presents concerned that his Fitbit often reads his heart rate in the 50s. He read on the internet that this can be caused by hypothyroidism and is worried he might have it, because his mother has hypothyroidism. His TSH comes back 2.0 (0.3-4.5). What do you suggest?

options.html: FT4 to rule out central hypothyroidism

answer:
The correct answer is A. ⭐ A normal TSH rules out thyroid dysfunction, and that is the end of the workup in someone with no reason to suspect pituitary disease. He has a family history, which is a legitimate reason to check a TSH periodically, and that is all this needs.

The distractors are three different ways of not accepting a normal result:

  • B — anti-TPO in a euthyroid man changes nothing. It is sensitive but not specific, and it almost never influences a clinical decision
  • C — ultrasound answers a structural question. He has no nodule and no mass
  • D — this is the one worth thinking about, because ⭐ central hypothyroidism is the single exception to "stop at a normal TSH". But it applies when there are other pituitary deficiencies or a known pituitary mass, and he has neither. A fit 24-year-old with a resting pulse in the 50s is describing athletic bradycardia, not pituitary failure

This is also a Choosing Wisely question: ⭐ only order tests that will change management, and none of B, C or D would.

stem: A 32-year-old healthy woman presents with palpitations, heat intolerance, 5 kg weight loss in the last month, normal appetite, tremor and anxiety. Thyroid is symmetrically moderately enlarged. TSH is <0.01 (0.35-4.5), FT4 is 44 (11-22), FT3 is 19.2 (3.5-6.5). Her mother and two sisters have Hashimoto's disease. You plan to prescribe methimazole. What is the next best step?

options.html: Check anti-TPO and TSH receptor antibody levels
Pregnancy test, liver enzymes and a complete blood count

answer:
The correct answer is D. Note what the stem has already settled: a young woman, symmetric goiter, strong family history of autoimmune thyroid disease, florid thyrotoxicosis. ⭐ When clinical suspicion of Graves disease is high enough you may diagnose it on signs and symptoms alone, and the question tells you the plan is already made. So the next step is not more diagnosis, it is the safety workup before starting the drug.

Each of the three tests maps onto a specific hazard of methimazole:

  • ⭐ Pregnancy test — thionamides can cause birth defects, and she is 32 with no contraception mentioned
  • ⭐ Liver enzymes — liver dysfunction is a recognised serious adverse effect
  • ⭐ Complete blood count — a baseline count before a drug whose feared complication is agranulocytosis

A and C would confirm what is already clinically clear. B is the sharper trap: RAI uptake would tell you the etiology, but it is ⛔ contraindicated in pregnancy, and you have not yet excluded pregnancy — which is precisely the test in option D.

stem: A 44-year-old man presents with peripheral vision loss and presyncope and is found to have a 2 cm pituitary adenoma and adrenal insufficiency. He is started on hydrocortisone and booked for surgery. He still feels fatigue and is developing constipation and cold intolerance. What tests would you order?
answer:
The correct answer is B. This is ⭐ the one situation where TSH alone is not enough. He has a known pituitary mass and an established second pituitary deficiency (adrenal insufficiency), and he is now describing hypothyroid symptoms. That is central hypothyroidism until proven otherwise.

⚠ ⭐ In central disease the TSH moves WITH the hormone, or not at all — it can be low or normal alongside a low FT4, because the pituitary making the TSH is the broken part. Ordering A, TSH alone, would return a normal-looking number and falsely reassure you.

C adds an antibody test for autoimmune thyroid destruction, which is not the mechanism here. D adds a structural test for a gland that is structurally fine.

⚠ One more thing the stem is quietly checking: he was started on hydrocortisone first. That is the correct order, because ⭐ giving levothyroxine in uncorrected adrenal insufficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis by increasing cortisol metabolism.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding parathyroid hormone and vitamin D metabolism is FALSE?

options.html: PTH is released in response to a low calcium concentration in blood
PTH causes conversion of 25-hydroxy to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Major sources of vitamin D include exposure to sunlight or dietary sources
PTH promotes absorption of calcium and phosphate in the kidney

answer:
The correct answer is D, and it is false for two separate reasons, either of which is enough:

  • ⭐ PTH is PHOSPHATURIC. It increases renal phosphate excretion. Pairing calcium and phosphate as if PTH retained both is the classic error, and it is what separates PTH from vitamin D, which does increase reabsorption of both
  • the word absorption belongs to the gut, not the kidney; the kidney reabsorbs

The other three are all true:

  • A — the calcium-sensing receptor on the chief cell is quiet when calcium falls, and PTH is released
  • B — PTH raises 1α-hydroxylase activity in the kidney, the rate-limiting, PTH-regulated step converting calcifediol to calcitriol
  • C — sunlight on 7-dehydrocholesterol and diet are the two sources

⭐ And note what B implies: PTH's effect on gut calcium is entirely INDIRECT, through calcitriol, because there are no PTH receptors in the GI tract at all.

stem: All of the following are indications for surgical treatment for patients with primary hyperparathyroidism except:

options.html: Corrected calcium > 0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit of normal

answer:
The correct answer is D, and the trap is that ⭐ age is an indication, but in the opposite direction: it is age UNDER 50 that argues for parathyroidectomy, not age over 60.

The logic is that a younger patient has decades of chronic hypercalcemia ahead of them, so the cumulative renal and skeletal cost of leaving it is high. Conversely, ⭐ an asymptomatic patient over 50 is generally NOT treated.

The full indication list, of which A, B and C are three:

  • calcium > 0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit
  • bone mineral density T-score < −2.5 at lumbar spine, femoral neck, total hip or ⅓ radius
  • vertebral fracture, and fragility fractures generally
  • creatinine clearance < 60 mL/min
  • 24-hour urine calcium > 10 mmol/day with raised stone risk
  • nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis
  • ⭐ age < 50

stem: Which is the most specific test for hypocalcemia?
answer:
The correct answer is B. ⭐ Trousseau's sign is the more specific of the two.

  • Trousseau's sign — inflate a blood pressure cuff above systolic for about 3 minutes and the hand goes into carpopedal spasm. Occluding the limb provokes the latent neuromuscular irritability that the low calcium has created, and it is uncommon in people with normal calcium
  • Chvostek's sign — tapping over the facial nerve twitches the lip or face. ⚠ It appears in a substantial minority of people with entirely normal calcium, which is what costs it specificity

Both come from the same mechanism: ⭐ less calcium interacting with sodium channels means cells depolarize more easily, so nerves and muscle become hyperexcitable. That single idea also explains the rest of CATS go Numb — convulsions, arrhythmia, tetany, spasm and stridor, and perioral numbness.

Worth holding onto for the ward: these are the signs of mild hypocalcemia. The severe picture is frank tetany, laryngeal spasm, seizures and a prolonged QT.

lectureMeta: Q109-110, from the Elentra module titled `P1 Clinical Presentation & Investigation of Thyroid Masses`. ⚠ **The module is titled "P1"**, so it may be the PoM 1 version of this lecture, but its content is what [[05 - Pathology of Thyroid Masses]] teaches in week 2, and **a question is filed under the week whose lectures it tests**, so it sits here. The module holds 5 questions; ⚠ **three of them (Akio ×2, Kiaria) are the same questions already banked from the slide deck as Q87-89** and are not banked twice. Both below were **select-all** in the module and are rewritten as single-answer MCQs over complete sets, per the house rule.
stem: Which of the following are common differentials for a thyroid mass? (originally a select-all-that-apply; rewritten as an MCQ over complete sets)

options.html: All of cyst, adenoma, hyperplasia, Hashimoto's, carcinoma and lymphoma are equally common

answer:
The correct answer is A. The module's four correct selections were cyst, adenoma, hyperplasia/sporadic and Hashimoto's thyroiditis; carcinoma and lymphoma were deliberately not selected.

⭐ The question is about what is COMMON, not about what matters most. Carcinoma and lymphoma belong on the differential of a thyroid mass, but they belong on the life-threatening and urgent columns rather than the common one:

| Common | Life / QoL threatening | Urgent | | --- | --- | --- | | hyperplasia / sporadic · cyst · Hashimoto's (real nodules and pseudonodules) · adenoma | differentiated (papillary, follicular) · poorly differentiated · medullary carcinoma | anaplastic carcinoma · lymphoma |

⭐ Most thyroid nodules are benign — a 0.1% annual incidence and a 10% lifetime probability — which is the frame the whole risk-adapted pathway is built on. D fails for that reason alone.

flags.title: Do not read "common" as "safe"
flags.html: Sorting the differential by frequency is a triage tool, not a reassurance. The entire point of TI-RADS and Bethesda is that the uncommon diagnoses are the ones the workup exists to exclude.

stem: Which of the following are included in the ACR TI-RADS? (originally a select-all-that-apply; rewritten as an MCQ over complete sets)

options.html: Composition, shape and margin, but not size

answer:
The correct answer is A. The module's correct selections were composition, shape and margin; ⚠ ⭐ size was deliberately not selected.

TI-RADS scores what a nodule looks like, not how big it is. The ACR categories are composition (cystic, spongiform, mixed, solid), echogenicity, shape (specifically taller-than-wide), margin (smooth, ill-defined, lobulated, extra-thyroidal extension) and echogenic foci (including microcalcifications). Points across those give the TR level.

⭐ Size enters afterwards, as the threshold for what to do about a given TR level — it decides whether to biopsy or to follow, not how suspicious the nodule is. That distinction is the whole point of the question: a small nodule with suspicious features can outrank a large bland one.

It is also why the pathway runs TSH → ultrasound and TI-RADS → FNAB → Bethesda, with the imaging risk and the cytology risk read together. A benign cytology sitting under a TR5 ultrasound is discordant, and the answer to discordance is repeat the biopsy, not accept the reassuring half.

stem: What type of epithelium lines the labia majora?
answer:
The correct answer is E. ⭐ The labia majora are skin: keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with hair follicles and eccrine, apocrine and sebaceous glands.

⭐ C is the labia minora, and the pair is the highest-yield contrast in vulvar histology: keratinized with adnexa (majora) versus non-keratinized with usually NO adnexal structures (minora).

Being skin is also what gives the majora their pathology: cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma and lichen sclerosus, the equivalent of BXO on the penis.

stem: What are the layers of the vaginal wall? (originally a select-all-that-apply; rewritten as an MCQ over complete sets)
answer:
The correct answer is A. The vagina has mucosa → muscularis → adventitia:

  • mucosa — non-keratinizing squamous epithelium, a barrier
  • muscularis — thick smooth muscle
  • ⭐ adventitia — loose connective tissue with elastic fibres

⭐ The discriminator is the outer layer. An adventitia is loose connective tissue anchoring an organ to its surroundings; a serosa is a peritoneal covering. The vagina is not draped in peritoneum, so it has the former.

B and C import myometrium and endometrium, which are uterine. D is the near-miss, correct until its final word.

stem: Where is the transformation zone located in the gynecologic tract?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Transcribed from the module: "The transformation zone is located in the uterine cervix and marks the transition of squamous epithelium (ectocervix) to glandular epithelium (endocervix)."

⭐ It matters because it is the most common site of cervical cancer, and because both epithelia meet there, the cancer can be either squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma. A zone of squamous metaplasia — one mature epithelium replacing another — is where malignant transformation is most likely.

stem: What cell types are found in the cervical transformation zone? (originally a select-all-that-apply; rewritten as an MCQ over complete sets)

options.html: Squamous metaplasia, squamous epithelium and columnar (glandular) epithelium

answer:
The correct answer is A. All three of squamous metaplasia, squamous epithelium and columnar (glandular) epithelium are present; ⚠ urothelium is not — that is bladder and ureter.

⭐ The zone contains all three because it is a border in motion. The ectocervix brings non-keratinizing squamous, the endocervix brings mucus-secreting columnar, and where the junction has migrated, columnar has been replaced by squamous metaplasia. Finding all three together is what defines the zone histologically.

stem: Match the type of endometrium with the phase of the menstrual cycle. (originally a drag-and-drop matching activity; rewritten as an MCQ whose options are complete mappings)

options.html: Secretory → luteal phase · proliferative → follicular phase
Secretory → follicular phase · proliferative → luteal phase
Secretory → luteal phase · proliferative → menstrual phase
Secretory → follicular phase · proliferative → menstrual phase

answer:
The correct answer is A, which is the module's own pairing: secretory endometrium ↔ luteal phase, proliferative endometrium ↔ follicular phase.

Name each phase from the hormone driving it and the mapping cannot invert:

  • ⭐ Follicular = estrogen = PROLIFERATIVE. Oestrogen from the growing follicle thickens the endometrium, and the glands are tubular and straight
  • ⭐ Luteal = progesterone = SECRETORY. The corpus luteum primes the lining for implantation, and the glands become tortuous with luminal secretions

⭐ Under the microscope the gland shape is the tell: straight and tubular means oestrogen, coiled and secreting means progesterone. B inverts them, which is the whole point of the distractor.

stem: In what phase of the menstrual cycle would you expect menstrual endometrium? (originally a fill-in-the-blank; rewritten as an MCQ, with distractors drawn from the adjacent teaching point)

options.html: The secretory phase, at its peak

answer:
The correct answer is A. Transcribed from the module: "Menstrual endometrium is present during menses which falls on Day 1-Day 7 of the menstrual cycle (Follicular Phase) in a woman with a 28 day cycle."

⭐ This is the one that catches people out, because menstruation feels like an ending but is counted as a beginning. Day 1 of bleeding is day 1 of the cycle, and the follicular phase runs from there to ovulation. So the menstrual endometrium of days 1-7 sits inside the follicular phase, alongside the earliest follicular recruitment.

The shedding itself is the consequence of the previous luteal phase ending: the corpus luteum regresses, oestrogen and progesterone both fall, the spiral vessels contract, and the functionalis becomes ischemic and sheds. ⭐ The basalis is not shed, and it is what regenerates the functionalis during the proliferative phase that follows.

stem: On a histologic image of the Fallopian tube, what is the structure on the luminal surface of the epithelial cells? (the module posed this against a labelled histology image that the Rise export does not ship; the stem is rewritten to stand on its own)
answer:
The correct answer is D. The Fallopian tube mucosa is ciliated and secretory epithelium.

⭐ The cilia are functional, not decorative: together with the peristaltic action of the smooth muscle muscularis, they move the ovum toward the uterus and sperm toward the ampulla. Lose ciliary function and you raise the risk of an ectopic pregnancy, because the fertilized ovum does not complete the journey.

A, keratin, belongs to skin such as the labia majora. C, stroma, is supporting connective tissue, not a surface structure. B is the near-miss worth being careful with: microvilli are absorptive brush-border projections, not motile — the tube needs motility, so cilia.

stem: A labelled figure of the Fallopian tube marks four positions, A to D, running from the uterine end outward. Which mapping is correct? (originally a drag-and-drop matching activity against a labelled image the Rise export does not ship; rewritten as an MCQ whose options are complete mappings, using the module's own pairings)

options.html: A = isthmus · B = ampulla · C = infundibulum · D = fimbriae
A = ampulla · B = isthmus · C = fimbriae · D = infundibulum
A = infundibulum · B = fimbriae · C = ampulla · D = isthmus
A = fimbriae · B = infundibulum · C = isthmus · D = ampulla

answer:
The correct answer is A, which is the module's own mapping: A = isthmus, B = ampulla, C = infundibulum, D = fimbriae.

The order is anatomical, running from the uterus outward to the ovary:

  • intramural — within the uterine wall
  • ⭐ isthmus — the thinnest, narrowest segment
  • ⭐ ampulla — the widest, most central segment, and where fertilization usually occurs
  • infundibulum — the funnel nearest the ovary
  • fimbriae — the finger-like projections at its mouth

⭐ Getting the isthmus and ampulla the right way round is the examinable half, because the ampulla being widest is the same fact that explains both normal fertilization and why 96-98% of ectopic pregnancies are tubal.

flags.title: Reconstructed from the module's pairings, not from its figure
flags.html: The lettering here follows the module's stated matches. The original image is not in the export, so the stem states the orientation (uterine end outward) explicitly rather than relying on a picture.

stem: Where does fertilization most commonly occur? (the module asked this against the same labelled figure; rewritten to name the segments)
answer:
The correct answer is B. Transcribed from the module: "Fertilization most commonly occurs in the widest portion of the fallopian tube (the ampulla)."

⭐ Widest is the reason. The ampulla gives the most room and the slowest transit, so the sperm and the ovum have the best chance of meeting there. Sperm reaching it release acrosomal enzymes to cross the corona radiata and zona pellucida, and once one penetrates, the zonal reaction re-forms the zona and blocks polyspermy.

⚠ The same anatomy explains the pathology: ⭐ the tube is where 96-98% of ectopic pregnancies implant, because the fertilized ovum is already there and only reaches the uterus if transport works.

stem: What hormone secreted by the ovary is responsible for inducing changes in the endometrium to prepare for implantation?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Transcribed from the module: "Following ovulation, during the luteal phase, the mature ovarian follicle develops into a corpus luteum and secretes progesterone causing the endometrium to have a secretory appearance and primes it for implantation."

⭐ Oestrogen builds the endometrium; progesterone prepares it. Oestrogen drives the proliferative thickening; progesterone converts it to a secretory lining producing glycogen and glycoproteins, which is what an implanting blastocyst needs.

⭐ But the two are sequential, not independent: oestrogen induces the progesterone receptors, so progesterone can only act on tissue oestrogen has already primed. That receptor dependency is the molecular reason the luteal phase has to follow the follicular one.

stem: Order the stages of ovarian follicle development from first to last. (originally a drag-and-drop ordering activity; rewritten as an MCQ whose options are complete orderings)
answer:
The correct answer is A, the module's own ordering: oocyte (1) → primordial follicle (2) → primary follicle (3) → secondary follicle (4) → mature Graafian follicle (5).

What defines each step is the granulosa and theca around the oocyte:

  • primordial — dormant, and what is present at birth. At puberty monthly ovarian factors recruit 30-50 into primary follicles
  • primary — acquires one layer of granulosa cells
  • secondary — granulosa proliferate into another layer
  • ⭐ tertiary/Graafian — a double layer of theca outside, a fluid-filled antrum, and thickened granulosa over the oocyte. It takes 6-8 months to reach this stage

⭐ The follicle with the most FSH receptors becomes dominant, because there is only so much FSH to go round — which is exactly the competition that ART defeats by flooding the system with supraphysiological FSH so several follicles mature at once.

lectureMeta: Q111-132, the Elentra module knowledge checks (22 questions, the largest module in the block). **Keyed** by the module; **only 6 carry written feedback**, transcribed where present, and the rest are reasoned from [[08 - Embryology & Histology]]. ⚠ **Four items were not natively single-answer MCQs** and are rewritten per the house rule, each marked under its stem: two select-alls (Q112, Q114), two matching activities (Q115, Q121) and one fill-in-the-blank (Q116). ⚠ **Three questions depended on a module image that the Rise export does not ship** (the labelled fallopian tube and the ciliated epithelium); their stems are rewritten to stand on their own.
stem: What structure produces the largest amount of progesterone?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Transcribed from the module: "Following ovulation and release of the oocyte from the ovary, the Graafian follicle develops into the corpus luteum and produces and secretes progesterone."

⭐ The switch is in the receptors. Near ovulation the granulosa cell starts expressing LH receptors and loses its FSH receptors; after ovulation both granulosa and theca convert into corpus luteum cells expressing LH receptors, and LH is what then drives progesterone output.

C is the same structure after it has failed: with no implantation the corpus luteum regresses into a corpus albicans, a scar, and progesterone falls, which is what brings on menstruation. If implantation does succeed, hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast rescues the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over at about week 8.

lectureMeta: Q111-132, the Elentra module knowledge checks (22 questions, the largest module in the block). **Keyed** by the module; **only 6 carry written feedback**, transcribed where present, and the rest are reasoned from [[08 - Embryology & Histology]]. ⚠ **Four items were not natively single-answer MCQs** and are rewritten per the house rule, each marked under its stem: two select-alls (Q112, Q114), two matching activities (Q115, Q121) and one fill-in-the-blank (Q116). ⚠ **Three questions depended on a module image that the Rise export does not ship** (the labelled fallopian tube and the ciliated epithelium); their stems are rewritten to stand on their own.
stem: What ovarian cell type would give rise to a germ cell tumour?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Transcribed from the module: "An oocyte is a germ cell that could give rise to germ cell tumours in the ovary."

⭐ Ovarian tumours are classified by the cell they come from, and the name tells you the cell. The ovary's cortex holds all of them side by side:

  • germ cells — the oocytes → germ cell tumours
  • sex cord / stromal cells — granulosa and theca → granulosa cell tumours, thecomas, which may be hormonally active
  • surface epithelium — low cuboidal → the epithelial tumours, which are the commonest ovarian malignancies overall

So A, C and D are all real origins, just of different tumour families, which is what makes them good distractors.

stem: Female calico cats exhibit three different colours of fur, typically caused by random silencing of one of the two X chromosomes in each cell during the 32-cell stage of development. What is the cluster of cells called at this stage?
answer:
The correct answer is D. ⭐ The morula is the solid ball of blastomeres produced by cleavage — division with no overall growth, so each daughter cell is smaller than the last and the whole cluster stays about the size of the original zygote. At 32 cells, that is where the embryo is.

The distractors are the stages either side, and they are worth being able to order:

  • B, blastula/blastocyst — by day 4 a fluid-filled cavity forms and the cells sort into embryoblast (inner cell mass → the embryo) and trophoblast (outer → the placenta). It has reached the uterus by then
  • C, gastrula — week 3, when the bilaminar disc becomes trilaminar
  • A, neurula — later still, when the notochord induces the neural tube

⭐ Sequence: zygote → cleavage → morula → blastocyst → implantation → bilaminar disc → gastrulation → neurulation.

lectureMeta: Q111-132, the Elentra module knowledge checks (22 questions, the largest module in the block). **Keyed** by the module; **only 6 carry written feedback**, transcribed where present, and the rest are reasoned from [[08 - Embryology & Histology]]. ⚠ **Four items were not natively single-answer MCQs** and are rewritten per the house rule, each marked under its stem: two select-alls (Q112, Q114), two matching activities (Q115, Q121) and one fill-in-the-blank (Q116). ⚠ **Three questions depended on a module image that the Rise export does not ship** (the labelled fallopian tube and the ciliated epithelium); their stems are rewritten to stand on their own.
stem: Individual blastomeres were isolated from the embryo at the 4-cell stage. Each was cultured in vitro to the blastocyst stage and individually implanted into four pseudopregnant foster mothers. What would you expect to observe 9 months later?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Two properties of early blastomeres give this away:

  • ⭐ They are totipotent. At the 4-cell stage each blastomere can still form a complete embryo and its extra-embryonic membranes, so none of them is missing anything. That rules out D and E
  • ⭐ They are clones. All four descend by mitosis from one zygote, so they are genetically identical. That rules out C

A would be the answer if only one blastomere were viable, which is exactly what totipotency denies.

⭐ This is the mechanism of monozygotic twinning, taken to four. It is also the reason the calico-cat question above works: the coat pattern comes from random X-inactivation happening later, in each cell independently, so genetically identical animals still differ in appearance.

lectureMeta: Q111-132, the Elentra module knowledge checks (22 questions, the largest module in the block). **Keyed** by the module; **only 6 carry written feedback**, transcribed where present, and the rest are reasoned from [[08 - Embryology & Histology]]. ⚠ **Four items were not natively single-answer MCQs** and are rewritten per the house rule, each marked under its stem: two select-alls (Q112, Q114), two matching activities (Q115, Q121) and one fill-in-the-blank (Q116). ⚠ **Three questions depended on a module image that the Rise export does not ship** (the labelled fallopian tube and the ciliated epithelium); their stems are rewritten to stand on their own.
stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with spotting and lower abdominal ache. She has not had her period for 5 weeks. Beta-hCG is elevated, confirming pregnancy. Ultrasound reveals an empty uterine cavity. Which of the following would most likely explain the condition?

options.html: An ectopic pregnancy, most commonly a mesenteric implantation
She is not pregnant and may have appendicitis
An ectopic pregnancy, most commonly a tubal implantation

answer:
The correct answer is C. A positive hCG with an empty uterus is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise, and ⭐ 96-98% of them are tubal.

The full distribution: Fallopian tube 96-98% · ovary 4% · abdominal cavity 1% · internal cervical os 1% · endocervical canal 1%. ⚠ A is the trap — it names the right diagnosis with the wrong site; mesenteric implantation is vanishingly rare.

B contradicts the elevated hCG. D contradicts the empty cavity: by 5 weeks of amenorrhea with a positive test, an intrauterine gestation should be visible.

⭐ Why the tube: fertilization normally happens in the ampulla, so the conceptus starts there and only reaches the uterus if tubal transport works. Anything that damages the cilia or the tube lumen leaves it to implant where it already is. Worth pairing with the other hCG discriminator: ⚠ a LOW hCG also suggests ectopic.

lectureMeta: Q111-132, the Elentra module knowledge checks (22 questions, the largest module in the block). **Keyed** by the module; **only 6 carry written feedback**, transcribed where present, and the rest are reasoned from [[08 - Embryology & Histology]]. ⚠ **Four items were not natively single-answer MCQs** and are rewritten per the house rule, each marked under its stem: two select-alls (Q112, Q114), two matching activities (Q115, Q121) and one fill-in-the-blank (Q116). ⚠ **Three questions depended on a module image that the Rise export does not ship** (the labelled fallopian tube and the ciliated epithelium); their stems are rewritten to stand on their own.
stem: Which of the indicated processes establishes the three distinct germ layers?
answer:
The correct answer is B. ⭐ Gastrulation converts the bilaminar disc (epiblast + hypoblast) into the trilaminar disc (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), in week 3, and it is the only process here that creates germ layers.

The three steps, in order:

  • ① epiblast cells invade the hypoblast and replace it → endoderm
  • ② epiblast cells migrate laterally and cranially between endoderm and epiblast → intraembryonic mesoderm
  • ③ the epiblast cells left behind → ectoderm

The distractors are all real processes at the wrong moment: A, neurulation acts on a germ layer already made, when the notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural tube. C and D, folding, turn a flat disc into a three-dimensional body. E, organogenesis, builds organs from layers that already exist.

lectureMeta: Q111-132, the Elentra module knowledge checks (22 questions, the largest module in the block). **Keyed** by the module; **only 6 carry written feedback**, transcribed where present, and the rest are reasoned from [[08 - Embryology & Histology]]. ⚠ **Four items were not natively single-answer MCQs** and are rewritten per the house rule, each marked under its stem: two select-alls (Q112, Q114), two matching activities (Q115, Q121) and one fill-in-the-blank (Q116). ⚠ **Three questions depended on a module image that the Rise export does not ship** (the labelled fallopian tube and the ciliated epithelium); their stems are rewritten to stand on their own.
stem: The epiblast is capable of forming which of the following germ layers?
answer:
The correct answer is D. ⭐ All three germ layers derive from the epiblast — which is exactly what the three steps of gastrulation describe: the epiblast supplies the cells that become endoderm, then mesoderm, and what remains becomes ectoderm.

⚠ The intuitive answer is A, and it is wrong. The epiblast is often labelled "future ectoderm" and the hypoblast "future endoderm", which is a useful shorthand for week 2 but false as a statement of fate. ⭐ The hypoblast does not become the embryonic endoderm at all — it is displaced by epiblast cells and contributes to the yolk sac lining.

That is the whole point of the question: the definitive endoderm is epiblast-derived, not hypoblast-derived.

lectureMeta: Q111-132, the Elentra module knowledge checks (22 questions, the largest module in the block). **Keyed** by the module; **only 6 carry written feedback**, transcribed where present, and the rest are reasoned from [[08 - Embryology & Histology]]. ⚠ **Four items were not natively single-answer MCQs** and are rewritten per the house rule, each marked under its stem: two select-alls (Q112, Q114), two matching activities (Q115, Q121) and one fill-in-the-blank (Q116). ⚠ **Three questions depended on a module image that the Rise export does not ship** (the labelled fallopian tube and the ciliated epithelium); their stems are rewritten to stand on their own.
stem: Which structure is derived from the same embryonic primordium as the kidney?
answer:
The correct answer is A. ⭐ The kidney and the gonads both arise from INTERMEDIATE MESODERM, as the urogenital ridge. The shared origin is why the two systems develop together and why their anomalies travel together.

The others come from elsewhere:

  • B, epidermis — surface ectoderm
  • C, mammary gland — also surface ectoderm, a specialised skin appendage
  • D, liver — endoderm, budding off the foregut
  • E, adrenal medulla — ⭐ neural crest, which is why it is chromaffin tissue making catecholamines. Note the adrenal is two organs in one: the cortex is mesodermal and the medulla neural crest

Recall the mesoderm's three columns and this becomes systematic: paraxial (somites → axial skeleton, muscle, dermis) · ⭐ intermediate (urogenital) · lateral plate (body wall, limbs, serous membranes).

stem: An infant is born with congenital anomalies of the special senses, including cataracts and sensorineural deafness. Which teratogen do you suspect?

options.html: Maternal exposure to diagnostic radiation (e.g. x-ray)

answer:
The correct answer is A. ⭐ Congenital rubella syndrome is the classic triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness and cardiac defects (typically patent ductus arteriosus). Two of the three are in the stem.

⭐ The risk of fetal rubella infection is greatest early, when the eye and the inner ear are forming — which is the same principle as the week-by-week teratogen windows.

The distractors each have their own signature, and none of it is this:

  • B, alcohol — fetal alcohol spectrum: midface hypoplasia, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, microcephaly, neurodevelopmental impairment
  • C, diagnostic radiation — diagnostic doses rarely reach a teratogenic threshold; the concerning data are from acute high-dose exposure
  • D, undernutrition — growth restriction, and neural tube defects with folate deficiency
  • E, nicotine — growth restriction, prematurity, placental complications

lectureMeta: Q111-132, the Elentra module knowledge checks (22 questions, the largest module in the block). **Keyed** by the module; **only 6 carry written feedback**, transcribed where present, and the rest are reasoned from [[08 - Embryology & Histology]]. ⚠ **Four items were not natively single-answer MCQs** and are rewritten per the house rule, each marked under its stem: two select-alls (Q112, Q114), two matching activities (Q115, Q121) and one fill-in-the-blank (Q116). ⚠ **Three questions depended on a module image that the Rise export does not ship** (the labelled fallopian tube and the ciliated epithelium); their stems are rewritten to stand on their own.
stem: A 22-year-old pregnant woman at 20 weeks of gestation has an ultrasound revealing spina bifida in the fetus. At what week of gestation did this defect most likely occur?
answer:
The correct answer is B. ⭐ spina bifida is a failure of the CAUDAL neuropore to close, and that closure happens on day 26 — inside weeks 4 to 6. A defect cannot arise after the process it disrupts has finished.

The neural tube closes from the middle outward toward both ends:

  • ⭐ cranial neuropore closes day 24 → failure gives anencephaly
  • ⭐ caudal neuropore closes day 26 → failure gives spina bifida

A is excluded by the teratogen windows themselves: ⭐ weeks 1-2 are "all or nothing" — an insult either kills the conceptus or does nothing, because the cells are still totipotent and can replace losses. C, D and E all fall in the fetal period, where insults cause minor morphologic and functional defects rather than major structural ones.

⭐ Weeks 3-8 are the critical period, when organogenesis and morphogenesis peak and major congenital anomalies are made. This question is that principle applied to one date.

lectureMeta: Q111-132, the Elentra module knowledge checks (22 questions, the largest module in the block). **Keyed** by the module; **only 6 carry written feedback**, transcribed where present, and the rest are reasoned from [[08 - Embryology & Histology]]. ⚠ **Four items were not natively single-answer MCQs** and are rewritten per the house rule, each marked under its stem: two select-alls (Q112, Q114), two matching activities (Q115, Q121) and one fill-in-the-blank (Q116). ⚠ **Three questions depended on a module image that the Rise export does not ship** (the labelled fallopian tube and the ciliated epithelium); their stems are rewritten to stand on their own.
stem: A 26-year-old woman has consumed excessive quantities of alcohol almost every weekend for the last few years. Three weeks ago she missed her second consecutive period, and a pregnancy test is positive. Should you as her physician be concerned about the effects of her binge-drinking episodes on her baby?

options.html: You need not be concerned, as it is so early in development
You should be concerned, as alcohol at an early stage in development may have a pronounced impact on the fetus
She is not an alcoholic, so you have nothing to worry about
She has been eating well and exercising, so you need not be concerned

answer:
The correct answer is B. ⭐ Early is precisely when it matters most. Two missed periods puts her at roughly 8 weeks, so the binge episodes have spanned the embryonic period, weeks 3-8 — the critical period, when cell division, differentiation, organogenesis and morphogenesis are all at their peak and teratogens produce major congenital anomalies.

⚠ A inverts the "all or nothing" rule. That rule applies to weeks 1-2 only, and she is well past it.

C and D are the socially comfortable answers, and both are wrong for the same reason: ⭐ there is no established safe threshold, safe pattern, or safe drinker profile for alcohol in pregnancy. Binge drinking delivers high peak concentrations, which is if anything the more damaging pattern, and good nutrition does not offset a teratogen.

The clinical move is to say so plainly and without blame, and to arrange follow-up — she is still pregnant, and what she does from here still changes the outcome.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lectureMeta: Q133-134, the Elentra module knowledge checks (2 questions). **Keyed, and both carry the module's own written feedback**, transcribed below.
stem: Measurement of gonadotrophins in serum can give an indication of the function of all of the following except:
answer:
The correct answer is B. Transcribed from the module: "The answer is B as the uterus does not have FSH or LH receptors and is normally not a target for direct FSH/LH action. Of course, the anterior pituitary; ovary/testes and hypothalamus are targets for FSH/LH action and all have gonadotrophin receptors."

⭐ The uterus responds to steroids, not to gonadotrophins. Its cycle is driven by estrogen and progesterone made by the ovary; LH and FSH act one step upstream, on the gonad. So a gonadotrophin level reports on the axis, not on the endometrium.

That is also why gonadotrophins are so informative diagnostically: reading them together with the sex steroids localises the problem. High FSH and LH with low oestrogen puts the fault in the gonad (the pituitary is shouting at a gland that cannot answer); low or inappropriately normal gonadotrophins with low oestrogen puts it in the pituitary or hypothalamus.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lectureMeta: Q133-134, the Elentra module knowledge checks (2 questions). **Keyed, and both carry the module's own written feedback**, transcribed below.
stem: The rate of secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH):

options.html: decreases if GnRH is injected every two hours
is increased by a peptide hormone (inhibin) secreted by Sertoli cells
is increased along with LH during the middle of the menstrual cycle
is high throughout the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle

answer:
The correct answer is C. Transcribed from the module: "The answer is c; GnRH pulse would increase FSH and or LH release; inhibin decreases FSH release; LH and FSH both surge in the mid cycle; FSH and LH levels rise to their highest levels in menopausal women; FSH levels decline during the follicular phase due to increasing oestradiol negative feedback. So only C can be correct."

Each distractor inverts a real mechanism, and they are worth taking one at a time:

  • A — ⭐ pulsatile GnRH stimulates. A pulse every 2 hours is the physiological pattern; it is continuous GnRH that suppresses, which is how a GnRH agonist ends up causing chemical castration
  • B — ⭐ inhibin INHIBITS FSH, which is what its name says. Sertoli and granulosa cells make it, and it brakes FSH specifically rather than the whole axis
  • D — ⭐ postmenopausal FSH is HIGH, because the ovary is no longer producing the oestrogen and inhibin that restrain it. Low is the opposite of the truth
  • E — ⭐ FSH FALLS through the follicular phase, suppressed by the rising oestradiol from the very follicle it grew. That negative feedback is also what starves all but the dominant follicle

C survives because the mid-cycle surge is the one moment oestradiol's feedback flips from negative to positive, and both gonadotrophins rise together.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lectureMeta: Q135-136, the Elentra module knowledge checks (2 questions). **Keyed** by the module, with **no written feedback**, so the explanations are reasoned from [[10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle]].
stem: A 25-year-old woman with normal menstrual cycles wishes to become pregnant. In her monthly cycle, fertility is likely to be maximal when her:

options.html: basal body temperature has reached its highest value
plasma estradiol is at its lowest point
plasma progesterone is increasing toward its highest value

answer:
The correct answer is C. ⭐ Progesterone starts rising at ovulation, as the follicular remnants luteinize, so "increasing toward its highest value" marks the peri-ovulatory window — which is exactly when fertility peaks.

The distractors are all real events at the wrong point in the cycle:

  • A — the temperature rise is progesterone-mediated and ⚠ lags ovulation. By the time it has reached its highest value, the fertile window is closing. This is the classic limitation of temperature charting: it confirms ovulation retrospectively
  • B — oestradiol is lowest around menstruation, furthest from ovulation
  • D — ⚠ inverted. Around ovulation, oestrogen makes cervical mucus thin, clear and stretchy to let sperm through; thick mucus is the progesterone-dominant luteal pattern, which is hostile to sperm
  • E — falling progesterone is the end of the luteal phase, immediately before menstruation

⭐ B, D and E all describe times remote from ovulation; A describes the right event too late.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lectureMeta: Q135-136, the Elentra module knowledge checks (2 questions). **Keyed** by the module, with **no written feedback**, so the explanations are reasoned from [[10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle]].
stem: Detection of a peak of estradiol in blood lasting about 12 hours, unaccompanied by a rise in progesterone, suggests which of the following will likely occur within the next 3 days?
answer:
The correct answer is D. ⭐ An oestradiol peak with progesterone still low is the pre-ovulatory signature. Sustained high oestradiol is what flips oestrogen's feedback from negative to positive, triggering the LH surge, and ovulation follows.

The two halves of the stem both matter:

  • the oestradiol peak places her at the end of the follicular phase, where the dominant follicle is producing heavily
  • ⭐ progesterone NOT yet risen proves ovulation has not happened. Progesterone only climbs once the corpus luteum forms

The distractors all belong to the luteal phase or its end: E, corpus luteum regression, and C, menstruation, come about two weeks later; B, a falling temperature, accompanies that regression as progesterone withdraws. A is simply out of sequence.

⚠ The threshold is worth carrying with the concept: oestradiol must exceed roughly 300-500 pg/mL and stay there for about 48 hours to trigger the surge. Level and duration both, which is what makes partial versions of this fact into good distractors.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lectureMeta: Q137-139, the Elentra module knowledge checks (3 questions). **Keyed** by the module; Q139 carries its own written feedback, ⚠ **and that feedback contradicts the option the module flags as correct** — see the warning on that question.
stem: What characterizes spermatogenesis?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Spermatogenesis takes a diploid spermatogonium through meiosis to ⭐ four haploid gametes.

Each distractor is true of something adjacent, which is what makes them work:

  • A — spermatogenesis happens in the seminiferous tubules. The epididymis is where sperm are stored and mature further, not where they are made
  • B — ⭐ this is oogenesis, not spermatogenesis. The oocyte is arrested twice, at prophase I until recruitment and at meiosis II until fertilization. Male meiosis runs to completion without arrest
  • D — ⭐ also oogenesis. The female reservoir is laid down before birth and never replenished; spermatogenesis begins at puberty and continues throughout life from a self-renewing stem cell

⭐ Three of the four options are describing the female side. Sorting them is the whole question: 4 gametes versus 1, continuous versus finite, no arrest versus two arrests.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lectureMeta: Q137-139, the Elentra module knowledge checks (3 questions). **Keyed** by the module; Q139 carries its own written feedback, ⚠ **and that feedback contradicts the option the module flags as correct** — see the warning on that question.
stem: Testosterone affects which of the following?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Testosterone acts on all four, and the lecture groups them as non-reproductive tissues, secondary sex characteristics and reproductive function:

  • A, muscle — it is anabolic, building muscle. It also acts on bone, driving chondrocyte proliferation at the epiphyseal plate and then its closure, and on skin, activating sebaceous glands
  • B, spermatogenesis — ⭐ required for it, which is the point most easily forgotten because testosterone is thought of as a systemic hormone. Leydig cells make it under LH, and it acts locally in the seminiferous tubules
  • C, hair follicles — it alters body hair distribution, and ⭐ via DHT, made by 5-α reductase, which has receptors in hair follicles, accessory sex glands and external genitalia. This is why altered androgen signalling causes baldness
  • D, larynx — it relaxes the larynx, deepening the voice

⭐ Two conversions decide where testosterone acts: 5-α reductase → DHT, ten times more potent, for hair, glands and external genitalia; and aromatase → estradiol in the CNS and adipose tissue, which is what closes the epiphyseal plates in males.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology
lectureMeta: Q137-139, the Elentra module knowledge checks (3 questions). **Keyed** by the module; Q139 carries its own written feedback, ⚠ **and that feedback contradicts the option the module flags as correct** — see the warning on that question.
stem: Folliculogenesis is characterized by:

options.html: the recruitment of developing follicles from the resting primordial pool
the growth of the follicle wall by the development of granulosa and theca cell layers
usually the selection and growth of a single mature Graafian preovulatory follicle
the meiotic maturation to produce an oocyte with a haploid chromosomal complement
A, B and C are all correct

answer:
The correct answer is E. Transcribed from the module: "Answer E is correct as follicle recruitment from a resting pool; growth of the follicle by developing theca and granulosa cell layers and selection of a mature preovulatory follicle are all characteristics of folliculogenesis. Meiotic maturation occurs after ovulation and is normally only completed if spermatozoa entry during fertilization occurs."

⭐ D is the one excluded, and the reason is timing. Folliculogenesis is about the follicle, the somatic envelope around the oocyte; the oocyte's own meiotic maturation is a separate process that finishes later. The oocyte is arrested in prophase I throughout follicular growth, resumes at ovulation, and then ⭐ arrests again at meiosis II until a sperm actually enters — so the haploid complement is not achieved during folliculogenesis at all.

A, B and C are the three phases in order: recruitment of 30-50 primordials each month, growth as granulosa and theca layers develop, and selection of the single dominant follicle, won by whichever has the most FSH receptors.

flags.title: The module's own key contradicts its explanation
flags.html: The Rise export flags option A as the correct answer, while the module's written feedback states plainly that "Answer E is correct" and explains why. The prose is authoritative and E is banked as the key, since A alone would make B and C false, which the same feedback denies. Flagged rather than silently resolved.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 50-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of weight loss (~40 lbs) despite an increased appetite, frequent palpitations, and shakiness. She feels very hot and sweaty and can't get to sleep at night. She is on no medications. On exam: heart rate 120/min, BP 148/70, skin warm and moist, fine tremor in her hands. She has a noticeable stare and lid lag in both eyes but no chemosis, scleral injection, or diplopia on range of motion testing. Her thyroid is not tender but is diffusely enlarged and has a systolic bruit over both lobes. There is a Grade III/VI mid-systolic murmur heard best at the aortic area. TSH < 0.01 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 51 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 16.5 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: What diagnosis is most consistent with this history, physical exam, and lab tests? Justify your answer.
answer:
C. ⭐ Thyrotoxicosis is the lab picture from any cause; hyperthyroidism claims the gland is OVERPRODUCING. thyroiditis releases preformed hormone - thyrotoxic, but not hyperthyroid.

She is hyperthyroid, and Graves specifically:

  • ⭐ Diffusely enlarged gland - symmetric, not nodular
  • ⭐ Systolic bruit - increased vascularity, a driven gland
  • Eye findings, which are Graves-specific

Supported by weight loss despite increased appetite, tremor, heat intolerance, and the cardiovascular set: HR 120, ⭐ wide pulse pressure (148/70), palpitations.

A - subacute thyroiditis is ⭐ painful; hers is not tender. B - TMNG needs discrete nodules. D - she is on no medications.

stem: What is the relevance of her eye findings on the physical exam?

options.html: Adrenergic signs seen in any thyrotoxicosis, not specific to Graves
They point to Graves; the absent findings exclude active disease
A sign of imminent visual loss, so an ocular emergency needing referral
Unrelated to the thyroid, pointing to a separate neurological cause

answer:
B. ⭐ Thyroid eye disease is specific to Graves disease - the antibodies stimulate the retro-orbital tissue as well as the gland.

She has a stare and lid lag. ⭐ What she lacks is the point: no chemosis, no scleral injection, no diplopia - the findings that mark clinically ACTIVE disease and decide whether she needs ophthalmology, steroids, or surgery.

⚠ The orbit runs on its own clock: eye disease can persist or progress after the gland is removed and the hyperthyroidism resolves.

C - she has no visual loss. D - wrong mechanism. > [!warning] A is not simply wrong > 03 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis calls stare, lid retraction and lid lag ⭐ adrenergic and non-specific, reserving proptosis, diplopia and visual loss for Graves orbitopathy. On that split her particular findings are the non-specific ones. ⭐ Worth checking with the lecturer.

stem: What are other possible causes of elevated free T4 and free T3 levels and suppressed TSH levels

options.html: Central hypothyroidism, or failure of the anterior pituitary
Increased synthesis, or leakage of preformed hormone

answer:
D. ⭐ The split is synthesis versus leakage.

Overproduction - Graves disease · ⭐ toxic adenoma, one hot nodule with the rest of the gland quiet · TMNG, several nodules

Leakage (thyroiditis) - post-partum · subacute, where ⭐ pain is the discriminator · post-surgical · infectious

Exogenous - levothyroxine over-replacement · ⚠ ⭐ over-the-counter animal-thyroid supplements (porcine or bovine, unregulated, T3:T4 wrong for humans). ⭐ Take a supplement history - patients often do not know these contain hormone.

Iodine load, the substrate - ⭐ the Jod-Basedow effect: ⭐ iodinated contrast after a CT · ⭐ amiodarone, which ⚠ persists up to a year past the last dose, so ask what cardiac drugs they were on before

⭐ hCG resembles TSH: a first-trimester TSH of ~0.1 with normal free hormones is ⭐ physiological, not hyperthyroidism. Rarely, TSH-producing tumours.

A and B are hypothyroid states; C is a calcium disorder.

stem: Are further tests needed to confirm the diagnosis? If yes, what tests would you do and how could they help?

options.html: Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, to confirm Graves
A radioactive iodine uptake scan, read on its pattern of uptake
A thyroid ultrasound, which is definitive for the etiology
No further testing is needed; the clinical picture is diagnostic

answer:
B. ⭐ The pattern of uptake names the cause:

UptakeDiagnosis
One bright spotToxic adenoma
Multiple spotsTMNG
⭐ Diffuse⭐ Graves disease - expected in her
Decreasedthyroiditis

Radioactive iodine is swallowed and imaged at 24 hours. ⭐ The thyroid is the only organ that takes up iodine at that level, because it is the only one iodinating tyrosine to build T3 and T4.

⚠ Low uptake is not "Hashimoto's" - Hashimoto's is by definition hypothyroid. In a thyrotoxic patient, low uptake means thyroiditis.

A - anti-TPO is a Hashimoto's antibody; TRAb is the Graves-specific blood test. C - ultrasound is for a nodule, not etiology. D - the scan is what proves which cause.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 50-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of weight loss (~40 lbs) despite an increased appetite, frequent palpitations, and shakiness. She feels very hot and sweaty and can't get to sleep at night. She is on no medications. On exam: heart rate 120/min, BP 148/70, skin warm and moist, fine tremor in her hands. She has a noticeable stare and lid lag in both eyes but no chemosis, scleral injection, or diplopia on range of motion testing. Her thyroid is not tender but is diffusely enlarged and has a systolic bruit over both lobes. There is a Grade III/VI mid-systolic murmur heard best at the aortic area. TSH < 0.01 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 51 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 16.5 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: List the 4 main treatment options for this problem. For each, explain how they work and summarize the pros and cons (risks, side-effects).

options.html: Beta-blockers, NSAIDs, steroids and watchful observation

answer:
C. Four aims:

AimTreatmentDetail
Supportivebeta-blockerspalpitations, tachycardia, tremor - ⚠ does not lower production
↓ production⭐ thionamides: methimazole > PTU⭐ 1st line for Graves, the one that can REMIT. 4-6 weeks. ⭐ agranulocytosis, liver dysfunction, ⚠ birth defects
↓ productionRAI⭐ 1st line for adenoma and TMNG. Permanent cure, but ⭐ permanent hypothyroidism; ⚠ worsens eye disease, especially in smokers; ⛔ not in pregnancy
↓ productiontotal thyroidectomy⭐ rarely - large symptomatic goiter, suspected malignancy, or refractory thyroid storm

⭐ Only Graves remits, which is why a thionamide goes first there and RAI first in nodular disease. ⚠ Her eye findings bear on the choice - RAI may worsen them.

A is the hypocalcemia regimen. B is supportive only. D omits RAI and surgery.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 72-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his son. He has lived on his own since his wife died last year, and his son is concerned he has become more forgetful. Between them you get a further story of weight gain, poor appetite, cold intolerance, voice hoarseness, and leg puffiness. Past history: an inferior MI 5 years ago, for which he is on ASA, bisoprolol and atorvastatin; he also has SL NTG for angina though he can't remember the last time he needed it. On exam he is oriented, responsive (though slow), and not in distress. BP 140/90, heart rate 52 beats/min, RR 16, O2 saturation 94% on room air, T 36.2 C. Skin cool and dry. Non-pitting edema in both legs up to his knees. Heart sounds hard to hear, dullness at the right lung base with decreased tactile fremitus. You can't see his neck veins, nor see or feel his thyroid. ⭐ The relaxation phase of the DTRs at his knees is delayed.

stem: What diagnosis is consistent with this history and physical exam? Justify your answer.

options.html: Congestive heart failure from his previous MI

answer:
B. ⭐ The delayed relaxation phase (Woltman sign) is the most specific sign, and the rest follows the hypothyroid column: cold intolerance, ⭐ weight GAIN despite DECREASED appetite, slow mentation, bradycardia at 52, ⭐ diastolic hypertension with a narrow pulse pressure (140/90), cool dry skin.

⚠ An impalpable thyroid does not argue against it - the signs are not sensitive, and an atrophic gland is an ordinary end state of Hashimoto's.

A - ⚠ his neck veins are not visible, hard to square with congestive failure; heart failure sits under "both can do", so the edema does not discriminate. C - depression causes neither bradycardia nor a delayed relaxation phase. D is the opposite column.

⚠ Watch for myxedema coma - obtundation and hypothermia with hypotension and hyponatremia. He is bradycardic and cool but oriented and normothermic.

stem: What tests would you order?

options.html: Free T4 and free T3, without a TSH
serum TSH first, with free T4 to confirm

answer:
D. ⭐ TSH case-finds; free hormone confirms. Expect TSH HIGH with free T4 LOW - ⭐ free T3 is not needed.

For etiology, ask about past thyroid treatments and pituitary risk; ⭐ otherwise assume Hashimoto's.

A - ⚠ anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin almost never influence clinical decisions. B - ⚠ ultrasound is not sensitive, not specific and not required, only for a coincident nodule. C is the protocol for suspected central disease, where ⭐ TSH moves WITH the hormone - he has no pituitary risk.

stem: Based on your answer to Q1, and assuming the results of the lab tests you ordered in Q2 confirm your diagnosis, how would you treat him?

options.html: Oral levothyroxine, started low and titrated up
Oral levothyroxine at the full ~1.5 mcg/kg/day dose
Methimazole, titrated to a normal TSH
No treatment; replacement is of no proven benefit

answer:
A. Standard replacement is ⭐ ~1.5 mcg/kg/day titrated to a normal TSH, with the modifier ⭐ start low and titrate up if elderly or with heart disease. He is 72 with an inferior MI and angina.

⭐ Recheck TSH at 4-6 weeks, because ⭐ levothyroxine's half-life is 1 week - sooner reads a level short of steady state. ⚠ Do not monitor free T4 or T3 once you are the one replacing them.

Taken ≥ 1 h before or ≥ 2 h after eating, and ⭐ 4 h away from calcium, iron or magnesium.

B is the dose for a well young patient. C treats the opposite disease. D misapplies the subclinical rule - his free T4 is low, so this is overt.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 26-year-old female delivered a healthy baby 10 weeks ago and now presents complaining of palpitations that started 3 weeks ago, worse at night. She says the palpitations are getting better, but at first "my heart was going to jump out of my chest". She has had no chest pain, dyspnea, or lightheadedness. She has also been feeling warm and is tired, though she is up most nights at least once to breast feed. She is on no medications other than an iron supplement. On exam: BP 136/78, pulse 80 and regular, tremor in her hands. Her thyroid is immediately felt on palpation and might be a bit enlarged, but it is not tender and she has no nodules. TSH < 0.05 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 21.2 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 5.0 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: Intrepret her TFTs.
answer:
C. ⚠ Read the free hormones against their ranges before naming the pattern.

HersRange
TSH< 0.050.3-4.5⭐ suppressed
Free T421.29-22⚠ normal
Free T35.03.1-6.8normal

⭐ Suppressed TSH with normal free hormones is subclinical hyperthyroidism; overt disease needs free hormone above range. It carries a risk of bone loss and atrial fibrillation.

⚠ "Subclinical" describes the labs, not the patient - she is plainly symptomatic.

A needs a high free T4. B is the wrong direction. D would need ⭐ TSH normal or HIGH with a high free T4. > [!warning] Spelling in the source > The handout writes "Intrepret". Quoted verbatim, flagged not corrected.

On exam: BP 136/78, pulse 80 and regular, tremor in her hands. Her thyroid is immediately felt on palpation and might be a bit enlarged, but it is not tender and she has no nodules. stem: What is the most likely cause of her thyroid problem?
answer:
B. She is 10 weeks post-partum, and ⭐ post-partum is a listed thyroiditis trigger.

  • Goiter in thyroiditis may be ⭐ asymmetric, symmetric or absent - hers is barely enlarged
  • ⚠ Not tender: ⭐ pain belongs to the subacute, post-viral form
  • ⭐ Already improving, which is what burning out looks like

A - Graves disease is the main differential but expects a symmetric goiter, often eye signs, and ⭐ does not spontaneously improve at 3 weeks. C needs a nodule; she has none. D - iron is not thyroid hormone, though ⚠ it blocks levothyroxine absorption if she later needs replacement.

stem: Describe the natural history of this disorder according to its clinical and laboratory features.

options.html: Progressive worsening thyrotoxicosis, requiring definitive treatment
Permanent hypothyroidism, present from the outset
A single thyrotoxic episode with no later consequence
A thyrotoxic phase that burns out, then a hypothyroid phase

answer:
D. ⭐ Thyroiditis leaks preformed hormone, and that store is finite - which is why ⭐ it burns out.

  • Thyrotoxic phase - suppressed TSH with raised or high-normal free T4, while the gland leaks
  • Hypothyroid phase - TSH rises and free T4 falls, the damaged gland unable to synthesise

⭐ The hypothyroid phase is the one to watch for; low-uptake disease is treated supportively while you wait for it. Her improving symptoms and high-normal free T4 put her at the end of the thyrotoxic phase.

A describes Graves, which does not burn out. B skips the phase she is in. C is the dangerous version of the right answer - it drops the hypothyroid phase, which is the reason to keep monitoring.

TSH < 0.05 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 21.2 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 5.0 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: Do you need further tests to confirm the diagnosis? If yes, what test(s) would you do and how will they help?

options.html: An RAI uptake and scan; low uptake would mean leakage
Anti-TPO antibodies, which would establish Graves
A thyroid ultrasound, definitive for the etiology
No test can separate a thyroiditis from Graves disease

answer:
A. ⭐ RAI uptake is the best single test for the etiology of thyrotoxicosis:

  • ⭐ LOW uptake → leakage → thyroiditis → supportive care only
  • ⭐ HIGH uptake → synthesis → Graves, TMNG, adenoma → a thionamide, RAI or surgery

⚠ It is expensive, a 2-day test, and ⛔ contraindicated in pregnancy.

⭐ Whether she needs it is separate from what it would show. A painless small goiter 10 weeks post-partum, already improving, is typical enough that the result would not change management - which is supportive care either way. It becomes worth doing if she fails to improve or worsens.

B - anti-TPO is a Hashimoto's marker, often positive here too, so it separates nothing; ⭐ TRAb is the Graves-specific antibody. C - ultrasound is not required. D is false.

stem: Does she need to be monitored? If so, what would you recommend?

options.html: No monitoring, once the thyrotoxicosis has settled
Monitor free T4 and free T3 monthly, indefinitely
Yes - follow her TSH for the hypothyroid phase
Yes - repeat the RAI uptake scan at intervals

answer:
C. ⭐ Low-uptake disease is treated supportively, plus monitoring for the hypothyroid phase - the monitoring is half the treatment.

⭐ Follow TSH, since the transition being watched for is a rising TSH.

⚠ This is the step most easily dropped. She is improving, so she looks like someone who can be discharged - and the hypothyroidism arrives months later, in a woman whose fatigue will be put down to a new baby.

A is the error the rule exists to prevent. B - ⚠ free T4 and T3 are not what you follow. D repeats a 2-day test that has already answered its one question.

preamble.html: The case. A 26-year-old female delivered a healthy baby 10 weeks ago and now presents complaining of palpitations that started 3 weeks ago, worse at night. She says the palpitations are getting better, but at first "my heart was going to jump out of my chest". She has had no chest pain, dyspnea, or lightheadedness. She has also been feeling warm and is tired, though she is up most nights at least once to breast feed. She is on no medications other than an iron supplement. On exam: BP 136/78, pulse 80 and regular, tremor in her hands. Her thyroid is immediately felt on palpation and might be a bit enlarged, but it is not tender and she has no nodules. TSH < 0.05 mU/L (0.3-4.5), free T4 21.2 pmol/L (9-22), free T3 5.0 pmol/L (3.1-6.8).

stem: Does she need to be treated?

options.html: Yes - methimazole, to bring the free T4 down
Supportive care only, with a beta-blocker if needed
Yes - levothyroxine, to pre-empt the hypothyroid phase
Yes - radioactive iodine ablation of the gland

answer:
B. ⭐ You cannot block a gland that is not synthesising - her hormone is leaked and preformed, so a thionamide has nothing to act on.

Supportive means beta-blockers for palpitations, tachycardia and tremor. Hers are mild and improving with a pulse of 80, so this is a judgement call rather than an obligation.

⚠ NSAIDs then steroids are for the PAIN of subacute thyroiditis - her gland is not tender.

A would do nothing for the leak and ⚠ deepen the hypothyroid phase. C treats a phase she is not in - she is currently thyrotoxic. D ablates a gland that is already burning out.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
The case. A 68-year-old man is critically ill in the ICU. TSH 1.0 mU/L (0.3-4.5), Free T4 8.0 (9-22), Free T3 1.5 (3.5-6.5). Your resident tells you that the TFTs can be explained by Non-Thyroidal Illness (NTI) Syndrome.

> [!warning] Error in the source material > The handout gives his free T4 and free T3 in `mmol/L`. Free thyroid hormones are reported in `pmol/L`, as the same handout does in Cases #1 and #3. Flagged, not corrected. (The free T3 reference range also differs between cases - 3.5-6.5 here against 3.1-6.8 elsewhere - but either is a plausible lab-specific range.)

stem: What is NTI syndrome? Outline the 3 main patterns in the TFTs in patients with NTI syndrome.

options.html: Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid in critical illness
Thyroid hormone resistance, unmasked by critical illness
Pituitary infarction occurring during critical illness
Abnormal thyroid tests in illness, with a normal thyroid

answer:
D. ⭐ The abnormality belongs to the illness, not the thyroid - the pattern seen in a critically ill patient whose thyroid is intrinsically normal.

⚠ The three TFT patterns are not covered anywhere in the Week 2 material, so they are left open here rather than filled in from elsewhere.

⭐ What his numbers DO support is in Q87, and it is the clinically important half: the same panel fits central hypothyroidism, which is a diagnosis rather than an adaptation.

A is an intrinsic thyroiditis - the opposite of "non-thyroidal". B is hormone resistance, which runs high free hormones. C names one specific pituitary event, not the syndrome.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 35-year-old woman noticed a lump on the left side of her neck when she was brushing her teeth. It moved up and down when she swallowed, and she has found that she experiences some pressure swallowing solids but not liquids. She has not noted any change in her voice or other discomfort. She is concerned that the mass seems to have enlarged since she first found it. She has been otherwise well and denies symptoms of hyper- or hypothyroidism. There is no family history of thyroid disease. On exam you confirm a palpable nodule on the left side of her neck in or near the thyroid gland. It is non-tender, moves with swallowing, and you do not feel any enlarged lymph nodes.

stem: Describe the four tests beyond the history and physical by which to investigate this nodule.

options.html: Ultrasound, CT neck, MRI neck and a PET scan
TSH, an RAI scan, ultrasound with TI-RADS, and FNA
Needle core, punch, excisional biopsy and frozen section

answer:
C. ⭐ Biochemistry → imaging → pathology, with the imaging branch decided by the TSH:

StepTestDecides
1⭐ TSHwhich imaging comes next
2a. TSH LOWRAI scan⭐ a HOT nodule is NEVER cancer
2b. normal or HIGHultrasound + TI-RADSwhether to biopsy
3⭐ FNABcytology, by Bethesda category

⭐ TSH is first because a low result diverts the whole pathway - biopsying a hyperfunctioning nodule is the error the sequence prevents.

A tests thyroid function, not a structural nodule. B has no role in initial evaluation. D - ⚠ needle core biopsy is the wrong instrument for the neck and punch biopsy is for skin.

There is no family history of thyroid disease. On exam you confirm a palpable nodule on the left side of her neck in or near the thyroid gland. It is non-tender, moves with swallowing, and you do not feel any enlarged lymph nodes.

stem: The ultrasound report describes a "2.3 cm left-sided, solid hypoechoic nodule with normal borders and shape and no microcalcifications. American College of Radiology TI-RADS 4, American Thyroid Association - Intermediate Suspicion." What do you now recommend?

options.html: Clinical follow-up only, given the reassuring features
Total thyroidectomy, on the TI-RADS score

answer:
B. ⭐ TI-RADS decides whether to biopsy, on risk score AND size together:

TI-RADS⭐ FNA ifFollow if
TR3≥ 2.5 cm≥ 1.5 cm
⭐ TR4⭐ ≥ 1.5 cm≥ 1.0 cm
TR5≥ 1.0 cm≥ 0.5 cm

⭐ She is TR4 at 2.3 cm, past the threshold. Note the shape of the table: the higher the suspicion, the smaller the nodule needs to be.

⚠ The reassuring features are a distractor - normal borders and absent microcalcifications already fed into the TR4 score, so re-reading them double-counts them, which is what A does.

C - ⭐ TI-RADS decides whether to biopsy, not whether to operate. D applies the surveillance threshold when she has met the biopsy one, in a nodule that is already growing.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 35-year-old woman noticed a lump on the left side of her neck when she was brushing her teeth. It moved up and down when she swallowed, and she has found that she experiences some pressure swallowing solids but not liquids. She has not noted any change in her voice or other discomfort. She is concerned that the mass seems to have enlarged since she first found it. She has been otherwise well and denies symptoms of hyper- or hypothyroidism. There is no family history of thyroid disease. On exam you confirm a palpable nodule on the left side of her neck in or near the thyroid gland. It is non-tender, moves with swallowing, and you do not feel any enlarged lymph nodes.

stem: You arrange a fine needle aspiration of the nodule that is read as "Bethesda 4 - Follicular Neoplasm (indeterminate)." What does this mean in terms of possible malignancy? What do you recommend?

options.html: 97-100% risk; total thyroidectomy and node dissection
5-20% risk; the sample was inadequate, so repeat it

answer:
D. ⭐ Bethesda IV is indeterminate, at 23-34%:

Bethesda⭐ Risk of malignancy
I non-diagnostic5-20%
II benign2-7%
III AUS12-30%
⭐ IV follicular neoplasm⭐ 23-34%
V suspicious67-83%
VI malignant97-100%

⭐ Repeating the aspirate cannot resolve it. A follicular adenoma and a follicular carcinoma have identical nuclei; only ⭐ capsular or vascular invasion separates them, and that is visible solely in the resected specimen. ⚠ A cytology sample contains no capsule. ⚠ The opposite of papillary carcinoma, where the nuclei are the diagnosis.

So: ⭐ molecular analysis or a diagnostic hemithyroidectomy, which is also the cure if it is an adenoma. Her enlarging, symptomatic nodule points the same way.

A is Bethesda II, B is VI, C is I.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. A 47-year-old woman has Graves disease with a large goitre and has opted for a total thyroidectomy. She is discharged three days post-op, but two days later is brought to hospital following a seizure. Her family notes that since she's been home she's been complaining of pins and needles in her fingers, toes, and around her lips. Labs: TSH 2.4 mU/L (0.3-4.5), Ca 1.71 mmol/L (2.12-2.62), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), Na 137, K 4.1, glucose 4.8.

stem: She has recovered from her seizure and is awake. What three clinical signs can you check for?

options.html: Trousseau's sign, Chvostek's sign, a prolonged QT
Hyporeflexia, a short QT interval, and an Osborn wave
Proptosis, lid lag and a systolic thyroid bruit
Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's sign and papilledema

answer:
A. ⭐ Hypocalcemia makes nerve and muscle hyper-excitable.

SignHow
⭐ Trousseau's signcuff above systolic for 3 min → carpopedal spasm. ⭐ More specific
Chvostek's signtap over the facial nerve → facial twitch
⭐ Prolonged QTon ECG - ⚠ risks torsades de pointes

Trousseau's and Chvostek's appear in MILD disease; convulsions, perioral paresthesias, carpopedal spasm and laryngeal spasm mark SEVERE. ⚠ She has already seized, and ⚠ laryngeal spasm is immediately life-threatening.

B is the ⭐ hyperCALCEMIA column - weakness, hyporeflexia, a short QT and an Osborn wave. C is thyroid, and she no longer has one. D is meningeal.
