preamble.title: The case - James
preamble.html:
The case - James (Q148-Q151). "James is a 3.5-year-old male referred for short stature. He was born at 34+3, and spent 3 weeks in the NICU for jaundice, hypoglycemia, and poor feeding. He has met his developmental milestones appropriately but seems to lag behind other children in growth. His growth chart is shown on the next page."

Given at Q150: "You obtain previous growth parameters. At age 3 years James' height was 89 cm and weight was 12 kg."

stem: The most important next step is to
answer:
[!success]- Answer

A. ⭐ Red in Noor's annotated copy, whose legend says red is the right answer - Obtain further history ** (initially have stuff).

⚠ This overturns the reasoning banked here first, which argued for B. That argument leaned on the document answering itself two questions later ("You obtain previous growth parameters") and on the fact that a velocity needs two points. ⭐ But the stem carries its own annotation - "(but should have all of them)" - and that reframes the question: all four are things you will do, and it is asking which comes first.

⭐ "Initially have stuff" is the argument. You already hold a history: 34+3 weeks, three weeks in the NICU for jaundice, hypoglycemia and poor feeding. ⭐ Every one of those is a thread, and taking them further is free - Noor's margin note on the stem reads "probably nutrition prob", which is a hypothesis generated from the history alone and which Q150 goes on to confirm as celiac disease.

⭐ And B collapses into A on its own annotation: "Obtain previous growth charts (if they didn't come in with them, would get hx beforehand)". The charts may simply not be in the room. The history always is.

⭐ Worth reading against Q140, where the official answer IS "obtain previous growth charts". Same question, different case, opposite answer - because Samantha's history is explicitly "non-contributory" and there is nothing further to take, while James's neonatal history is loaded. ⚠ So the rule is not "always get the charts" or "always take a history"; it is take whichever one the case has left on the table.

C needs two measurements a year apart and cannot be done today. D needs parental heights, which this case never gives.

preamble.title: The case - James
preamble.html:
The case - James (Q148-Q151). "James is a 3.5-year-old male referred for short stature. He was born at 34+3, and spent 3 weeks in the NICU for jaundice, hypoglycemia, and poor feeding. He has met his developmental milestones appropriately but seems to lag behind other children in growth. His growth chart is shown on the next page."

Given at Q150: "You obtain previous growth parameters. At age 3 years James' height was 89 cm and weight was 12 kg."

stem: How do you classify his growth problem(s)?

options.html: Short stature with decreased weight for age
Deceleration of growth with normal weight for height

answer:
[!success]- Answer

C. Read the chart first, then the previous parameters against it:

Age 3.0Age 3.5 (chart)Change
Height89 cm~90 cm, at about the 3rd percentile+1 cm in six months
Weight12 kg~11 kg, ⚠ below the 3rd percentile⚠ −1 kg

⭐ He has lost weight while barely growing, and the weight is the more affected of the two. That is the block's chronic-illness pattern verbatim: "usually weight loss (or at least a lack of weight gain) precedes the changes in linear growth."

A is the endocrine pattern and the exact opposite - the block's "short and relatively chubby" child, which is Samantha. ⭐ The two CHSG cases are deliberately built as a matched pair, and getting this row right is the whole session.

B requires disproportion - the block means limb length against trunk, which is skeletal dysplasia and FGFR3. Nothing here is described as disproportionate, and prematurity is not a classification of a growth pattern. ⭐ Noor's note on it is the useful objection: "was a premature baby, but disproportionate could refer to limbs / weight - not sure what disproportionate means", which is exactly why the word has to be pinned to limb against trunk and not to weight.

⭐ D is what the group chose, and her note on why it is wrong is better than the option is. Marked green - "group decides" - with the reasoning: ⚠ "not enough to conclude deceleration, there is no definition of deceleration, would be going from NORMAL growth velocity to deceleration, basically a created term". ⭐ Deceleration is a claim about a trajectory and you need two points to make it; at this moment you have one chart and one earlier reading, and the weight is what has actually moved.

He has met his developmental milestones appropriately but seems to lag behind other children in growth. His growth chart is shown on the next page."

Given at Q150: "You obtain previous growth parameters. At age 3 years James' height was 89 cm and weight was 12 kg."

stem: What diagnostic test be most helpful in determining the diagnosis?
answer:
[!success]- Answer

B. Q149 has already placed him in the weight-fell-first column, and that column is chronic illness or undernutrition. The block lists celiac disease first under impaired absorption, puts celiac serology in the standard screen for a short child ("CBC, ferritin, renal function, TSH, celiac serology"), and gives a gluten-free diet as the treatment that fixes the growth.

⭐ Celiac is the diagnosis that rewards testing more than any other on that list, because a cheap serology finds a cause that a diet reverses completely - and it is the one whose growth pattern is exactly his.

A is the workup for a pituitary cause, which belongs to the other arm of the split - the short, chubby child. D is in every short-stature workup, and his would be delayed, but ⚠ bone age does not name a disease. The block uses it to separate familial (on time) from constitutional delay (behind), and it is delayed in celiac, chronic disease and GH deficiency alike. C is ruled out by a child who has crossed percentiles and lost a kilogram.

He has met his developmental milestones appropriately but seems to lag behind other children in growth. His growth chart is shown on the next page."

Given at Q150: "You obtain previous growth parameters. At age 3 years James' height was 89 cm and weight was 12 kg."

stem: What lab finding is most likely?
answer:
[!success]- Answer

A. ⭐ A and D are the same haemoglobin and differ only in the MCV, so the question is entirely about the size of the red cell. Celiac disease damages the proximal small bowel, which is where iron is absorbed, so the anaemia it causes is iron-deficient and therefore microcytic - a low MCV. D's MCV of 90 is normal, and would point somewhere else entirely.

B is hypothyroidism, which is the endocrine arm - the block's "slow growth with weight gain". James lost weight. C would be a late consequence of long-standing malabsorption rather than the first thing to turn up at 3½.

flags.title: The session supplies the step the block does not
flags.html:
⚠ Grep the endocrinology block for "microcytic", "MCV" or "iron deficiency" and there is nothing - it gives only the screen, "CBC, ferritin, renal function, TSH, celiac serology", where ferritin beside the CBC is the hook. ⭐ The session closes that gap itself: Noor's annotated copy marks the answer "(microcytic) (bc iron deficiency)", so the chain from celiac to iron deficiency to a low MCV was taught in the room even though it is not written in the block. ⭐ Flagged here because it is worth knowing which of your sources a fact came from.

Two more notes she took on this question: ⭐ "Celiacs may present with isolated short stature", and, on option B, "(high TSH, normal FT4) >> BMI tends to increase with endocrine reaction" - which she then writes out as the line of the session: ⭐ "KEY: BMI increases with endocrine causes!!!!!!" That is the same discriminator as Samantha's, stated from the other side.

lecture: Deck Case - Andrew, 4y8m: Precocity with Asymmetric Testes (Gallego After-Class Cases)
lectureMeta: Q152-Q154, the first case of `ph_gallego_cases_puberty_and_growth_aferclass_` (pp. 2-9). ⭐ **Keyed by the lecturer's own worked slides** - the deck poses each question and then answers it on the following slide. Q154's stem and its six options are verbatim from the deck; Q152 and Q153 are posed as open prompts in the deck, so their options are written here and the key taken from the answer slide. Banked here rather than in [[Module Questions - Endocrinology]] because it is a patient case.

preamble.title: The case - Andrew, 4 years 8 months
preamble.html:
The case. Andrew, 4 years 8 months, referred for assessment of precocious puberty. Body odour for 6 months (using deodorant) · pubic hair 4 months · increased penile size 4 months · rapid growth for 6 to 12 months - +20 lb and +6-8 inches in a year · no previous heights available · a year ago he was shorter than his 6-year-old sister and is now a few inches taller. Mother 171 cm (menarche 16), father 183 cm, normal puberty.

Physical. Height 122.6 cm, >97th · ⭐ height-age 7 years (CA 4 y 8 m) · weight 26.5 kg, >97th · "muscular" appearance and deep voice · pubic hair Tanner II, penile length Tanner IV · ⭐ testicular volume: right 2 mL soft, left 8 mL firm.

stem: What investigations would you propose for Andrew?

options.html: An MRI of the head, on the grounds that under half of precocious boys are idiopathic
A 17-hydroxyprogesterone and adrenal imaging, to find the source of the androgen
LH and FSH, a serum testosterone, and a bone age taken at the left wrist
A GnRH stimulation test, since a single random gonadotropin is pulsatile and insensitive

answer:
C. The deck answers itself on the next slide: ⭐ LH/FSH · Testosterone · Bone age. The block's first-line panel is the same list - "random LH (>0.3 mIU/L suggests CPP) · FSH · estradiol or testosterone · bone age".

⭐ Three tests, three different questions. The gonadotropins say whether the brain is driving it. The testosterone says how much androgen is actually there. The bone age says what it has already cost him in final height - and his comes back at 11.5 years against a chronological 4.8.

D is the gold standard, for the wrong question. A GnRH stimulation test confirms central precocity; you do not run it before the random pair tells you which way to look. The deck does run one - on Sarah, after her LH came back borderline.

A is mandatory in a boy whose precocity is central, and that fact is the trap: it is true, it is high-yield, and it is not yet applicable. ⚠ The deck never images Andrew's head at all. B names a real peripheral source - CAH or a virilising tumour - but ⭐ an adrenal source virilises without touching the testis, and his left testis is 8 mL and firm.

preamble.title: The case - Andrew, 4 years 8 months
preamble.html:
The case. Andrew, 4 years 8 months, referred for assessment of precocious puberty. Body odour for 6 months (using deodorant) · pubic hair 4 months · increased penile size 4 months · rapid growth for 6 to 12 months - +20 lb and +6-8 inches in a year · no previous heights available · a year ago he was shorter than his 6-year-old sister and is now a few inches taller. Mother 171 cm (menarche 16), father 183 cm, normal puberty.

Physical. Height 122.6 cm, >97th · ⭐ height-age 7 years (CA 4 y 8 m) · weight 26.5 kg, >97th · "muscular" appearance and deep voice · pubic hair Tanner II, penile length Tanner IV · ⭐ testicular volume: right 2 mL soft, left 8 mL firm.

Results (deck p. 6): FSH <1 (low, suppressed) · LH <0.3 (low, suppressed) · Testosterone 25.3 nmol/L (ref. prepubertal <1.0, adult 10.5-35) · Bone age 11.5 yrs (CA 4.8 yrs).

stem: Is this Precocious puberty? If so, central or peripheral?

options.html: Central precocity: the bone age is advanced, which only an activated axis can produce
Peripheral precocity: the androgen is high while both gonadotropins are suppressed
Premature adrenarche: body odour and pubic hair without true pubertal axis activation
Not precocity: a testosterone within the quoted adult range is normal at any age

answer:
B. The deck's own summary: "Low LH and FSH · Very high Testosterone · Bone age is too advanced for CA" ⭐ "= Consistent with GnRH Independent PP or Peripheral PP."

The block reduces the whole distinction to which direction the two move: ⭐ central = gonadotropins HIGH and steroid HIGH; peripheral = gonadotropins LOW and steroid HIGH.

⭐ Suppressed gonadotropins beside a testosterone of 25.3 is negative feedback working perfectly, on a source it cannot switch off. The pituitary sees an adult testosterone in a four-year-old and shuts down - and shutting down changes nothing, because the androgen was never coming from its instruction.

A treats the bone age as if it were specific. It is not: ⭐ bone age is advanced by androgen exposure from any source, which is why the block lists precocious puberty and hyperthyroidism together under advanced bone age. It tells you how long this has been going on, not where it comes from.

C is the block's benign variant - pubic hair alone, adrenal, with no growth spurt and no bone-age advance. He has a deep voice, Tanner IV penile length, a height-age of 7 and a bone age of 11.5. D misuses a reference range: quoting an adult interval for a 4-year-old is the abnormality, not the reassurance - his prepubertal ceiling is 1.0.

Body odour for 6 months (using deodorant) · pubic hair 4 months · increased penile size 4 months · rapid growth for 6 to 12 months - +20 lb and +6-8 inches in a year · no previous heights available · a year ago he was shorter than his 6-year-old sister and is now a few inches taller. Mother 171 cm (menarche 16), father 183 cm, normal puberty.

Physical. Height 122.6 cm, >97th · ⭐ height-age 7 years (CA 4 y 8 m) · weight 26.5 kg, >97th · "muscular" appearance and deep voice · pubic hair Tanner II, penile length Tanner IV · ⭐ testicular volume: right 2 mL soft, left 8 mL firm.

Results (deck p. 6): FSH <1 (low, suppressed) · LH <0.3 (low, suppressed) · Testosterone 25.3 nmol/L (ref. prepubertal <1.0, adult 10.5-35) · Bone age 11.5 yrs (CA 4.8 yrs).

stem: What is the most likely cause for Andrew's precocious puberty?

options.html: This is a normal variation and I am not worried about his pubertal development

answer:
C. The deck's management slide: ⭐ left orchidectomy · histology confirmed a benign Leydig cell tumour · post-op testosterone <0.3 nmol/L.

⭐ The asymmetry was the finding all along - 2 mL on the right, 8 mL firm on the left. The block puts it twice: "asymmetric testis suggests a Leydig tumour", and the Leydig cell tumour sits at the head of its gonadal causes of peripheral precocity.

⭐ Why the asymmetry has to mean a local cause. LH travels in the blood and reaches both gonads, so central activation enlarges both. A source inside one testis enlarges that one, and the contralateral testis stays where it was - his is still 2 mL and soft, which is prepubertal.

B and D would virilise him with BOTH testes small. The block: androgen arriving from a peripheral source elsewhere gives acne, pubic hair, increased penile length and accelerated growth ⚠ "with NO change in testicular volume (<3 mL)". His left is 8 mL.

E causes central precocity, which his suppressed LH and FSH exclude - and it is the tempting wrong answer, because the block's own line about boys ("<50% idiopathic, image the CNS") is exactly the fact a well-prepared reader reaches for. ⭐ It applies only once the gonadotropins have said "central", which is why they are measured first. A and F are excluded by the same numbers; a post-operative testosterone of <0.3 settles it retrospectively.

lecture: Deck Case - Sarah, 3y6m: Rapidly Progressive Precocity (Gallego After-Class Cases)
lectureMeta: Q155-Q157, the second case of the same deck (pp. 10-18). ⭐ **Keyed by the lecturer's own worked slides.** Q157's stem and its six options are verbatim; Q155 and Q156 are open prompts in the deck, so their options are written here and the key taken from the answer slide. ⭐ **Read this case against [[#152|Andrew]] - same presentation, opposite gonadotropins, opposite everything downstream.**

preamble.title: The case - Sarah, 3 years 6 months
preamble.html:
The case. Sarah, 3 years 6 months. Breast bud noticed since 18 months, with ⭐ rapid progression in the last 6 months · vaginal discharge for 6 months · pubic hair 6 months ago · always tall, but a recent growth spurt in the last 6 months. Family history: mother 157 cm, ⚠ menarche age 9-10 yrs; father 180 cm, normal puberty.

Physical. Height 118.6 cm, >97th · ⭐ height-age 6 y 10 m (CA 3.6 y) · mid-parental height on the 50th percentile · weight 24.5 kg, >97th · breasts Tanner III · pubic hair Tanner III · no clitoromegaly · leukorrhea and estrogenisation of the vaginal mucosa.

Results (deck p. 13): Random LH 0.32 IU/L (pre-pubertal <0.31) · FSH 5.3 IU/L (high) · Estradiol 70 pmol/L (ref <30) · TSH 1.34 mIU/L (0.45-4.8) · fT4 15 (11-18) · Prolactin 15 µg/L (<20) · Bone age 7.9 yrs (CA 3.6 yrs).

stem: Is Sarah in Puberty? If so, is it Central or peripheral?

options.html: Not puberty: an estradiol of 70 is too low to account for Tanner III breast development
Premature thelarche: isolated breast tissue, which regresses without any treatment
Peripheral: a random LH of 0.32 is pre-pubertal and cannot be driving this picture
Central: the LH is over the pre-pubertal cut-off, with a high FSH and estradiol

answer:
D. The deck's reading of its own panel: "Borderline LH of 0.32 · High estradiol level · Normal thyroid function and prolactin · Advanced bone maturation" → ⭐ "In puberty = likely GnRH dependent PP or CPP."

The block gives the threshold: ⭐ a random LH >0.3 mIU/L is consistent with the onset of central puberty. Hers is 0.32 against a stated pre-pubertal ceiling of 0.31 - ⚠ the thinnest margin the number can have, which is why the deck calls it borderline and goes on to a stimulation test in Q156.

⭐ The asymmetry of that threshold is the thing to hold onto. The block warns that an undetectable random LH has low sensitivity, because secretion is pulsatile - so ⭐ a LOW random LH proves very little, while a value over the cut-off, beside a high FSH and a high estradiol, points central. One direction of this test is informative and the other is not.

C reads 0.32 as low. It is over the line - and in peripheral precocity the gonadotropins are suppressed, not borderline, as Andrew's <0.3 and <1 were.

A misreads the reference: 70 against <30 is more than double, and the tissue has already responded - leukorrhea and an estrogenised mucosa are estrogen effect you can see. B is excluded by the block's own definition: premature thelarche is breast only, ⚠ with NO growth spurt and NO bone-age advance. She has a growth spurt, pubarche, and a bone age of 7.9 at 3.6.

Physical. Height 118.6 cm, >97th · ⭐ height-age 6 y 10 m (CA 3.6 y) · mid-parental height on the 50th percentile · weight 24.5 kg, >97th · breasts Tanner III · pubic hair Tanner III · no clitoromegaly · leukorrhea and estrogenisation of the vaginal mucosa.

Results (deck p. 13): Random LH 0.32 IU/L (pre-pubertal <0.31) · FSH 5.3 IU/L (high) · Estradiol 70 pmol/L (ref <30) · TSH 1.34 mIU/L (0.45-4.8) · fT4 15 (11-18) · Prolactin 15 µg/L (<20) · Bone age 7.9 yrs (CA 3.6 yrs).

stem: How to confirm Central PP?

options.html: A GnRH stimulation test, taking a peak LH above 5 mIU/L as confirmation
A repeat random LH drawn in the early morning, when secretion is highest
An MRI of the head, since a structural lesion is what defines central precocity
A pelvic ultrasound, to show a uterus that has responded to circulating estrogen

answer:
A. The deck runs the test and prints the table:

min0306090
LH0.3⭐ 15149
FSH3.571013

"Diagnosis: LH Peak > 5 mIU/L · Confirmed: GnRH dependent precocious puberty (CPP)." The block says the same: ⭐ "the GnRH stimulation test is the gold standard - an exaggerated LH response with a peak LH >5 confirms CPP." Hers peaks at 15.

⭐ The architecture is worth memorising once and reusing. To prove an axis is switched ON, stimulate it and show it over-responds. To prove one is switched OFF, stimulate it and show it barely moves. ⭐ The same test appears again in this deck on the 14-year-old Andrew, where the peak is 0.7 and the verdict is the exact opposite.

B repeats a test the block calls insensitive - a random LH screens, and its low values are uninformative because secretion comes in pulses. Repeating it earlier in the day does not change that.

C is the next step, not this one - and the deck takes it, finding a normal hypothalamic/pituitary MRI. ⭐ A normal MRI does not unmake central precocity, which is precisely why the confirmation comes before the imaging. D demonstrates an estrogen effect that her mucosa has already demonstrated.

stem: What is the most likely cause of Sarah's precocious puberty?
answer:
A. The deck's MRI slide: "Normal description of hypothalamic/pituitary regions; no evidence of tumor or any other [vascular] abnormalities" - and it goes straight on to management with an LHRH analogue.

The block gives the epidemiology that makes idiopathic the answer rather than a shrug: ⭐ in girls, central precocious puberty is mostly idiopathic; in boys, under 50% is - which is why the head MRI is mandatory in a boy and confirmatory in a girl.

F is what the MRI was done to exclude, and it came back clean. C, D and E are the whole peripheral column, and a stimulation test that confirmed GnRH-dependent precocity rules the column out in one move - peripheral steroid is made independently of GnRH. B is excluded by her growth spurt and her bone age.

⭐ "Idiopathic" is a positive finding here, not an absence of one. It is what is left after a borderline LH was pushed to a peak of 15 and a head MRI came back normal - and it is what makes the LHRH analogue the entire management. The deck's three aims for it are worth keeping: ⭐ suppress LH to pre-pubertal and arrest progression · drop growth velocity back to pre-pubertal · avoid further bone acceleration so final height is less compromised. ⚠ Untreated idiopathic CPP costs an average 5-6 cm of adult height.

lecture: Deck Case - Denise, 15.5y: Short Stature with Primary Amenorrhea (Gallego After-Class Cases)
lectureMeta: Q158-Q159, the third case of the same deck (pp. 19-23). ⭐ **Keyed by the lecturer's own worked slides.** Both prompts are open in the deck (*"INVESTIGATIONS?"*, then a stated diagnosis), so the options are written here and the keys taken from the answer slides.

preamble.title: The case - Denise, 15.5 years
preamble.html:
The case. Denise, 15.5 years, referred for assessment of short stature and amenorrhea. ⭐ Shortest girl in the class since grade 3 · breast bud started at age 13 yrs; not much progression · no menses · surgery for a cleft mitral valve at age 5 · history of multiple ear infections, myringotomy tubes. Mother 172 cm, menarche 14; father 176 cm.

Physical. Height 146 cm, <3rd · weight 50 kg, 25-50th · multiple pigmented nevi face and body · ⭐ cubitus valgus · ⭐ breast development Tanner II · pubic hair Tanner V.

stem: Investigations?

options.html: An MRI of the head, on the basis that absent puberty points at the hypothalamus
LH, FSH and estradiol, thyroid function, bone age, pelvic ultrasound, a karyotype
IGF-1 and two provocative growth hormone tests, since she is below the 3rd percentile
A GnRH stimulation test first, to establish whether the axis can be driven at all

answer:
B. The deck's list, in its own order: ⭐ CBC and ferritin · LH/FSH and estradiol · thyroid function · bone age · pelvic / abdomen US · karyotype.

⭐ The gonadotropins are the branch point for every hypogonadism - the block: high means the gonad failed, low means the brain did. Hers come back LH 59.4 and FSH 156.9, which sends you to the gonad.

⭐ And the karyotype is not optional here. The block says it flat: "karyotype every short girl" - which is the single line that makes this case, and the reason the deck closes it with "the only feature of Turner syndrome may be short stature."

A and D are both downstream of the gonadotropins. You image the head or stimulate the axis once you know which way the pair points, and hers point away from the brain. C is the growth-hormone workup, and the block reserves it for a child who is short with otherwise normal puberty and no other explanation. Hers is not isolated short stature - it comes with primary amenorrhea, a stalled thelarche and a dysmorphic feature.

stem: Results: LH 59.4 IU/L (high) · FSH 156.9 IU/L (high) · Estradiol <40 pmol/L · IGF-1 243 (237-996) · Bone age 15 yrs · Karyotype 45,XO · Pelvic US: small pre-pubertal uterus and small (? streak) ovaries, normal kidneys. What is the diagnosis?

options.html: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty, the commonest cause of delayed puberty
Growth hormone deficiency, her IGF-1 sitting at the bottom of the reference range
Secondary hypogonadism from a hypothalamic lesion, with a low estradiol to match
Turner syndrome - primary ovarian failure, with the karyotype and the phenotype

answer:
D. The deck states it: ⭐ "Diagnosis: Primary Ovarian Failure (Primary hypogonadism); Turner syndrome" - and then spends a whole slide on three lines worth memorising: ⭐ "The only feature of Turner syndrome may be short stature" · "Consider Turner syndrome in short slowly growing girls" · "Early diagnosis and referral important to optimize growth and final height."

The block's Turner column reads back through her almost item by item:

Block saysDenise
⭐ Short stature in 95-100% - the commonest feature146 cm, <3rd since grade 3
45,X in 60%karyotype 45,XO
Gonadal failure complete in 90% - "streak ovaries"small (? streak) ovaries, pre-pubertal uterus
Thelarche 10-15%, menarche only 1%breast bud at 13, stalled at Tanner II; no menses
⭐ Pubarche 100%, because the adrenal glands are normal⭐ pubic hair Tanner V
Cubitus valgus, short 4th metacarpals, webbed neckcubitus valgus

⭐ The split between Tanner V pubic hair and Tanner II breast is the most useful thing in the case. It looks self-contradictory until you know the two come from different glands: ⭐ pubarche is adrenal and her adrenals are normal; thelarche is ovarian and her ovaries are streaks. A girl fully developed for pubic hair and barely developed for breast is that dissociation made visible.

A requires low-normal gonadotropins and a delayed bone age. Hers are enormous and her bone age is 15 at 15.5. C inverts the level entirely - secondary hypogonadism has LOW LH and FSH; hers are the loudest possible evidence of a failed gonad. B misreads a number inside its range, and the block requires an inadequate response to two provocative tests, which was never done.

flags.title: What the deck records that the block does not
flags.html: Her cleft mitral valve repair and recurrent ear infections both belong to Turner's associated burden - the block says to screen a Turner girl lifelong for congenital heart disease, renal anomaly, autoimmune thyroid disease, celiac, T1DM and hearing loss. ⚠ The multiple pigmented nevi the deck records are not mentioned anywhere in the block, and are not reasoned from here.

preamble.title: The case - Andrew, 14 years
preamble.html:
The case. Andrew, 14 years, referred for assessment of delayed puberty. ⭐ Puberty - no changes noted · undescended testis noted at birth, orchidopexy at 18 months · ⭐ shortening of the metacarpals · no family history of delayed puberty - mother menarche 12, father completed growth by 16. Mother 160 cm, father 180 cm, ⭐ mid-parental target 176.5 cm (50th percentile).

Physical. Height 168 cm (50-75th) - ⭐ at his parental target · weight 62 kg, 85th · stretched penile length Tanner I (4 cm) · pubic hair Tanner I · ⭐ testicular volume 2-3 mL bilaterally.

Results (deck p. 29): LH <0.1 IU/L and FSH <0.1 IU/L · Testosterone <0.4 nmol/L · Karyotype 46,XY · ⭐ Bone age 14 yrs (CA 14 yrs) · normal CBC and ferritin · TSH 1.23, fT4 16 (11-18) · Prolactin 15 (<20).

stem: Andrew - unifying diagnosis?

options.html: Central hypogonadism: gonadotropins and testosterone low, with a bone age on time
Klinefelter syndrome, the commonest cause of testicular failure in boys by some way
Constitutional delay, the commonest cause of delayed puberty in boys, needing no more
Primary hypogonadism: the undescended testis and 2 mL volumes mean the gonad failed

answer:
A. The deck's own unifying slide: "Absent signs of puberty · Cryptorchidism and small penile length · Mild dysmorphic features: short metacarpals · Pre-pubertal LH, FSH, Testosterone · Bone age consistent with chronologic age" → ⭐ "Diagnosis: Central hypogonadism."

The block gives the rule in one line: ⭐ LOW LH and FSH with a low sex steroid is SECONDARY (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism - "the brain never sent the signal."

⭐ The bone age is what excludes the normal variant, and it is the single most useful number in the case. The block says CDGP is diagnosed on a DELAYED bone age - "the test that makes the diagnosis". His is ⭐ 14 at 14. A boy whose skeleton is exactly on time but whose puberty has not started is not running late; ⚠ he is not starting. His height sitting at his mid-parental target says the same thing from the other direction - CDGP tracks at or below the 3rd percentile, and he is 50-75th.

C is the commonest cause of delayed puberty in boys, which is exactly what makes it the dangerous answer - ⚠ it is the diagnosis of a normal variant, and treating this boy as a normal variant means never replacing his testosterone.

B and D both require HIGH gonadotropins. A failed gonad removes the feedback and the pituitary shouts; his are <0.1, which is the opposite of shouting. B is further excluded by a 46,XY karyotype - the block puts Klinefelter at 47,XXY in 80%.

stem: GnRH test - LH 0 / 30 / 60 / 90 min: <0.1 → 0.7 → 0.4 → 0.4. FSH over the same points: 0.3 → 3.0 → 3.1 → 3.2. How do you read it?

options.html: Constitutional delay: the gonadotropins did rise, so the axis is intact and merely late
Primary gonadal failure, the flat LH reflecting a gonad that cannot make testosterone
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: the pituitary barely responds, LH peaking at 0.7
A normal pubertal response, the FSH having risen tenfold from its baseline value

answer:
C. The deck labels the table exactly that: ⭐ "Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism."

⭐ The number to read it against is Sarah's, five slides earlier. Her peak LH was 15 against a threshold of 5. ⭐ His is 0.7. Same test, same units, opposite verdict - and that symmetry is why the deck runs it on both patients.

Stimulated peak LHReading
Sarah, 3.6 y15⭐ axis switched ON early - CPP confirmed
Andrew, 14 y⚠ 0.7⭐ axis will not switch ON at all

A misreads a move from <0.1 to 0.7 as a response. In CDGP the axis is intact and merely late, so a stimulated pituitary responds when asked. ⚠ A pituitary that cannot get its LH past 1 on direct stimulation is not late.

D is true about the FSH - 0.3 to 3.2 is a real rise - but ⭐ LH is the informative gonadotropin for pubertal onset, which the block states outright: "LH is more useful than FSH for assessing the onset of puberty." A normal pubertal response is an LH-dominant one.

B inverts the level, for the same reason it did in Q160: a failed gonad leaves the pituitary unrestrained, so LH and FSH would already be high before any stimulation was given.

stem: Further information: he reports "no sense of smell". MRI: "underdevelopment of olfactory bulbs". What is the diagnosis?

options.html: A craniopharyngioma compressing the pituitary stalk, found on the same MRI scan
Prader-Willi syndrome, in which hypogonadism accompanies hyperphagia and obesity
Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome, a congenital cause of the hypogonadotropic picture
Kallmann syndrome - hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia and absent bulbs

answer:
D. The deck: "He reports 'no sense of smell' · MRI: 'Underdevelopment of olfactory bulbs'" → ⭐ "Diagnosis: Kallmann Syndrome." The block carries it in six words: ⭐ Kallmann = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism + anosmia.

⭐ The point of the case is that nobody asked about the smell until the end. It is one line of history, it costs nothing, and it converts an unexplained hypogonadotropic hypogonadism into a named diagnosis with a known inheritance and a known set of associations. ⭐ That is why "anosmia" sits in the history skeleton of both Week 3 puberty notes - it is only ever found if it is asked for.

B is the block's Prader-Willi: failure to thrive in infancy, then ⚠ hyperphagia and severe obesity in early childhood, with a chromosome 15 microdeletion. His weight is 85th and nothing else fits. C is on the block's list of congenital causes of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, but it is defined by retinal dystrophy, polydactyly and obesity, none of which is described. A would be an acquired cause, and the MRI found no mass - his other pituitary axes (TSH, fT4, prolactin) are all normal too.

flags.title: The deck's Kallmann associations are broader than the block's
flags.html: Its final slide lists cleft palate and lip · kidney malformations · metacarpal malformations and pes cavus · sensorineural deafness · cerebellar ataxia and epilepsy · colour blindness, nystagmus · mirror motions. ⚠ The block names only the anosmia. So his shortened metacarpals - flagged on the deck's own unifying slide - are the deck's association, not the block's: the block links short metacarpals to pseudohypoparathyroidism ("knuckle-knuckle-dimple-dimple", Archibald's sign) and to Turner, and does not list them under Kallmann.

lecture: Deck Case - Baby Tyler, 3 weeks: Salt-Losing Crisis (Stein DSD Review Session)
lectureMeta: Q191-196, the worked case running through `stein_dsd_review_afterclass_` (Dr. Robert Stein, Pediatric Endocrinology), slides 5-16. ⭐ **Stems verbatim - the deck poses all six as its own questions.** ⭐ **Keyed from the deck's own answer slides**, which follow each question directly. preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The case. ⭐ Baby Tyler is 3 weeks old, assigned male at birth. Vomiting intermittently for 7 days, ⭐ loose frequent stools 6-8 per day, poor feeding, irritable, and ⚠ failing to gain weight. History - birth weight 3.7 kg, birth length 55 cm, normal pregnancy, labour and delivery; no other pregnancies; ⭐ parents unrelated and non-consanguineous. Examination - dehydrated, cold, ⭐ hyperpigmented, ⭐ NORMAL appearance of the male genitalia, ⚠ HR 150, BP 50.

stem: You see Tyler in the emergency Department. Before doing any investigations, is there anything else that you want to know about him on history or physical examination?

options.html: A detailed feeding and formula-preparation history, with an abdominal examination
A developmental and immunisation history, with a full neurological examination
A maternal medication history alone, since drugs are the commonest cause here
Birth and family history, plus genitalia, hydration and pigmentation on exam

answer:
D. ⭐ The deck answers its own question on the two slides that follow it, and both are in the note's workup skeleton already:

The deck asks forIt reports
birth measurements3.7 kg, 55 cm - ⭐ normally grown, so this is acute, not antenatal
pregnancy, labour, deliverynormal
other pregnancies⭐ none - ⚠ so there is no earlier neonatal death to have raised the alarm
⭐ consanguinityparents unrelated - ⚠ asked because CAH is autosomal recessive, and a negative answer does not exclude it
hydration and perfusiondehydrated, cold, HR 150, BP 50
⭐ hyperpigmentation⭐ present - this is the ACTH excess, visible on the skin
⭐ the genitalia⭐ NORMAL male appearance

⭐ Two of those findings are the whole case. ⚠ Hyperpigmentation in a collapsing neonate is ACTH excess, and ⭐ normal-looking genitalia is not reassurance - it is the expected finding in a 46,XY infant with CAH. The note puts it as the block's highest-yield point: ⭐ "the 46,XX infant looks ambiguous and is caught at birth; the 46,XY infant looks normal and presents in crisis a fortnight later."

⚠ The note's PEx line would also have you palpate for gonads - "a palpable gonad is almost always a testis" - which is how the same examination serves an ambiguous-genitalia presentation.

A and B are the reasonable general-paediatric work-ups for vomiting and failure to thrive, and ⚠ both would miss this, because neither looks at the skin or the genitalia. C asks a question the note does list - maternal medications and maternal virilisation - but ⭐ as one line of a history, not instead of one, and transplacental androgen is not the commonest cause.

stem: What investigations will help determine the cause of his symptoms?

options.html: Electrolytes, glucose and cortisol, then 17-hydroxyprogesterone and a karyotype

An abdominal ultrasound and contrast study to exclude malrotation with volvulus
A sweat chloride test and stool studies, given the diarrhoea and failure to thrive

answer:
A. ⭐ The deck's next slide is exactly this list, and it matches the note's Ix line:

TestWhat it is for
⭐ sodium, potassium⭐ Na↓ and K↑ are the mineralocorticoid failure
⭐ glucosehypoglycaemia in a salt-losing crisis
⭐ cortisolthe glucocorticoid failure
⭐ 17-hydroxyprogesterone⭐ the diagnostic marker - markedly raised in 21-OHD
karyotype and pelvic ultrasound⭐ the note asks for these in every case

⭐ The order is not arbitrary. The electrolytes and glucose are the ones that change what you do in the next ten minutes; the 17-OHP and the karyotype name the disease but will not come back in time to treat him.

⚠ A septic workup is not a wrong instinct - a 3-week-old who is vomiting, irritable and shocked gets cultures, and B would often be started in parallel. ⭐ It is wrong as the answer to "what will determine the cause", because it would not find this one. ⭐ Na 110, ⭐ K 8.4⭐ ALDOSTERONE deficiency - sodium not retained, potassium not excreted
⭐ Cortisol 40 (119-618)⭐ CORTISOL deficiency - ⚠ and this is a shocked child, in whom it should be at the top of the range, not below it
Glucose 2.5hypoglycaemia - the consequence of the cortisol deficiency

⭐ Losing both at once is what localises the lesion. The adrenal note makes this the discriminator between primary and secondary disease: ⭐ "Primary insufficiency loses aldosterone as well as cortisol - so K⁺ is high, ACTH is high, and fludrocortisone is required; secondary spares all three." ⚠ A potassium of 8.4 is therefore not an incidental abnormality - it is the finding that says the problem is at the adrenal.

⭐ It also fits the hyperpigmentation, which is ACTH driven, and which secondary insufficiency does not produce.

A and B each take half the panel. D is the one worth taking seriously, because ⚠ he genuinely has been vomiting and stooling for a week - but ⭐ GI losses do not drive potassium UP, and they do not suppress cortisol in a shocked infant. The direction of the potassium is what rules it out.

History - birth weight 3.7 kg, birth length 55 cm, normal pregnancy, labour and delivery; no other pregnancies; ⭐ parents unrelated and non-consanguineous. stem: What is your diagnosis? Be as specific as possible Testosterone 10.5 nmol/l (<0.03) · 17OHP 1365 nmol/l (<7.8)

options.html: Simple virilising congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia presenting in the neonatal period
Primary autoimmune adrenal insufficiency presenting in the neonatal period
Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency

answer:
D. ⭐ "As specific as possible" is the whole instruction - and the diagnosis has three parts, each earned by a different result:

PartEarned by
⭐ CAH⭐ 17-OHP 1365 against a normal <7.8 - over 170x, with testosterone 10.5 where it should be undetectable
⭐ 21-hydroxylase deficiency⭐ the 17-OHP is the substrate immediately above the block, and the note puts 21-OHD at ≈95% of CAH
⭐ SALT-WASTING form⭐ Na 110, K 8.4, and a crisis at 3 weeks

⭐ The mechanism runs in one chain, as the note has it: cortisol blocked → ACTH excess → adrenal hyperplasia → blocked precursors shunted into androgen → virilisation, with ⭐ aldosterone lost as well because the same enzyme sits on the mineralocorticoid limb.

⚠ His testosterone of 10.5 is an adult male level in a 3-week-old, and it has produced no visible sign, because there is nothing left to virilise in a 46,XY infant.

A is the same enzyme with 1-5% residual activity - ⚠ cortisol deficiency and androgen excess WITHOUT significant salt loss, which a sodium of 110 excludes. B is the mild end, which the note says presents as ⭐ premature pubarche and later hirsutism and oligomenorrhoea, not as neonatal collapse. C would give low cortisol and high potassium, but ⚠ not a 17-OHP of 1365 - and the note lists autoimmune disease as 80-90% of primary insufficiency in the West while naming CAH separately as its own cause.

stem: How would you manage this acute presentation of CAH?

options.html: Potassium-containing maintenance fluid with oral hydrocortisone started next day
Dextrose-saline without potassium, intravenous hydrocortisone, and fludrocortisone
Insulin and dextrose to lower the potassium, deferring steroids until results return
Normal saline alone, with steroid replacement withheld until the karyotype returns

answer:
B. ⭐ The deck's answer slide gives the crisis protocol in three parts, and each doses against a problem already on the panel:

ComponentThe deck's numbersAgainst
⭐ Fluid⭐ 5% dextrose / normal saline (D5/NS), NO potassium, resuscitate at 20 ml/kg, continue at 1.5-2x maintenance⚠ Na 110 and Glu 2.5 in one bag; the potassium is omitted because his is 8.4
⭐ hydrocortisone IV⭐ bolus 2 mg/kg, then an infusion of 100 mg/m²/daythe cortisol of 40
⭐ fludrocortisone0.1-0.3 mg/daythe aldosterone deficiency

⭐ Leaving the potassium out of the fluid is the detail most easily lost, and it is the one that would do immediate harm: ⚠ adding potassium to a child at 8.4 is the opposite of the treatment.

⭐ Hydrocortisone is the glucocorticoid of choice here rather than dexamethasone, and the adrenal note's potency table is why: ⭐ hydrocortisone carries mineralocorticoid activity, dexamethasone carries none.

⭐ The adrenal note's crisis line is the same instinct in one phrase - "Crisis: saline + hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, do not await results."

A gets the potassium exactly wrong and defers steroid in a shocked child. C treats the hyperkalaemia as the diagnosis: ⚠ it is real and it is dangerous, but the potassium falls when the missing hormones are replaced, and deferring steroid is what kills. D misses the dextrose in a hypoglycaemic infant, omits both hormones, and ⭐ waits on a test that will take days and change nothing about tonight.

stem: What would be the presentation of a female patient (46XX) with the same diagnosis?

options.html: Normal female genitalia, with the diagnosis made only at puberty on investigation
Undervirilised genitalia with palpable gonads in the inguinal canals on examination
Virilised genitalia, clitoral enlargement, fused folds and one urogenital opening
Normal female genitalia and an identical salt-losing crisis at one to three weeks

answer:
C. ⭐ The deck answers with a second baby, A.H., and the findings are the answer:

Baby A.H.
⭐ 3 cm phallusthe clitoral hypertrophy
⭐ hyperpigmented, FUSED, rugated labio-scrotal folds⚠ the fusion is the virilisation
⭐ single uro-genital sinus at the base of the phallusthe note's "single urogenital opening", its most severe form
⭐ NO gonads palpable⭐ consistent with 46,XX - there are ovaries, and they are intra-abdominal

⭐ This is the asymmetry the block calls its highest-yield point, and it is the reason the deck asks the question at all: ⭐ "The 46,XX CAH infant looks ambiguous and is caught at birth; the 46,XY CAH infant looks normal and presents in salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks." ⚠ Same enzyme, same severity, same salt loss - the only difference is whether anyone noticed before the crisis.

⭐ The note's own examination language applies here: describe and diagram the gonads, phallus and labio-scrotal folds in neutral terms, ⚠ delay assignment of the sex of rearing, do not assign a name, and do not register the birth until the investigations are complete.

A and D both keep the genitalia normal, which is the 46,XY picture. ⚠ D is the sharpest distractor, because the salt-losing crisis half of it is true - the girl is at the same risk - ⭐ but she does not look normal at birth, which is exactly what buys her the earlier diagnosis. B is undervirilisation with palpable gonads, which is the 46,XY differential - 5α-reductase deficiency or androgen insensitivity - and ⭐ a palpable gonad is almost always a testis.

stem: What are the long-term considerations in gthe management of a patient with CAH?

options.html: Glucocorticoid for the first two years only, then weaning once growth is complete
Mineralocorticoid alone lifelong, since cortisol recovers once hyperplasia resolves
No ongoing treatment once the acute crisis resolves, with annual electrolytes only
Lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid with stress dosing and surveillance

answer:
D. ⭐ The note's long-term management callout is Stein's own earlier slide, and it answers this directly:

ComponentDose
⭐ hydrocortisone⭐ 10-15 mg/m²/day divided bid or tid - set against a normal cortisol secretion rate of 12.5 ± 3 mg/m²/day; prednisone or dexamethasone in older adolescents
⭐ fludrocortisone (Florinef)⭐ 0.05-0.20 mg daily, with ⭐ additional oral saline in infants
⚠ Stress dosing⭐ increase the glucocorticoid during illness or stress, to prevent a salt-losing crisis
Plusgenital surgery where indicated, education, and surveillance

⭐ Stress dosing is the part that has to be taught to the family rather than prescribed, and it is what the education is for: ⚠ the child's next crisis will begin at home, during an ordinary childhood illness.

⭐ The dose is deliberately physiological, not pharmacological. It is pegged to what the adrenal would have made - which is why ⚠ it is replacement for life rather than a course that finishes.

A and C both treat the crisis as the illness. ⚠ The enzyme defect does not resolve, and stopping replacement returns the child to the state they presented in. B keeps the half that fixes the sodium and drops the half that prevents hypoglycaemia and ⭐ allows the ACTH drive - and so the androgen excess - to continue unopposed.

stem: What factors would you need to consider when discussing gender assignment in a baby with a DSD?

options.html: The karyotype alone, which determines the assignment in every case of this kind
Diagnosis, genital appearance, fertility, replacement needs and family views
The appearance of the external genitalia alone, assessed by the surgical team only
The parents' stated preference alone, recorded before investigations are complete

answer:
B. ⭐ This is the one closing question the deck does answer, and its list is reproduced in the note verbatim:

Factor
⭐ underlying diagnosis⚠ which is why the karyotype and the 17-OHP come first
genital appearance and surgical options⭐ and the note is explicit that assignment does NOT inevitably mean surgery
need for lifelong replacement therapy
⭐ potential for fertility
⭐ views of the family, and sometimes circumstances relating to cultural practices

⭐ The deck opens the slide with the thing that is not a factor but governs the conversation: ⚠ "Initial gender uncertainty is extremely unsettling and stressful for families." ⭐ And it closes by making the team non-optional - "involvement of a multidisciplinary team including psychology / social work essential."

⭐ The expected outcome is part of the discussion, and the block carries the numbers: 90% of CAH girls raised female identify as female, against ⚠ 60% of 5α-reductase deficiency patients raised female who identify as MALE - which is exactly why the underlying diagnosis heads the list.

⚠ The note's procedural instructions run alongside all of this: delay assignment of the sex of rearing, do not assign a name, do not register the birth, use neutral terms throughout, and warn the family that a final diagnosis may take several weeks.

A, C and D are each one real factor promoted to be the only one. ⭐ D is the most tempting, because the family's views are genuinely on the list - ⚠ but "before investigations are complete" is the error, and it is the one the note guards against most explicitly.

stem: Akio has a 2 cm palpable enlarging thyroid nodule. He has a family history of thyroid cancer in his father. Your next steps will be:
answer: The correct answer is C. This nodule needs investigation given enlargement and family history of cancer. Remember to choose the least invasive and most cost-effective test first for a mass. Ultrasound is an important first step for a thyroid nodule to determine risk of malignancy and need for nodule sampling. A CT scan would not be indicated as a first line test here, since thyroid nodule sampling cannot be performed with the CT scan and it is an expensive test. Needle core biopsy (NCB) is not used to sample neck nodules in general, and especially thyroid nodules. The needle is large bore, and there is a risk of tumour seeding and hematoma. One exception is for lymphoma in a neck lymph node, where NCB is first line sampling in some patients.

weekLabel: Week 2 - Thyroid, Parathyroid, Bone & Reproductive Physiology

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (5 questions).
stem: The imaging report indicates a TIRADs score of 4. What type of nodule sampling would you choose for Akio?
answer: The correct answer is C. For thyroid, which is a vascular organ, FNAB is the preferred biopsy type for sampling a nodule. As well, given the risk of tumour seeding and hematoma formation the large bore needles (needle core biopsy) would be avoided if possible. Incisional biopsies are not performed for thyroid, due to the vascularity of the organ, such that surgery would either be a lobectomy or thyroidectomy. Punch biopsy is used only for skin related lesions, not for deep lesions under the skin. FNAB needs to be performed first for risk stratification before any decision about surgery usually.

stem: Kiaria has a 2.7 cm mildly symptomatic thyroid nodule, normal TSH. The ultrasound report indicates a mixed cyst and TIRADs score 2. You remove clear fluid with a fine needle aspiration biopsy and the cyst disappears. On follow-up the cyst does not reappear. The most likely diagnosis is:
answer: The correct answer is B. With disappearance of the cyst with aspiration, a not suspicious TIRADs score and no reappearance of the cyst, this is in keeping with a benign cyst. An abscess is unusual in the thyroid, and the aspirate should reveal pus. The clinical features do not indicate the classic signs of inflammation. Papillary carcinoma can be cystic, but would show increase in size on follow-up and some solid component. An adenoma, which can be cystic would not disappear with aspiration in that there would be a solid component left. Lymphoma is typically firm solid tissue, and not a cyst.

stem: Pure gonadal dysgenesis, characterized by a 46, XX karyotype, normal external genitalia, and bilateral streak gonads, results if primordial germ cells fail to invade the gonadal ridges. These germ cells migrate from which of the following locations?
answer: The correct answer is E. During the 4th to 6th weeks primordial germ cells migrate from the neck of the yolk sac along the hindgut mesentery to the mesoderm of the posterior body wall and onto the gonadal ridges. If there is no migration of the germ cells, functional gonads are unable to develop.

stem: Sex determination occurs initially via which of the following.
answer: The correct answer is D. The SRY gene is the initial factor for sex-determining factor. If the SRY gene is present it will initiate the male development pathway by producing TDF. If SRY gene is not present, and TDF is not produced the default female development pathway will occur.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (11 questions), plus Q212 written from the lecture deck's What Caused These Anomalies? slide, which names hematometrocolpos but poses no question of its own.
stem: Hematometrocolpos is a collection of blood and fluid within the uterus and/or vagina. Which of the following developmental occurrences would result in this condition?

options.html: Failure of canalization of the vaginal plate
Failure of one paramesonephric duct to develop
Failure of complete fusion of the paramesonephric ducts
Failure of degeneration of the uterine septum

answer:
The correct answer is A. The lower two thirds of the vagina forms when the sinovaginal bulbs fuse into a vaginal plate and that plate canalizes. If it never canalizes the vagina is blocked, which is vaginal atresia, and menstrual blood cannot get out. It collects behind the obstruction and distends the vagina and then the uterus, which is hematometrocolpos. Two blockages do it: a transverse vaginal septum at the junction of the upper third and lower two thirds, and an imperforate hymen at the caudal end.

B, C and D are the paramesonephric duct anomalies: unicornuate, bicornuate and septate. None of them obstructs outflow, so none of them dams blood.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (21 questions).
stem:
Match the correct function to the labelled structures. Each function below pairs with one label A–G on the diagram.

Function
1. Hormone producer
2. Childbirth passage
3. Carries ovarian vessels
4. Home to developing fetus
5. Common site of fertilization
6. Anchors ovary to uterus
7. Site of Pap smears
answer:
The correct answer is C. The full set of pairings:

FunctionLabelStructure
Hormone ProducerEOvary
Childbirth PassageCVagina
Carries Ovarian VesselsGSuspensory ligament of the ovary
Home to Developing FetusABody of the uterus
Common Site of FertilizationDAmpulla of the uterine tube
Anchors Ovary to UterusFLigament of the ovary
Site of Pap SmearsBCervix

The reasoning below is mine — the module keyed the letters and gave none.

  • F and G are the pair worth separating. The ligament of the ovary (F) runs medially from the ovary to the uterus and is a gubernaculum remnant carrying nothing. The suspensory ligament (G) runs laterally over the pelvic brim and is the one holding the ovarian artery, vein and nerves — which is why it is the pedicle clamped in an oophorectomy, and why the ureter running beneath it is what gets injured.
  • D is the uterine tube, and fertilization happens in its ampulla, the widest part; the fimbriae at its lateral end only sweep the oocyte in. A tubal ectopic implants here for the same reason.
  • B is the cervix because a Pap samples the transformation zone, where columnar endocervical epithelium meets squamous ectocervical epithelium. That junction is where HPV transforms cells — not the uterine body (A), and not the vagina (C).

stem: There are many myths surrounding PMOS and your patients will look to you to dispel these. Which of the following statements about PMOS are TRUE? Click all that apply.

options.html: Women with PMOS are more prone to subfertility and early miscarriage.
Women with PMOS cannot lose weight.
Women with PMOS are more likely to have “metabolic syndrome” correlates: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, elevated lipids.
Women with PMOS have an increased appetite and are constantly hungry.
Eating organic or vegan will help as it is additives in food that cause PMOS.
Women with PMOS are more prone to developing endometrial cancer.
Women with PMOS are at a higher risk of developing mood disorders.

answer:
The correct answers are A, C, F and H. The module keys each statement individually, and the four it marks correct are the four real clinical risks: subfertility and early miscarriage, the metabolic syndrome correlates, endometrial cancer, and mood disorders.

⭐ The four false statements are all patient-blaming in structure — she cannot lose weight, she is always hungry, she eats the wrong food, she cannot conceive. The four true ones are all real clinical risks. That is the discrimination the exercise is training, and it is why the module pairs it with “no body shaming”.

⚠ B and G are the two to counsel against explicitly. She can lose weight, and she can conceive spontaneously — which is why contraception still has to be discussed in the same breath as the subfertility diagnosis.

stem: The prescription of ergocalciferol should be avoided or prescribed with caution in which of the following patient/s (could be multiple correct answers)?

options.html: A patient with hyperparathyroidism due to renal insufficiency

answer: The correct answer is A, B, D. Furosemide promotes calcium excretion, thus it is helpful in preventing hypercalcemia when taking vitamin D. Ergocalciferol requires both hepatic and renal metabolism to become the active calcitriol. A patient with renal insufficiency can convert ergocalciferol into calcifediol (hepatic), but can’t effectively convert calcifediol into calcitriol (renal). Thiazide increases calcium reabsorption, thus it should be taken with caution in conjunction with vitamin D to prevent hypercalcemia. Vitamin D increases both calcium and phosphate absorption, thus can worsen hypophosphatemia.

stem: What would be a consequence of malfunctioning chief cells in the parathyroid gland

options.html: Decreased levels of parathyroid hormones despite normal or low calcium levels.
Desensitization of parathyroid hormone receptors in the intestines.
Increased calcium absorption in the intestines despite normal or low calcium levels
Increased calcium reabsorption in the kidneys despite normal or high calcium levels.

answer: The correct answer is D. The chief cells are responsible for responding to high levels of calcium by shutting down parathyroid hormone release. If the chief cells malfunction, they will fail to detect hypercalcemia and the parathyroid hormone levels will remain high, which induces the kidneys to reabsorb even more calcium.

stem: A patient presents with decreased heart rate, cold intolerance, and weight gain despite decreased appetite. Their lab results demonstrate high TSH and low FT4. You inquire the patient about past thyroid diseases and thyroid treatments (radiation, surgery), which are negative. You also screened the patient for risk of pituitary disease, which is also negative. What is your next appropriate step?

options.html: Order anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibody levels
Order a radioactive iodine uptake test
Make the diagnosis of Hashimoto’s disease

answer: The correct answer is D. If you have excluded past thyroid disease and treatment and pituitary disease as causes of hypothyroidism, you can assume the diagnosis of Hashimoto’s disease based on the elevated FSH and low FT4 level. You do not need to order FT3 for assessing hypothyroidism. Radioactive iodine uptake test is ordered to assess causes for low TSH levels. Anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibodies are sensitive for Hashimoto’s disease, but they almost never influence clinical decisions in hypothyroidism, so they don’t need to be ordered.

Using radioactive iodine to treat a patient with thyroid adenoma
Using radioactive iodine to treat a patient with toxic multinodular goiter

answer: The correct answer is D. A large symptomatic goiter should be treated with surgery. stem: Your patient with osteoporosis and a previous hip fracture has been treated with romosozumab for 6 months. Their bone mineral density has been stable and they experienced no fracture events so far. How would you continue the management?

options.html: Romosozumab seem to be working well for the patient, so you will keep them on romosozumab until their osteoporosis progress or they experience a fracture
Follow up with zoledronic acid after 1 year of romosozumab therapy.
Follow up with raloxifene after 1 year of romosozumab therapy.

answer: The correct answer is C. Romosozumab, a bone formation therapy, should be followed with anti-resorptive therapy after 1 year. Both zoledronic acid and raloxifene are anti-resorptive therapies, but raloxifene is not effective for hip fractures.

stem: WHich of the following is true regarding bone diseases?

options.html: Paget’s disease involves a defect in bone mineralization while osteomalacia involve a defect in bone remodeling
Cotton wool appearance is a clinical presentation of osteogenesis imperfecta
Teriparatide can be used to treat Paget’s disease.
Hearing loss can be a clinical presentation for both Paget’s disease and osteogenesis imperfecta.

answer: The correct answer is D. Skull abnormalities in Paget’s disease and osteogenesis imperfecta can lead to compression and damage of cranial nerves, resulting in hearing loss. Osteomalacia involves a defect in bone mineralization while Paget’s disease involves a defect in bone remodeling. Cotton wool appearance is seen in Paget’s disease, representing increased and abnormal bone remodeling. Bone formation therapies, such as teriparatide, should be avoided in Paget’s disease since there is already increased bone formation.

stem: If a teratogen is introduced during week 6 of embryogenesis, which of the following will be the most likely effect on the developing embryo.

options.html: The teratogen either kills the embryo or has no effect on it
The teratogen could induce major congenital heart abnormalities
The teratogen could induce minor morphological abnormalities
The teratogen could induce minor functional abnormalities.

answer: The correct answer is B. Week 3-8 is the most critical period for cell differentiation, organogenesis, and morphogenesis, thus a teratogen exposure at week 6 can potentially introduce a major congenital abnormality. Teratogens have an all or nothing effect during the first 2 weeks of development. Teratogens introduced during the fetal period (week 9 onwards) could potentially introduce minor morphological and functional abnormalities.

stem: For a 25 year old female who has a regular menstrual cycle, which of the following is correct

options.html: We can’t be certain of the duration of her luteal phase since it varies across women, but her follicular phase is likely 14 days.
Her FSH levels are the lowest after she ovulates.
Her estrogen levels will continuously decrease following ovulation
There is one developing follicle in her ovaries during each menstrual cycle

answer: The correct answer is B. FSH levels are at the lowest after ovulation due to negative feedback from estrogen and progesterone. The length of the follicular phase varies across women, but the luteal phase is usually consistently 14 days. The estrogen level has another surge in the luteal phase. There are multiple follicular waves in development during each cycle.

stem: Which of the following is correct regarding oocyte development

options.html: The oocyte undergoes both mitosis and meiosis in a women of reproductive age
There is an even division of DNA and cellular content upon completion of meiosis I
Following ovulation, the oocyte rests in metaphase of meiosis I and transits through the fallopian tube, awaiting fertilization.
Nondisjunction in oocytes can occur upon fertilization with a sperm.

answer: The correct answer is D. Upon fertilization, the oocyte undergoes completion of meiosis II, where nondisjunction can occur. Oocytes only undergo mitosis during gestation, women are born with a set number of oocytes. There is an even division of DNA with meiosis I, but the first polar body contains very little oocyte cytoplasm. Following ovulation, the oocyte rests in metaphase of meiosis II.

stem: When examining a 14 year old boy, which of the following findings would make you most concerned about abnormal growth?

options.html: His height is >2 SD below the average for his age and sex
An X ray of wrists shows delayed bone age despite his short stature
His puberty has been delayed despite his short stature
He is currently significantly below his genetic potential

answer: The correct answer is D. While having a height >2 SD below the average could be an indicator for abnormal growth, having short stature alone is not enough to indicate abnormal growth; he could just be on the shorter end of normal. Delayed bone age and delayed puberty indicate normal growth variants in individuals with shorter stature.
